8.5 AWS Compute Decision Flow — What to Use When

The most common question: "Which compute service should I use?" This decision tree answers it:

❓ START: Do you want to manage servers?
▼ YES
▼ NO
Need full OS control or specific hardware?
▼ YES
▼ NO
✅ EC2 — Full control, any OS, any software
✅ EKS — Kubernetes (or ECS for simpler)
Running containers or just code?
▼ Containers
▼ Just Code
✅ Fargate — Serverless containers (ECS/EKS)
✅ Lambda — Event-driven, pay-per-use
ServiceControlScalingPricingBest For
EC2Full OSASG (manual rules)Per second (instance)Legacy apps, custom OS config
ECSContainer-levelService Auto ScalingEC2 or Fargate pricingAWS-only, simpler than K8s
EKSKubernetes APIHPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler$0.10/hr + worker nodesMicroservices, multi-cloud, K8s ecosystem
LambdaNone (code only)Automatic (per-invocation)Per ms + requestsEvent-driven, sporadic workloads
FargateContainer spec onlyService Auto ScalingPer task per secondContainers without managing servers
💡 THE DEVOPS RULE FOR COMPUTE

Start serverless, go to containers when needed, fall back to EC2 only when you must. Lambda/Fargate → less ops. ECS/EKS → orchestration. EC2 → maximum control, maximum responsibility. The exam answer is almost always the one requiring LESS operational overhead.

🔑 Compute is NOT about "which is better"

Every AWS compute service solves a DIFFERENT problem. The exam tests matching workload to service. Lambda at 14 minutes = WRONG (15-min limit). EC2 running 100ms/day = WRONG (paying for idle). Right-size your compute.

🧠 DEEP DIVE: Walking the Decision Tree for anihpj

Let's apply the decision tree to our anihpj Django application step by step:

1
Does anihpj need managed servers?

anihpj runs Django + PostgreSQL — it needs an OS, Python runtime, and persistent processes (not just short-lived functions). Decision: YES, we need some form of managed infrastructure. Lambda could handle individual API endpoints, but the full Django app with ORM, migrations, admin panel, and WebSocket support needs containers or VMs.

2
Do we need Kubernetes? Or simpler?

anihpj has multiple components: Django web, Celery workers, Redis cache, PostgreSQL. These need orchestration — health checks, rolling updates, service discovery. Decision: YES, Kubernetes is justified. ECS could work too, but EKS gives us Helm charts, Istio for traffic management, and the full K8s ecosystem for future expansion.

3
EC2 or Fargate for worker nodes?

anihpj needs GPU for resume parsing? No. Needs specific AMI customizations? Possibly (Image Builder for Golden AMI). But for simplicity: Start with Fargate for dev/staging, use EC2 for production (cost savings at scale, more control over node configuration).

4
Final Decision: EKS on EC2 + Fargate profile

Production: EKS with EC2 managed node group (t3.medium, 3-6 nodes). Dev: Fargate profile for cost savings (pay only when developing). Burst workloads: Lambda@Edge for CloudFront-triggered resume preview generation. This multi-compute strategy gives us the right tool for each job.

💰
EC2 Pricing

t3.medium: ~$30/month (1yr RI). Per-second billing. You pay even when idle. Best for: steady workloads with predictable capacity. Use Savings Plans for 30%+ discount.

📦
Fargate Pricing

0.25 vCPU + 0.5GB: ~$15/month per task. Per-second billing for actual usage. Best for: variable workloads, dev environments, batch jobs. ~1.5× EC2 cost but zero node management.

⚡
Lambda Pricing

1M requests: $0.20 + compute time ($0.0000166667 per GB-second). Best for: sporadic/event-driven workloads. At 100K requests/day, Lambda is cheaper than running EC2 24/7. At sustained high volume, EC2 wins.

🏢 REAL-WORLD COMPUTE — Who Runs What on AWS

🛒 Amazon.com — EC2 + ASG

Millions of EC2 instances

Stack: EC2 (custom Nitro instances) → Auto Scaling Groups → Elastic Load Balancing

Why: Full control over hardware for bare-metal performance. ASG scales automatically during Prime Day. Custom kernel optimizations impossible on serverless.

🏦 Coinbase — EKS

100% on Kubernetes

Stack: EKS → Helm charts → HPA + Cluster Autoscaler → Istio service mesh

Why: Crypto markets are 24/7 global. Zero-downtime rolling updates. HPA auto-scales during volatility. K8s ecosystem (Helm, Istio, Argo) essential for compliance.

📺 Disney+ — Lambda

100M+ subscribers

Stack: Lambda (video encoding) → S3 (media storage) → CloudFront (global delivery)

Why: Launch-day spikes (Hamilton premiere) handled without provisioning. Pay only for actual encoding time. Serverless = zero capacity planning for unpredictable streaming demand.

🚕 Lyft — ECS + Fargate

1000s of microservices

Stack: ECS Fargate → Service Auto Scaling → ALB → DynamoDB (ride tracking)

Why: Serverless containers = no node management. ECS is AWS-native (no K8s learning curve). Sub-second dispatch requires consistent latency — Fargate delivers.

8.6 Deploying anihpj on EC2 — The Traditional Way

Before Kubernetes, DevOps engineers deployed apps directly on EC2. Here's how you'd deploy the anihpj Django app on EC2 using a bootstrap script:

EC2 User Data — Bootstrap Script for anihpj
#!/bin/bash
# User Data script — runs ONCE when EC2 first launches
# This automates the entire anihpj setup

# 1. Update system & install Docker
yum update -y
amazon-linux-extras install docker -y
service docker start
usermod -a -G docker ec2-user
systemctl enable docker

# 2. Install Docker Compose
curl -L "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/latest/download/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose

# 3. Install nginx as reverse proxy
amazon-linux-extras install nginx1 -y

# 4. Pull anihpj from ECR (authenticated via IAM Role)
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker pull 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:latest

# 5. Create docker-compose.yml on the fly
cat > /home/ec2-user/docker-compose.yml << 'EOF'
version: '3.8'
services:
  web:
    image: 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:latest
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: anihpj.settings
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://user:pass@anihpj-db.xxx.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/anihpj
    restart: always
EOF

# 6. Start anihpj
cd /home/ec2-user
docker-compose up -d

# 7. Configure nginx as reverse proxy
cat > /etc/nginx/conf.d/anihpj.conf << 'EOF'
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name _;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    }
    location /static/ {
        alias /home/ec2-user/static/;
    }
}
EOF
systemctl enable nginx
systemctl start nginx

echo "✅ anihpj is running on port 80!"
📝 Key DevOps Principles in This Script

1. Automation: Zero manual steps — launch EC2, and anihpj is running. 2. No hardcoded secrets: ECR auth uses the EC2 IAM Role (no passwords!). 3. Immutable: If the instance has issues, terminate and launch a new one — the script rebuilds everything. 4. This is how we did it before Kubernetes. With EKS, these steps move into Dockerfile + Deployment YAML.

1
Launch EC2

AMI + User Data

2
Install Docker

User Data script

3
Pull Image

From ECR via IAM Role

4
Start Container

docker-compose up -d

5
Configure nginx

Reverse proxy :80→:8000

  • ✅ Lambda = zero ops, event-driven. Cost-effective for sporadic. NOT for long-running.
  • ✅ ECS = simpler than K8s, AWS-only. Free control plane. No K8s learning curve.
  • ✅ EKS = the Kubernetes standard. $0.10/hr. Helm, Istio, multi-cloud portability.
  • ✅ Fargate = containers without servers. No nodes to manage, pay per task.

anihpj has these components: (1) Django web server (long-running, needs Docker), (2) Resume image processor (triggered on S3 upload), (3) Nightly job cleanup (scheduled at 2 AM), (4) PostgreSQL database. For each component, choose the BEST AWS compute service and justify your choice.

# 2. Resume Image Processor → Lambda

#    Or: Kubernetes CronJob if already using EKS

# 4. PostgreSQL Database → RDS (not a compute decision!)

📝 Chapter 8 — AWS DevOps Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1

You need to run the anihpj Django application with full control over the OS, including custom kernel modules. Which AWS compute service should you choose?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud). EC2 gives you full root/administrator access, allowing custom kernel modules, specific OS configurations, and any software installation. No other AWS compute service provides this level of control.

📖 EXPLANATION

Lambda is serverless — no OS access. Fargate manages the underlying OS. ECS/EKS give container-level control only. EC2 is the only option when you need kernel-level customization. Use EC2 with Auto Scaling Groups for production resilience.

Q2

Your team is migrating from an on-premises Kubernetes cluster to AWS. You want to keep using Kubernetes tools (Helm, kubectl, Istio) and maintain multi-cloud portability. Which service should you use?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service). EKS runs standard, upstream Kubernetes — your existing Helm charts, kubectl commands, and Istio configuration work without modification.

📖 EXPLANATION

ECS is AWS-native — completely different API, no kubectl, no Helm. With EKS, you maintain K8s portability: move between AWS, GCP, Azure, or on-premises using the same manifests and tools. EKS is the right choice when Kubernetes expertise already exists in the team.

Q3

A startup wants to run containerized microservices on AWS without learning Kubernetes. They need service discovery, load balancing, and auto-scaling — but want to stay within the AWS ecosystem. Which service fits best?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service). ECS provides native container orchestration with service discovery (Cloud Map), load balancing (ALB integration), and auto-scaling — all using AWS concepts, not Kubernetes.

📖 EXPLANATION

ECS has a gentler learning curve than EKS. Task Definitions replace Pod specs, Services replace K8s Services. The control plane is FREE (unlike EKS at $0.10/hr). For AWS-only teams who don't need multi-cloud, ECS is often the simpler, cheaper choice.

Q4

You need to process user-uploaded resume files for anihpj. Processing takes 3 seconds per file, happens unpredictably throughout the day (0-100 uploads/hour), and involves calling AWS Rekognition. Which compute service minimizes cost?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

AWS Lambda. Lambda charges per millisecond of execution — you pay nothing when there are no uploads. With EC2/Fargate, you'd pay for idle capacity 24/7. Lambda also integrates natively with S3 triggers.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Lambda function — triggered by S3 upload
import boto3
def handler(event, context):
    bucket = event['Records'][0]['s3']['bucket']['name']
    key = event['Records'][0]['s3']['object']['key']
    # Process resume with Rekognition
    rekognition = boto3.client('rekognition')
    # ... process and save results ...
    # Cost: ~$0.0000002 per invocation + Rekognition API costs
    # If 0 uploads: $0.00!
Q5

You want to run anihpj containers on ECS but don't want to manage any EC2 instances. Which ECS launch type should you use?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Fargate launch type. With Fargate, you define CPU/memory per task, and AWS provisions the infrastructure automatically. No EC2 instances to patch, scale, or secure.

📖 EXPLANATION

ECS has two launch types: EC2 (you manage instances) and Fargate (serverless). Fargate is the DevOps-friendly choice — less operational overhead, per-task isolation, and pay-per-use pricing. Each ECS task gets its own ENI (Elastic Network Interface) for networking isolation.

Q6

Your EC2 Auto Scaling Group has min=2, desired=3, max=6. Three instances are running. One instance fails its health check. What happens?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The ASG terminates the unhealthy instance and launches a new one. After replacement, 3 instances are running again (maintaining the desired count).

📖 EXPLANATION

Auto Scaling Groups continuously perform health checks. If an instance fails (status check or ELB health check), the ASG: (1) marks it unhealthy, (2) terminates it, (3) launches a replacement. This happens automatically — the desired count of 3 is maintained without human intervention. If CPU spikes above your scaling policy threshold, the ASG scales OUT (up to max=6).

Q7

What is a Golden AMI, and why should DevOps engineers use EC2 Image Builder to create one?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

A Golden AMI is a pre-configured machine image with all software, dependencies, and security patches baked in. EC2 Image Builder automates the creation pipeline: base OS → install packages → run tests → produce AMI.

📖 EXPLANATION

Without Golden AMIs, each EC2 launch runs User Data scripts (5-10 minutes to configure). With Golden AMIs, instances launch in seconds — fully configured. Image Builder automates the pipeline: source OS → build components (install Docker, Python, nginx) → test → distribute AMI to regions. This is the DevOps pattern of immutable infrastructure.

Q8

You have a Lambda function that hasn't been invoked for 30 minutes. A new request arrives. What is a "cold start" and how does it affect this invocation?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

A cold start is the initialization latency (~1-3 seconds) when Lambda creates a new execution environment. After 30 minutes of inactivity, the previous environment was recycled, so this invocation experiences a cold start.

📖 EXPLANATION

Lambda execution environments persist for some time after invocation (typically 5-15 minutes). When a new request arrives and no warm environment exists, AWS: (1) downloads your code, (2) initializes the runtime, (3) runs your init code. This adds ~1-3 seconds. After that, subsequent requests reuse the warm environment (no cold start). For latency-sensitive apps, use Provisioned Concurrency to keep environments warm.

Q9

Your anihpj deployment on EC2 needs to pull Docker images from ECR. Where should you store the AWS credentials for aws ecr get-login-password?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Nowhere on the instance! Attach an IAM Role to the EC2 instance with ecr:GetAuthorizationToken and ecr:BatchGetImage permissions. The AWS SDK/CLI automatically retrieves temporary credentials from the instance metadata service.

📖 EXPLANATION
// IAM Role attached to EC2 instance (NO credentials on disk!)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": [
      "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",
      "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability",
      "ecr:BatchGetImage"
    ],
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}
// EC2 automatically gets temp creds via http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
// aws ecr get-login-password uses these automatically — no config needed!
Q10

Compare EC2 + Auto Scaling Group vs EKS with Cluster Autoscaler for running anihpj. Which provides better container orchestration and why?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

EKS provides better container orchestration. While both can scale, EKS adds: rolling updates (zero-downtime), self-healing (auto-restart crashed containers), service discovery (DNS), load balancing (Services), configuration management (ConfigMaps/Secrets), and the entire K8s ecosystem (Helm, Istio, ArgoCD).

📖 EXPLANATION
CapabilityEC2 + ASGEKS
ScalingASG (instance-level)HPA (Pod) + Cluster Autoscaler (Node)
UpdatesManual or CFN rollingkubectl rollout (zero downtime)
Self-healingASG replaces instanceRestart container (seconds)
Service DiscoveryManual (ALB targets)Built-in DNS + Services

Chapter 9: AWS Networking — VPC, Subnets & Connectivity

Networking is the backbone of every AWS deployment. If you don't understand VPCs, subnets, and routing, you can't secure your applications. In this chapter, you'll design the network architecture that runs anihpj on EKS — from VPC to Load Balancer to DNS.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 DOP-C02: Resiliency

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ VPC fundamentals — CIDR, subnets, route tables, gateways
  • ✅ Security Groups vs NACLs — and when to use each
  • ✅ VPC design patterns for EKS (public + private subnets across AZs)
  • ✅ Load Balancers — ALB vs NLB vs GWLB
  • ✅ Route 53 DNS, CloudFront CDN, and API Gateway

9.1 VPC Fundamentals — Your Private Cloud Network

A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your own isolated network in AWS. Think of it as your personal data center — you control IP ranges, subnets, routing, and firewall rules. Every AWS resource (EC2, RDS, EKS) lives inside a VPC.

Complete VPC Architecture — Public & Private Subnets
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  VPC: 10.0.0.0/16 (65,536 IPs) — us-east-1                          │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  us-east-1a                                                    │  │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐             │  │
│  │  │ PUBLIC SUBNET        │  │ PRIVATE SUBNET       │             │  │
│  │  │ 10.0.1.0/24          │  │ 10.0.10.0/24         │             │  │
│  │  │                     │  │                      │             │  │
│  │  │ ┌─────────────┐    │  │ ┌─────────────┐     │             │  │
│  │  │ │ NAT Gateway  │    │  │ │ EKS Worker   │     │             │  │
│  │  │ │ (elastic IP) │    │  │ │ Node         │     │             │  │
│  │  │ └──────┬───────┘    │  │ │ 10.0.10.45   │     │             │  │
│  │  │        │            │  │ └─────────────┘     │             │  │
│  │  │  ┌─────▼────────┐  │  │                      │             │  │
│  │  │  │ ALB (public)  │  │  │ Pods get IPs from    │             │  │
│  │  │  │ internet-     │  │  │ VPC CNI:             │             │  │
│  │  │  │ facing       │  │  │ 10.0.10.100-200      │             │  │
│  │  │  └──────────────┘  │  └─────────────────────┘             │  │
│  │  └─────────────────────┘                                       │  │
│  │  Route Table:            Route Table:                          │  │
│  │  10.0.0.0/16 → local    10.0.0.0/16 → local                   │  │
│  │  0.0.0.0/0 → IGW        0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway              │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                      │
│  Repeat in us-east-1b and us-east-1c for high availability!         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧬 DEEP DIVE: How VPC Isolation Works — Hardware-Level Enforcement

How does AWS ensure your VPC traffic CANNOT be seen by other customers on the same physical hardware? Through three layers of enforced isolation — all the way down to the silicon:

🖥️
LAYER 1: Nitro Card (Hardware)

Every packet is encapsulated with VPC metadata by a dedicated Nitro PCIe card. Functions like a hardware VPN tunnel per VPC. Other customers on the same physical wire cannot sniff your traffic — the Nitro card drops packets that don't match the VPC ID.

🔒
LAYER 2: Hypervisor (KVM)

Strict ENI-to-VM mappings enforced at the hypervisor level. Each Elastic Network Interface is bound to exactly one VM. No cross-talk possible — a VM cannot receive traffic destined for another VM's ENI, even on the same host.

🗺️
LAYER 3: Mapping Service

A global SDN controller tracks every VPC→Customer→Host mapping across all AWS regions. Every Nitro card queries this service: "Where does this encapsulated packet go?" The mapping service is the authoritative source of truth for the entire AWS network fabric.

🔗 WHY THIS MATTERS — It Enables Three Critical Services

🔗
VPC Peering

Two VPCs share routes directly — no physical connection needed. The Nitro encapsulation handles routing between VPCs transparently. Traffic stays on the AWS backbone.

🌉
Transit Gateway

A cloud router connecting 1,000s of VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect. All traffic flows through the Nitro encapsulation layer — no physical network reconfiguration.

🔌
PrivateLink / VPC Endpoints

Traffic to AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, ECR) stays on the AWS backbone. Never touches the public internet. Powered by the same Nitro encapsulation.

🔄 STATEFUL vs STATELESS — The SG/NACL Distinction

✅ Security Groups (Stateful)

Security Groups track connections. If you allow inbound :80, the return traffic on ephemeral ports is automatically allowed. No need to open outbound ephemeral ranges. This is why you rarely touch NACLs — SGs handle 99% of use cases.

Allow inbound :80 → return traffic auto-allowed ✅

⚠️ NACLs (Stateless)

NACLs do NOT track connections. You must explicitly allow BOTH directions: inbound on port 80 AND outbound on ephemeral ports (1024-65535). Forgetting the outbound rule is the #1 NACL misconfiguration.

Allow inbound :80 + outbound 1024-65535 😓

📦 THE ACTUAL PACKET FLOW — User → anihpj Pod

1
DNS Resolution

User types anihpj.example.com → Route 53 resolves to the ALB's public IP in the public subnet.

2
Internet Gateway

Packet arrives at the VPC's Internet Gateway → routed to the ALB in the public subnet.

3
TLS Termination

ALB terminates TLS, inspects the request (host/path), and forwards to the Target Group — a list of Pod IPs on worker nodes in private subnets.

4
Nitro Encapsulation

The Nitro card encapsulates the packet: "VPC-abc, target 10.0.16.45:8000". This encapsulation guarantees the packet can only reach its intended VPC and host.

5
Mapping Service Route

The encapsulated packet traverses the AWS backbone. The mapping service tells each hop: "VPC-abc lives on host X in AZ-a" → packet forwarded accordingly.

6
Pod Delivery

Worker node's Nitro card receives the packet, strips encapsulation, delivers to Pod 10.0.16.45:8000. The anihpj container processes the request and responds.

⚡ Latency Profile

Same AZ: ~2-5ms  |  Cross-AZ: ~10ms  |  Cross-Region: varies by distance. The packet NEVER touches the public internet after step 2 — all intra-VPC traffic flows over the AWS backbone via Nitro encapsulation. This is what makes VPC networking both secure AND fast.

🌐
CIDR Blocks

IP range in CIDR notation: 10.0.0.0/16 = 65,536 IPs. Subnets split this: /24 = 256 IPs each.

🚪
Internet Gateway

Allows resources with public IPs to reach the internet. Attached to VPC. Public subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW.

🔒
NAT Gateway

Allows PRIVATE resources to reach the internet (pull Docker images, updates) WITHOUT being reachable FROM the internet. Deployed in public subnet.

🛡️
Security Groups

Stateful firewall at the instance/ENI level. Allow inbound → return traffic auto-allowed. Default: deny all inbound, allow all outbound.

✅ Security Groups (Stateful)

Rules specify ALLOW only. If you allow inbound port 80, return traffic on ephemeral ports is automatically allowed. Attached to ENI/instance.

⚠️ NACLs (Stateless)

Rules specify ALLOW and DENY. Must explicitly allow BOTH inbound AND outbound (return traffic on ephemeral ports 1024-65535). Attached to subnet.

9.2 VPC Design Patterns for EKS

EKS requires careful VPC design. The recommended pattern: Public + Private subnets across 3 Availability Zones. EKS worker nodes go in private subnets. The control plane endpoint can be public, private, or both.

EKS VPC Layout — Recommended Architecture
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  VPC: 10.0.0.0/16 — EKS CLUSTER                                      │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌───────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────┐               │
│  │ us-east-1a            │  │ us-east-1b            │  us-east-1c   │
│  │ ┌───────────────────┐ │  │ ┌───────────────────┐ │  (same)       │
│  │ │ PUBLIC 10.0.0.0/24│ │  │ │ PUBLIC 10.0.1.0/24│ │              │
│  │ │ • NAT Gateway     │ │  │ │ • NAT Gateway     │ │              │
│  │ │ • Bastion Host    │ │  │ │                   │ │              │
│  │ └───────────────────┘ │  │ └───────────────────┘ │              │
│  │ ┌───────────────────┐ │  │ ┌───────────────────┐ │              │
│  │ │ PRIVATE 10.0.16.0 │ │  │ │ PRIVATE 10.0.17.0 │ │              │
│  │ │      /20          │ │  │ │      /20          │ │              │
│  │ │ • EKS Worker Nodes│ │  │ │ • EKS Worker Nodes│ │              │
│  │ │ • RDS Database    │ │  │ │ • ElastiCache     │ │              │
│  │ │ • Pods (via CNI)  │ │  │ │ • Pods (via CNI)  │ │              │
│  │ └───────────────────┘ │  │ └───────────────────┘ │              │
│  └───────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────┘               │
│                                                                      │
│  EKS Control Plane (AWS-managed account):                            │
│    • Endpoint: Private (recommended for production)                  │
│    • Worker nodes reach control plane via VPC endpoint               │
│    • kubectl reaches API via VPN/Direct Connect/bastion              │
│    • or: Public + Private endpoint for simpler access                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 VPC CNI Plugin — Pods Get Real VPC IPs

Unlike other K8s distributions that use overlay networks, EKS uses the AWS VPC CNI plugin. Every Pod gets a real, routable VPC IP address from the subnet's CIDR range. This means: Pods are directly addressable from other VPC resources, Security Groups work on Pods, and VPC Flow Logs show Pod traffic. The trade-off: each Pod consumes a VPC IP — plan your subnet sizes accordingly.

📊 DEEP DIVE: VPC Flow Logs — Network Monitoring

VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata flowing through your VPC. Think of it as "NetFlow for AWS" — you see WHO talked to WHOM, on which port, and whether it was accepted or rejected.

Flow Log Record Format — Captured per ENI, Subnet, or VPC
version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol packets bytes start end action log-status

# Example: anihpj Pod (10.0.16.45) accessing RDS (10.0.16.100) on port 5432
2 123456789 eni-abc123 10.0.16.45 10.0.16.100 45678 5432 6 15 2048 1623456789 1623456890 ACCEPT OK
📊
CloudWatch Logs

Real-time streaming + Metric Filters for alarms. Alert on REJECT records (blocked traffic). Best for: operational monitoring and troubleshooting.

🪣
S3

Long-term archive with Athena for SQL queries. Query years of flow data: "Show me all connections to port 22 last month." Best for: compliance auditing.

🔥
Kinesis Data Firehose

Real-time streaming to Splunk, ELK, Datadog. Correlate flow logs with application logs. Best for: SIEM integration and anomaly detection.

🔍
Troubleshoot Connectivity

Is traffic being blocked by a Security Group or NACL? Filter for action: REJECT — the flow log tells you exactly which rule blocked it.

🚨
Detect Anomalies

Spot unusual patterns: a Pod suddenly connecting to a foreign IP on port 22, or a spike in rejected traffic indicating a misconfigured SG.

📋
Compliance Auditing

Prove to auditors: "Only the application tier accessed the database tier on port 5432. No unauthorized access occurred."

🎯 EXAM TIPS
  • Flow Logs capture metadata only — not packet payloads. For payload inspection, use a Gateway Load Balancer with virtual appliance.
  • REJECT records = blocked by Security Group or NACL. ACCEPT = allowed through.
  • Published to CloudWatch OR S3, not both simultaneously from the same flow log. Use Kinesis if you need multiple destinations.
🔌 DEEP DIVE: VPC Endpoints — Keep Traffic Off the Internet

VPC Endpoints let AWS services communicate WITHOUT going through the public internet. Two types — know the difference for the exam:

🚪 GATEWAY ENDPOINT

FREE — S3 + DynamoDB only

Private Subnet ──▶ vpce-xxxx ──▶ S3/DynamoDB
via route table entry          private link
  • Add a route table entry in your subnet: destination = S3 prefix list, target = gateway endpoint ID.
  • No ENI created. Works at the route table level — any resource in the subnet can use it.
  • Traffic NEVER leaves the AWS network. No NAT Gateway needed, no internet exposure.
🔌 INTERFACE ENDPOINT

$0.01/hr + data — 100+ services

EKS Pod ──▶ ENI (private IP) ──▶ ECR/STS/CW
DNS: *.dkr.ecr      PrivateLink    
  • Creates an ENI with a private IP in your subnet. Uses PrivateLink — traffic stays on the AWS backbone.
  • DNS resolution automatically redirects service endpoints (e.g., *.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) to the ENI's private IP.
  • Supports security groups — you can restrict which resources can access the endpoint.
☸️ Essential EKS VPC Endpoints

For a fully private EKS cluster (no NAT Gateway), you need these endpoints:

📦
ECR (2 endpoints)

com.amazonaws.region.ecr.dkr (image pull) + ecr.api (repository metadata). Without these, Pods can't pull images.

🪣
S3 (Gateway)

For ECR's backing S3 layer image storage. Gateway endpoint — free, route table entry only.

🔐
STS + CloudWatch

STS: for IRSA token exchange. CloudWatch: for container logs. Both are interface endpoints.

🎯 EXAM TIPS
  • Gateway endpoints = route table entry (FREE). Only for S3 and DynamoDB.
  • Interface endpoints = ENI + DNS redirect ($0.01/hr + data). For everything else (100+ services).
  • Both keep traffic within the AWS network — no NAT Gateway, no internet gateway, no public exposure.
  • If a question asks "how to access S3 from private subnet without NAT Gateway?" → Gateway Endpoint (free).

9.3 Load Balancing on AWS — ALB vs NLB

7️⃣Layer 7 — ALBHTTP/HTTPS/gRPC. Path-based, host-based routing. WAF integration.Web AppsEKS IngressMicroservices
4️⃣Layer 4 — NLBTCP/UDP/TLS. Ultra-low latency, static IPs, TLS termination.Game ServersIoTStreaming
3️⃣Layer 3 — GWLBIP packets. Routes through virtual appliances for inspection.FirewallsIDS/IPSDeep Packet Inspect
FeatureALB (Application LB)NLB (Network LB)
OSI LayerLayer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC)Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS)
RoutingPath-based, host-based, header-basedIP + Port only
Performance~100ms overhead, good for web appsUltra-low latency, millions of RPS
Static IP❌ (DNS name only)✅ Fixed IP per AZ
TLS Termination✅ Native✅ Native
WebSockets✅✅ (TCP-level)
Best ForWeb apps, microservices, EKS IngressHigh-throughput, static IPs, non-HTTP
🔀
GWLB (Gateway Load Balancer)

Layer 3 (IP). Routes traffic to virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS) for inspection BEFORE reaching your app. Uses GENEVE protocol. Transparent — preserves source/destination IPs.

⚠️
CLB (Classic Load Balancer)

Legacy. Layer 4 + basic Layer 7. AVOID for new deployments. AWS recommends ALB or NLB for all new workloads. Only appears in exam for migration scenarios.

9.4 Route 53 — DNS & Traffic Management

Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service. It translates domain names (anihpj.example.com) into IP addresses (ALB endpoint). For DevOps, Route 53's routing policies enable advanced deployment patterns.

PolicyHow It WorksDevOps Use Case
📍Simple RoutingOne domain → one target. Basic DNS resolution with no health checks. The default policy.Single-region, non-critical endpoints. Quick prototyping.
⚖️Weighted RoutingSplit traffic by assigned weights: 90% → v1, 10% → v2. Weights must sum to any total — Route 53 normalizes them.Canary deployments! Shift 10% of users to new version, monitor error rates, then shift 100%. Also used for A/B testing.
⏱️Latency RoutingRoutes users to the AWS region with the lowest measured latency from their location. Uses live latency measurements, not geography.Multi-region active-active deployments. US users → us-east-1, EU users → eu-west-1, each with lowest latency.
🔄Failover RoutingActive-Passive: Primary target is healthy → all traffic goes there. Health check fails → auto-switch to secondary. Requires health checks on both.Disaster recovery. Primary region fails → Route 53 automatically redirects to DR region. Combined with cross-region replication.
🌍Geolocation RoutingRoute based on user's geographic location (continent, country, or US state). EU users → EU deployment, US users → US deployment.Compliance (GDPR: EU user data stays in EU). Localized content. Different pricing/features per region.
🔗Alias RecordsAWS-specific — points to AWS resources (ALB, CloudFront, S3 website, Elastic Beanstalk) for FREE. Resolves natively at the DNS level. Supports health checks.Always use Alias over CNAME for AWS resources. CNAME charges per query, Alias is free. Alias works at the zone apex (naked domain), CNAME does not.
🎯 EXAM TIP

Weighted Routing is the key policy for canary deployments and A/B testing on DOP-C02. Failover Routing is the key policy for disaster recovery (active-passive). Latency + Geolocation are often confused — latency is based on network performance, geolocation is based on the user's declared location. Alias records are ALWAYS the answer when routing to AWS resources like ALB, CloudFront, or S3 — they're free, support health checks, and work at zone apex.

9.5 CloudFront — Content Delivery Network

CloudFront caches your content at 600+ edge locations worldwide. Users get responses from the nearest edge, reducing latency from 200ms (cross-continent) to 10-20ms. For anihpj, CloudFront serves static files (CSS, JS, images) from S3 and routes dynamic requests to the ALB.

📁 Static Content (S3 + CloudFront)

CSS, JavaScript, images, user-uploaded files. Cached at edge locations with long TTL. Origin: S3 bucket with OAC.

⚡ Dynamic Content (ALB + EKS)

API calls, job post data, user authentication. NOT cached (or short TTL). Origin: ALB → EKS Pods.

🌐 DEEP DIVE: Lambda@Edge, CloudFront Functions & Cache Management

CloudFront has TWO serverless compute options at the edge — understanding when to use each is a DOP-C02 tested topic:

🧠 Lambda@Edge

More powerful, more latency, more triggers

  • Runs at Regional Edge Caches (13 locations, not all 600+ POPs)
  • Full Node.js / Python runtime — up to 30 seconds execution
  • 4 trigger points: Viewer Request, Origin Request, Origin Response, Viewer Response
  • Use cases: A/B testing (rewrite URLs), custom authentication at edge, dynamic content generation, header manipulation
⚡ CloudFront Functions

Lighter, faster, cheaper — 600+ locations

  • Runs at ALL 600+ edge locations — sub-millisecond startup
  • JavaScript only, lightweight (< 2ms execution time)
  • 2 trigger points only: Viewer Request, Viewer Response
  • Use cases: URL redirects, header manipulation, cache key normalization
  • ~1/6 the cost of Lambda@Edge — use when you don't need full runtime
🔐 OAC (Origin Access Control) — Replaces OAI

Ensures S3 objects can ONLY be accessed via CloudFront. Unlike the legacy OAI (which used S3 bucket policies), OAC uses IAM-based principal authentication. Users who try to hit the S3 bucket URL directly get a 403 Forbidden. Always use OAC for new CloudFront distributions — OAI is legacy.

Cache Invalidation — Purge Objects Before TTL Expires
# Invalidate specific files
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id E1ABCXYZ \
  --paths "/index.html" "/static/css/main.css"

# Invalidate everything (use sparingly — expensive at scale)
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id E1ABCXYZ \
  --paths "/*"

# Pricing: First 1,000 paths/month FREE, then $0.005 per path
⚠️ Cache Invalidation Reality

Invalidations are NOT instant — they can take a few minutes to propagate globally across all 600+ edge locations. For time-sensitive deployments, use versioned filenames instead (main.abc123.css) — this is instant because it's a new URL, not a cache purge. Invalidation is for emergencies; versioned filenames are for deployments.

9.6 API Gateway — Managed API Management

API Gateway is a fully managed service for creating, publishing, and securing APIs. It handles authentication, rate limiting, request transformation, and can integrate with Lambda, EKS, or any HTTP backend.

🔌
REST API

Full-featured: request validation, usage plans, API keys, caching. Best for public APIs.

⚡
HTTP API

Lightweight, cheaper (70% less), lower latency. Best for internal APIs, Lambda proxies.

🔗
VPC Link

Connects API Gateway to private resources inside VPC (EKS, internal ALB). No public exposure needed.

🎯 API Gateway Use Cases for anihpj
  • ✅ Public Job API: REST API → Lambda → DynamoDB — simple CRUD for jobpost listings with API keys for third-party integrators
  • ✅ Internal Microservices: HTTP API → VPC Link → NLB → EKS — cheaper, lower latency for service-to-service calls
  • ✅ WebSocket API: Real-time job posting notifications — WebSocket API → Lambda → DynamoDB Streams
  • ✅ Canary Deployments: Stage variables + deployment canaries — 10% traffic to new API version, monitor, roll forward or back

🏢 REAL-WORLD NETWORKING — How Companies Connect on AWS

🏢 Netflix — VPC + Transit Gateway

100,000+ VPC instances, 1000s of VPCs

Stack: VPC (per-service isolation) → Transit Gateway (inter-VPC routing) → Direct Connect (hybrid on-prem)

Why: Each microservice gets its own VPC for blast-radius isolation. Transit Gateway connects them without a mesh of peering connections.

🛒 Shopify — CloudFront + ALB

Sub-50ms page loads worldwide

Stack: CloudFront (600+ edge locations) → ALB (path routing) → EKS (dynamic content) + S3 (static)

Why: Every merchant's storefront cached at nearest edge. Dynamic cart/checkout routes through ALB to EKS. Static theme assets never touch origin servers.

🏦 Stripe — VPC Endpoints Only

Zero internet-exposed traffic

Stack: VPC Endpoints (all AWS services) → PrivateLink → No NAT Gateway → No IGW for internal services

Why: PCI DSS compliance demands NO traffic over public internet. Interface Endpoints for every AWS service. S3/DynamoDB via Gateway Endpoints.

📱 Tinder — Route 53 + NLB

Millions of concurrent WebSocket connections

Stack: Route 53 (latency-based routing) → NLB (Layer 4, WebSockets) → EKS (real-time matching engine)

Why: WebSockets need Layer 4 (NLB), not Layer 7 (ALB). Latency routing sends users to nearest region. NLB handles millions of persistent connections.

🧠 Chapter 9 — Core Takeaways

  • ✅ VPC = your private network. Everything runs inside one. Master public vs private subnets.
  • ✅ SGs are STATEFUL, NACLs are STATELESS. SGs handle 99% of firewall needs.
  • ✅ ALB for web apps (Layer 7), NLB for performance (Layer 4). GWLB for virtual appliances.
  • ✅ VPC Endpoints keep traffic on AWS backbone. Gateway (free, S3/DDB) vs Interface ($/hr, 100+ services).
  • ✅ Route 53 weighted routing = canary deployments. CloudFront = global edge caching.
⚠️ NETWORKING EXAM TRAP: Never expose RDS/DB to the internet!

Databases go in PRIVATE subnets. Only ALB (in public subnet) should be internet-facing. Use Security Groups to restrict: ALB SG → Worker SG → RDS SG. Each layer only trusts the layer above it.

⏱️ 20 minutes
Scenario: Design anihpj Network on AWS

Design a VPC architecture for anihpj running on EKS. Requirements: (1) Highly available across 3 AZs, (2) Worker nodes must not be directly accessible from the internet, (3) Pods must be able to pull images from ECR and reach external APIs, (4) Users access anihpj via HTTPS at anihpj.example.com, (5) Static files served via CDN.

💡 Hint: Public subnets for ALB + NAT Gateways. Private subnets for worker nodes. Route 53 → CloudFront → ALB (dynamic) + S3 (static). VPC CNI for Pod networking.
▼ Solution (Click to Reveal) 
# NETWORK ARCHITECTURE — anihpj on EKS
# ─────────────────────────────────────
# VPC: 10.0.0.0/16
# 3 AZs × (1 public + 1 private subnet) = 6 subnets
#
# PUBLIC SUBNETS (each AZ):
#   • ALB (internet-facing) — terminates HTTPS
#   • NAT Gateway — outbound for private subnets
#   • Bastion host (optional, for SSH access)
#
# PRIVATE SUBNETS (each AZ):
#   • EKS Worker Nodes (managed node group)
#   • RDS PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ)
#   • ElastiCache Redis
#   • Pods get VPC IPs via CNI
#
# DNS + CDN:
#   Route 53: anihpj.example.com → A Alias → CloudFront
#   CloudFront:
#     /static/* → S3 bucket (cached)
#     /api/*    → ALB (not cached, or short TTL)
#     /*        → ALB (dynamic)
#
# SECURITY:
#   ALB SG: allow 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
#   Worker SG: allow 8000 from ALB SG only
#   RDS SG: allow 5432 from Worker SG only
#   NAT Gateway: outbound only (no inbound rules)

📝 Chapter 9 — AWS DevOps Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1

Your EKS worker nodes are in private subnets. How do they pull container images from Amazon ECR (which is an AWS service on the internet)?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Via a NAT Gateway in a public subnet, or via VPC Endpoints for ECR (interface endpoints for ECR API + gateway endpoint for S3).

📖 EXPLANATION

Private subnets have no direct internet access. NAT Gateway (in public subnet) provides outbound-only internet access. Better: Use VPC Endpoints — traffic stays within AWS network, no NAT Gateway costs. ECR requires TWO endpoints: com.amazonaws.region.ecr.dkr (interface) for image pulls and com.amazonaws.region.ecr.api (interface) for API calls, plus S3 gateway endpoint for image layers.

Q2

What's the difference between a Security Group and a Network ACL (NACL)?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Security Groups are STATEFUL — allow inbound automatically allows return traffic. Attached to ENI/instance. ALLOW rules only. NACLs are STATELESS — must explicitly allow inbound AND outbound. Attached to subnet. ALLOW + DENY rules. Evaluated in rule number order.

📖 EXPLANATION

Use SGs as your primary firewall (instance-level, stateful). Use NACLs as a backup subnet-level defense. Common pattern: SG allows port 443 from anywhere; NACL blocks known bad IP ranges. Remember: NACLs evaluate rules by NUMBER (lowest first), and the first match (allow OR deny) wins.

Q3

You need to expose the anihpj EKS application with path-based routing: /api/* goes to backend service, /* goes to frontend service. Which AWS load balancer should you use?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Application Load Balancer (ALB). ALB supports Layer 7 routing — path-based, host-based, and header-based. NLB only supports Layer 4 (IP + Port) routing.

📖 EXPLANATION

On EKS, use the AWS Load Balancer Controller with a K8s Ingress resource. The controller automatically creates an ALB, Target Groups, and Listener Rules based on your Ingress YAML annotations. Path-based routing is configured in the Ingress spec.

Q4

You're deploying a new version of anihpj. You want to send 10% of users to v2 and 90% to v1. Which Route 53 routing policy enables this?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Weighted Routing. Create two records — one for v1 (weight 90) and one for v2 (weight 10) — both pointing to different ALBs or target groups.

📖 EXPLANATION

Weighted routing is perfect for canary deployments. Start with v2 at weight 1, monitor for errors, gradually increase to 100. If v2 has issues, set weight to 0 — all traffic instantly returns to v1. Combine with Route 53 health checks: if v2's endpoint fails health checks, Route 53 automatically removes it from rotation.

Q5

How does the VPC CNI plugin for EKS differ from traditional Kubernetes overlay networks like Flannel or Calico?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The VPC CNI plugin assigns actual VPC IP addresses to Pods — not overlay IPs. Pods appear as first-class citizens on the VPC network, directly routable from other VPC resources.

📖 EXPLANATION

With overlay networks (Flannel, Calico), Pods get virtual IPs (e.g., 10.244.x.x) encapsulated in VXLAN packets. With VPC CNI, Pods get real IPs from the subnet (e.g., 10.0.16.45). This means: Security Groups apply to individual Pods, VPC Flow Logs show Pod traffic, other VPC resources (RDS, Lambda) can reach Pods directly without NAT.

Q6

Your EKS cluster endpoint is set to "Private only." How do you run kubectl commands from your laptop?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Connect via VPN, AWS Direct Connect, or a bastion host in the VPC. Your laptop needs network reachability to the private endpoint IP address. Use aws eks update-kubeconfig to generate the kubeconfig.

📖 EXPLANATION

Private endpoint = control plane is only accessible from within the VPC. Options: (1) AWS Client VPN to VPC, (2) Direct Connect from corporate network, (3) SSH tunnel through a bastion host in public subnet. For development, use "Public and Private" endpoint setting — kubectl works from anywhere with IAM auth.

Q7

What's the difference between an Alias record and a CNAME record in Route 53?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Alias records are AWS-specific and can point to AWS resources (ALB, CloudFront, S3) at no charge. They work at the zone apex (root domain). CNAME records are standard DNS and cannot be used at the zone apex.

📖 EXPLANATION

RFC requires that a CNAME not coexist with other records at the zone apex (e.g., example.com). Alias records solve this — you can point example.com directly to your ALB. Always use Alias for AWS resources; CNAME for external domains.

Q8

How does CloudFront handle dynamic content that shouldn't be cached?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Set the Cache Behavior TTL to 0 (or use Cache-Control: no-cache headers). CloudFront forwards requests to the origin but still provides DDoS protection, TLS termination, and edge networking benefits.

📖 EXPLANATION

Even without caching, CloudFront adds value: AWS Shield Standard (free DDoS protection), TLS termination at the edge, persistent connections to origin (faster than user→origin directly), and geographic restriction capabilities. You're trading slightly higher latency for significant security and reliability gains.

Q9

You need to connect an API Gateway to an internal service running on EKS in a private subnet. How do you do this?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Use API Gateway VPC Link with a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of your EKS service. VPC Link allows API Gateway to reach private resources inside your VPC.

📖 EXPLANATION

VPC Link creates an elastic network interface in your VPC, giving API Gateway private connectivity. Architecture: API Gateway → VPC Link → NLB (internal, in private subnet) → EKS Pods. The NLB must be internal (not internet-facing). The EKS service type should be LoadBalancer with NLB annotations.

Q10

Your EKS cluster spans 3 AZs. You notice that in us-east-1a, the private subnet is running out of IP addresses for Pods. What can you do?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

(1) Add a secondary CIDR block to the VPC and create new subnets, (2) Use custom networking with the VPC CNI to assign Pods IPs from a different subnet than the node, or (3) Enable prefix delegation to assign /28 prefixes instead of individual IPs.

📖 EXPLANATION

The VPC CNI assigns one IP per Pod from the node's subnet. If subnet is /24 (256 IPs) shared with nodes + Pods, you can quickly exhaust IPs. Solutions: (1) Larger initial subnets (/20 = 4096 IPs), (2) Custom networking (Pod subnets separate from node subnets), (3) Prefix delegation (each ENI gets a /28 = 16 IPs, reducing ENI attachment count). Plan subnet sizes BEFORE creating the cluster!

Chapter 10: AWS IAM — Identity & Access Management

IAM is the #1 security topic on the AWS DevOps exam. If you don't understand IAM, you can't secure anything. This chapter covers IAM from the ground up — Users, Groups, Roles, Policies, and the EKS-specific IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) that lets individual Pods have their own AWS permissions.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 DOP-C02: Security (17%)

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ IAM Users, Groups, and Roles — the holy trinity
  • ✅ IAM Policy structure (Effect, Action, Resource, Condition)
  • ✅ Policy evaluation logic — why explicit DENY always wins
  • ✅ EC2 Instance Roles — no more hardcoded credentials
  • ✅ IRSA — per-Pod IAM roles on EKS
  • ✅ AWS Organizations & SCPs
Before IAM Roles (Pre-2012)

Hardcoded access keys on EC2. Rotating keys was manual. Keys leaked in GitHub repos. Compliance nightmare.

PAST
EC2 Instance Roles (2012)

Attach IAM Role to EC2. SDK auto-retrieves temporary credentials from metadata service. No keys on disk.

REVOLUTION
IRSA for EKS (2019)

Per-Pod IAM roles via OIDC. Pod → JWT → STS → temporary creds. Least privilege at the Pod level.

MODERN
IAM Roles Anywhere (2022)

On-premises servers get temporary AWS creds via X.509 certificates. No more long-lived access keys anywhere.

HYBRID

10.1 IAM Fundamentals — Users, Groups & Roles

IAM is GLOBAL (not regional) — a user created in any region works everywhere. The three core entities:

👤
IAM Users

Individual people or services. Has long-term credentials (password + access keys). DevOps rule: Use Roles, not Users, for applications.

👥
IAM Groups

Collections of Users. Attach policies to Groups, users inherit them. Example: "DevOps-Engineers" group gets CodePipeline, EKS, CloudWatch permissions.

🎭
IAM Roles

Temporary credentials, assumed by services (EC2, Lambda) or users. NO passwords or long-lived keys. The DevOps way: always use Roles for AWS access.

IAM Entity Relationships
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AWS ACCOUNT                                                         │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  IAM USERS                     IAM GROUPS                      │  │
│  │  ┌──────────┐                 ┌──────────────┐                │  │
│  │  │  alice   │────────────────▶│ DevOps-Engineers│              │  │
│  │  │ (human)  │     member of   │               │              │  │
│  │  └──────────┘                 │ Policies:     │              │  │
│  │  ┌──────────┐                 │  • EKSFullAccess│             │  │
│  │  │  bob     │────────────────▶│  • CodePipeline│              │  │
│  │  │ (human)  │     member of   │  • CloudWatch │              │  │
│  │  └──────────┘                 └──────────────┘                │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │  IAM ROLES (temporary, assumed)                                  │  │
│  │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐                    │  │
│  │  │ EC2 Instance Role │  │ Lambda Exec Role  │                    │  │
│  │  │ Assumed by: EC2   │  │ Assumed by: Lambda│                    │  │
│  │  │ Grants: S3, ECR   │  │ Grants: DynamoDB  │                    │  │
│  │  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘                    │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧬 DEEP DIVE: Why IAM is Global — The Architecture Behind It

IAM is GLOBAL (not regional). This confuses beginners — here's WHY:

🧠 Control Plane (Global)

The "brain" — where you manage things

  • IAM — users, roles, policies
  • Route 53 — DNS management
  • CloudFront — CDN configuration
  • Billing / Organizations — account management

These services don't run your workloads — they govern them. They're global because permissions and DNS need to work everywhere.

💪 Data Plane (Regional)

The "muscles" — where things actually run

  • EC2 — virtual machines
  • S3 buckets — object storage (bucket is regional)
  • RDS — managed databases
  • EKS clusters — Kubernetes

These services run your workloads. They're regional so data stays close to users and meets residency requirements.

🌍 How IAM's Global Architecture Works
  • IAM data lives in a global database replicated across all AWS regions. The authoritative copy is in us-east-1.
  • When EC2 in ap-southeast-1 calls S3 in eu-west-2, the IAM policy check happens at the global IAM service — not in either region.
  • This is WHY IAM is eventually consistent — writes propagate to the global replicas and may take a few seconds to be visible everywhere. If you create a role and immediately try to use it, you might get an AccessDenied for a few seconds.

🔑 CREDENTIALS — The Three Forms

👤
Username + Password

Console login — for humans. Used to sign into the AWS Management Console. Always enable MFA on these accounts. Never use for programmatic access.

🔑
Access Key ID + Secret

API/CLI — long-lived, 2 parts. AKIA... (public ID) + secret key (shown ONCE at creation). Used by aws configure. Rotate every 90 days.

⏳
Temporary Credentials (STS)

3 parts: AccessKeyId + SecretAccessKey + SessionToken. All three required. Automatically rotated by SDK. Valid 1–12 hours. The DevOps standard.

🔄 HOW STS GENERATES TEMPORARY CREDENTIALS

1. EC2 Requests Credentials

EC2 instance calls the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS): http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/role-name. This is a link-local address — only accessible from within the instance itself.

2. IMDS Forwards to STS

IMDS calls STS: "EC2 i-abc123 needs credentials for role anihpj-s3-read." IMDS acts as a proxy — the instance never talks directly to STS.

3. STS Verifies Trust

STS checks the role's TRUST POLICY: "Is EC2 i-abc123 trusted to assume anihpj-s3-read?" The trust policy is the gatekeeper — it defines WHO can assume the role.

4. STS Returns Temporary Credentials

STS generates: AccessKeyId + SecretAccessKey + SessionToken. Valid for 1–12 hours. The AWS SDK automatically refreshes these before they expire — your code never handles credential rotation.

5. SDK Caches & Uses

The SDK caches the credentials in memory and attaches them to every subsequent API call. You never see or manage these credentials — they're invisible, automatic, and secure by default.

💡 THE REVOLUTION — Why IAM Roles Changed Everything

Before IAM Roles (pre-2012), DevOps teams had to manually create IAM Users with access keys, copy those keys to every EC2 instance, and rotate them manually. Keys leaked in GitHub repos, sat in ~/.aws/credentials files, and were a compliance nightmare. With Roles, this entire process is automated, invisible, and secure by default — no keys on disk, no manual rotation, no credential leakage. This is why the DOP-C02 exam always prefers Roles over Users for any AWS-to-AWS communication.

10.2 IAM Policies — Deep Dive

Every IAM policy is a JSON document with four key elements:

IAM Policy Structure
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",           // Allow or Deny
    "Action": [                  // WHAT you can do
      "s3:GetObject",
      "s3:ListBucket"
    ],
    "Resource": [                // WHICH resources
      "arn:aws:s3:::anihpj-bucket",
      "arn:aws:s3:::anihpj-bucket/*"
    ],
    "Condition": {               // WHEN (optional)
      "IpAddress": {
        "aws:SourceIp": "10.0.0.0/8"
      }
    }
  }]
}
🧠 DEEP DIVE: IAM Policy Evaluation Logic
The evaluation order is CRITICAL for the exam:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POLICY EVALUATION FLOW (for every API call):                         │
│                                                                       │
│  1. EXPLICIT DENY? ──▶ YES ──▶ ❌ DENIED (stop!)                     │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ▼ NO                                                               │
│  2. SCP (Organizations) DENY? ──▶ YES ──▶ ❌ DENIED                  │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ▼ NO                                                               │
│  3. Resource-based policy ALLOW? ──▶ YES ──▶ ✅ ALLOWED              │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ▼ NO                                                               │
│  4. Identity-based policy ALLOW? ──▶ YES ──▶ ✅ ALLOWED              │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ▼ NO                                                               │
│  5. Permission boundary DENY? ──▶ YES ──▶ ❌ DENIED                  │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ▼ NO                                                               │
│  ❌ IMPLICIT DENY (default — everything is denied unless allowed)     │
│                                                                       │
│  🎯 GOLDEN RULE: Explicit DENY > ALLOW > Implicit DENY               │
│     One DENY anywhere in the chain = request is DENIED.               │
│     You can't "allow away" a deny.                                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

10.3 IAM Roles — The DevOps Essential

Roles are how AWS services get permissions without hardcoded credentials. This is one of the most important DevOps patterns — never put AWS access keys in code, config files, or environment variables.

🔴 BEFORE IAM ROLES — The Old "Hardcoded Keys" Nightmare
  • Create IAM User → generate Access Key + Secret Key → copy to server → store in ~/.aws/credentials → HOPE nobody leaks it
  • Keys committed to GitHub repos → AWS bill: $50,000 in crypto mining overnight
  • Rotating keys = manual process, often forgotten → expired keys break production
  • One key per server → all apps on that server share the same permissions → "why can the web server delete S3 buckets?!"
🟢 WITH IAM ROLES — The DevOps Way
  • ✅ Attach IAM Role to EC2 instance → SDK auto-retrieves temporary credentials from 169.254.169.254
  • ✅ No keys on disk. No keys in code. No keys in environment variables.
  • ✅ STS auto-rotates credentials every 1-12 hours. Application never knows the keys changed.
  • ✅ Each service gets its OWN role → Lambda has DynamoDB access, EC2 has S3 access, EKS Pod has Secrets Manager access
🖥️
EC2 Instance Role

EC2 instances assume a role to access S3, ECR, CloudWatch. Credentials auto-rotated, available at 169.254.169.254.

⚡
Lambda Execution Role

Lambda functions assume a role to access DynamoDB, S3, SNS. Defined in function configuration.

🔧
CodeBuild Service Role

CodeBuild assumes a role during builds to pull from ECR, push to S3, call AWS APIs.

🖥️EC2 InstanceSDK needs S3 access
→
🔗IMDS169.254.169.254
→
🔐STSAssumeRole
→
🔑Temp CredsValid 1-12 hrs
→
📦S3 API CallSigned with creds
💡 NEVER Put AWS Credentials in Your Code

The old (wrong) way: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA... in environment variables. The DevOps way: Attach an IAM Role to the EC2/EKS/Lambda resource. The SDK automatically retrieves temporary credentials. No keys to leak, no keys to rotate. This alone prevents 90% of AWS credential breaches.

10.4 IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts (EKS)

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) is the #1 EKS security feature on the DOP-C02 exam. It lets individual Kubernetes Pods assume their own IAM roles — without IRSA, every Pod on a worker node shares the node's single IAM role. One Pod needs S3? Every Pod gets S3. IRSA gives you per-Pod, least-privilege IAM.

❌ Without IRSA — Shared Node Role
  • All Pods on node share ONE IAM role (attached to EC2 instance profile)
  • anihpj Pod needs S3 → ALL Pods get S3 access
  • Sidecar containers inherit the same permissions
  • Security nightmare: a compromised logging sidecar can access your production database
  • No way to scope permissions per-application
✅ With IRSA — Per-Pod IAM Roles
  • Each K8s Service Account maps to a dedicated IAM Role
  • anihpj Pod → anihpj-sa → anihpj-s3-read role (S3 only)
  • Logging sidecar → logging-sa → CloudWatch Logs role (logs only)
  • Least privilege per Pod: compromise one Pod, you get only its narrow permissions
  • IAM conditions can scope by namespace, SA name, cluster ID
🔐 DEEP DIVE: The OIDC Trust Chain — How IRSA Actually Works

IRSA relies on OIDC (OpenID Connect) federation between your EKS cluster and AWS IAM. Here's the full trust chain:

1
EKS creates a signed JWT token

When a Pod annotated with a Service Account starts, EKS injects a projected service account token (JWT) into the Pod at /var/run/secrets/eks.amazonaws.com/serviceaccount/token. This token is signed by the EKS cluster's OIDC provider and contains the SA identity.

2
Pod exchanges JWT for AWS credentials via STS

The AWS SDK (in your Pod) calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, passing the JWT and the IAM Role ARN. AWS STS validates: (a) the JWT signature against the OIDC provider, (b) the IAM trust policy allows this specific SA.

3
STS returns temporary credentials

STS returns an AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken — valid for 1 hour (auto-refreshed by SDK). These are injected as environment variables: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN.

4
Pod accesses AWS with its own identity

The Pod now calls AWS APIs using those temporary credentials. CloudTrail logs show the specific IAM Role — you can trace every API call back to the exact Kubernetes Service Account and Pod that made it.

1 Create OIDC Provider in IAM

One-time setup per EKS cluster. Creates a trust relationship: "This EKS cluster is allowed to vouch for identities." The OIDC provider URL looks like: oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED123.... Each EKS cluster gets a unique OIDC issuer URL.

2 Create IAM Role with Trust Policy

The trust policy says: "Allow sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity ONLY for ServiceAccount anihpj:anihpj-sa from this specific EKS cluster." The condition StringEquals on :sub ensures only the exact SA can assume this role — not any other SA in the same cluster.

3 Annotate K8s Service Account

Add the annotation eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/ROLE-NAME to the K8s ServiceAccount. EKS's Pod Identity Webhook reads this annotation and injects the JWT token + role ARN into Pods using this SA.

4 Pod Starts — IRSA Activates Automatically

No code changes needed. The AWS SDK auto-discovers the injected token and credentials. Your Python/Node.js/Java app uses boto3/aws-sdk as usual — IRSA is transparent to application code.

IRSA Complete Setup — Service Account + IAM Trust + Pod
# 1. K8s Service Account (annotated with IAM Role ARN)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sa
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/anihpj-s3-read

---
# 2. Pod using that Service Account
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa  # ← This triggers IRSA!
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:v1
    # ENV vars automatically injected:
    # AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE
    # AWS_ROLE_ARN

# 3. IAM Role Trust Policy (in AWS, not K8s)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {
      "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED..."
    },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        "oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED...:sub": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-sa"
      }
    }
  }]
}
🎯 IRSA Exam Tips — What You MUST Know for DOP-C02

1. IRSA requires an OIDC provider in IAM — one per EKS cluster. 2. The trust policy condition :sub must match system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:SA-NAME. 3. IRSA replaces kiam and kube2iam — those are deprecated third-party solutions. 4. The annotation goes on the ServiceAccount, not the Pod. 5. For cross-account access, the trust policy can allow roles from another account's OIDC provider — useful for shared services.

10.5 AWS Organizations & SCPs — Multi-Account Governance

AWS Organizations lets you manage multiple AWS accounts centrally with consolidated billing and hierarchical policy enforcement. SCPs (Service Control Policies) are the ultimate guardrails — they define the maximum available permissions for every IAM principal in an account. Even if an IAM policy says "Allow," an SCP can say "No."

🧠 SCPs Do NOT Grant Permissions — They Only Remove Them

SCPs are permission boundaries at the account/OU level. They work like this: you attach IAM policies to grant permissions, then attach SCPs to restrict those permissions. An SCP alone gives nobody access to anything. Think of SCPs as the "ceiling" — IAM can grant up to that ceiling, but never above it.

🏢
Organization Root

Top-level container. All accounts live under it. SCPs attached here affect every account in the organization. Attach your "deny leaving org" guardrail here.

📂
Organizational Units (OUs)

Group accounts by function: Security, Dev, Staging, Prod. SCPs inherit down the tree — root → OU → sub-OU → account. Each level can only RESTRICT further, never loosen.

🔐
Management Account

The payer account. Run zero workloads here. Only used for billing, organization admin, and SCP management. Create member accounts for all actual resources.

🏢 Management Account (root)

Billing only. No workloads. Create all other accounts from here. The management account is outside any OU by default — SCPs attached to the root affect it too, so be careful.

📂 Security OU

Contains Audit Account (CloudTrail, Config aggregator) and Log Archive Account (centralized S3 for all logs). Attach SCP: "Deny deletion of CloudTrail trails and S3 log buckets." No one can tamper with audit evidence.

📂 Workloads OU — Dev/Staging

Contains anihpj-dev and anihpj-staging accounts. Attach SCP: "Deny resource creation outside us-east-1 and us-east-2." Prevents accidental multi-region sprawl. Developers can experiment freely but can't break compliance.

📂 Workloads OU — Production

Contains anihpj-prod. Attach SCP: "Deny EC2 instance types above t3.large and deny RDS deletion." Cost control + protection against accidental database destruction. Production changes require break-glass roles.

🔐 DEEP DIVE: How SCP Evaluation Works — The Full Chain

When a principal makes an AWS API call, the effective permissions are the intersection of all policies evaluated in this exact order:

1
SCP Evaluation (Account Boundary)

Is this action allowed by the SCPs on this account? If ANY SCP denies it → implicit deny, STOP. If all SCPs allow → continue to step 2.

2
Resource-Based Policy (if applicable)

Does the resource (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) allow this principal? An Allow here can bypass the need for identity-based policies, but SCPs still take precedence.

3
Identity-Based Policy (IAM)

Do the user/role's IAM policies allow this action? Combined with permission boundaries and session policies. The final result is the intersection of all allows minus all denies.

❌ If ANY SCP Denies...

The action is blocked immediately. It doesn't matter what IAM policies say. SCP deny is absolute. Example: SCP denies s3:DeleteBucket → no one in that account can delete a bucket, not even the root user.

✅ Effective Permissions Formula

Effective = SCP_Allows ∩ Resource_Allows ∩ Identity_Allows
Even if SCP allows and resource allows, identity must also explicitly allow. Then subtract any explicit denies at any level. Deny always wins.

🚫
SCP Example: Block Public S3
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "Action": ["s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock",
               "s3:PutBucketAcl",
               "s3:PutBucketPolicy"],
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        "s3:x-amz-acl": "public-read"
      }
    }
  }]
}

Prevents ANY account member from making an S3 bucket public — even if IAM allows it. This is the #1 SCP every organization should deploy.

🌍
SCP Example: Region Restriction
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "NotAction": [
      "cloudfront:*",
      "iam:*",
      "route53:*",
      "organizations:*"
    ],
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
      "StringNotEquals": {
        "aws:RequestedRegion": [
          "us-east-1",
          "us-east-2"
        ]
      }
    }
  }]
}

Locks accounts to specific regions. Global services (IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, Organizations) are exempted. DevOps teams can't accidentally deploy to unapproved regions.

🎯 DevOps SCP Strategy — The "Paved Road" Pattern

1. Root level: Deny leaving the organization (prevents account escapes). 2. Security OU: Deny CloudTrail/Config deletion. 3. Dev OU: Deny expensive instance types (keep costs predictable). 4. Prod OU: Deny resource deletion (require break-glass roles for emergencies). 5. All OUs: Deny public S3 buckets, require IMDSv2, deny root user usage. This creates a "paved road" where developers can move fast within safe guardrails — they can't accidentally nuke production or leak data.

10.6 IAM Best Practices for DevOps

These are the non-negotiable IAM rules every DevOps engineer must follow. They directly map to exam questions and real-world security practices:

🔐
Principle of Least Privilege

Start with NOTHING, add only what's needed. Never use "Resource": "*" or AdministratorAccess for applications. Scope to specific resources.

🎭
Use Roles, Not Users

Applications (EC2, Lambda, EKS) use Roles with temporary credentials. Humans use IAM Identity Center (SSO) with temporary credentials. No long-lived access keys.

🔑
Enable MFA

ALL human IAM users must have MFA. Use virtual MFA devices or hardware security keys (U2F/FIDO2). Enforce with an SCP or IAM policy condition.

🔄
Rotate Credentials

Rotate access keys every 90 days. Use IAM Credential Report to audit. For Roles, temporary credentials auto-rotate — no action needed.

🔍
Use IAM Access Analyzer

Identifies resources shared with external entities. Generates least-privilege policies based on CloudTrail activity. Free to use.

📊
Monitor with Credential Report

Generates CSV report of all IAM users: password age, access key age, MFA status. Audit weekly. Automate with AWS Config rules.

🚨 COMMON IAM MISTAKES ON THE EXAM

1. Putting AWS access keys in code/environment variables → Use IAM Roles. 2. Using root user for daily tasks → Create IAM users with MFA, lock away root credentials. 3. Using "Resource": "*" in policies → Always scope to specific ARNs. 4. Forgetting that IAM is GLOBAL → A user in any region can access resources in any region. 5. Not understanding the policy evaluation order → Explicit Deny ALWAYS wins.
