Chapter 20: Amazon EKS — Managed Kubernetes on AWS

Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) is AWS's managed Kubernetes offering. AWS runs the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) across 3 AZs for high availability — you only manage worker nodes and applications. This is the foundation for running Kubernetes in production on AWS.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~4 hours 🎯 Domain 1: SDLC 22% & Domain 3: Resiliency 15% 📝 10 Questions

20.1 What is Amazon EKS?

Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is a managed Kubernetes service that runs the upstream K8s distribution. Unlike self-managed K8s where you install and maintain every component, EKS splits responsibility: AWS manages the control plane, you manage the data plane.

🔧 Self-Managed K8s on EC2
  • You install and configure: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet, kube-proxy, CNI
  • You handle etcd backup/restore, API server scaling, certificate rotation
  • You patch OS, K8s version upgrades, security fixes
  • Full control, full responsibility. Good for learning, risky for production without a dedicated platform team.
☸️ Amazon EKS (Managed)
  • AWS runs the control plane across 3 AZs — auto-scaling, auto-healing, auto-upgrading
  • etcd is fully managed: encrypted, backed up, replicated across AZs
  • You manage: worker nodes (EC2 or Fargate), Pods, Deployments, Services
  • $0.10/hour per cluster + worker node costs. Production-ready in minutes.
🏢
AWS manages the Control Plane

API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager — all run in an AWS-managed VPC. You can't SSH into them, and you don't need to. AWS handles HA, scaling, upgrades, and security patches automatically.

🔗
You manage Worker Nodes

EC2 instances (or Fargate) that run your Pods. You choose the instance type, AMI, and scaling configuration. Managed Node Groups automate rolling updates and lifecycle management.

☸️
Upstream K8s, Not a Fork

EKS runs the same Kubernetes you'd run on-prem. No vendor lock-in — migrate your workloads between EKS, AKS, GKE, or on-prem K8s with minimal changes. All standard K8s tools (kubectl, Helm, ArgoCD) work as-is.

🧠 DEEP DIVE: Why EKS Costs $0.10/hour — What You're Actually Paying For

That $0.10/hour (~$73/month) flat fee per cluster covers: 3 highly-available control plane instances across 3 AZs, managed etcd with automated backups and encryption, integrated IAM authentication, automatic K8s version upgrades, and 24/7 AWS support. Compare to self-managed: running 3 t3.medium instances for the control plane alone costs ~$125/month — and you still have to manage everything yourself. EKS is actually cheaper than self-managed for production clusters when you factor in engineering time.

20.2 EKS Architecture — Who Manages What

The defining characteristic of EKS is the split architecture: AWS owns the control plane in an AWS-managed account, and you own the data plane in your account. They communicate via the kubelet → API server connection over an elastic network interface (ENI).

☸️ AWS-Managed Control Plane (You Don't Touch)

Runs in an AWS-owned VPC. Includes: API server (authenticates kubectl requests via IAM), etcd (encrypted at rest, auto-backup every 24 hours, replicated across 3 AZs), scheduler (assigns Pods to nodes), and controller manager (reconciles desired vs actual state). AWS handles all upgrades, patches, and scaling automatically. You access the API server via a public or private endpoint — the endpoint can be restricted to your VPC only for security.

🖥️ Your Data Plane — EC2 Worker Nodes

Runs in YOUR VPC. Each worker node is an EC2 instance running: kubelet (registers with the EKS API server, runs Pods), kube-proxy (maintains network rules for Services), containerd (container runtime), and the VPC CNI plugin (assigns real VPC IPs to Pods). Managed Node Groups automate patching, scaling, and graceful termination.

🔌 Communication — ENI Cross-Account

The kubelet on each worker node communicates with the EKS API server via a cross-account elastic network interface (ENI). The API server endpoint can be: Public (accessible from anywhere), Public + Private (accessible from within your VPC and the internet), or Private only (accessible only from within your VPC). For production, restrict to private-only with a VPN or Direct Connect.

📊
EKS Control Plane Scaling

AWS auto-scales the API server based on request load. etcd is a 3-node cluster across 3 AZs with automatic failover. If one AZ fails, the remaining 2 etcd nodes elect a new leader within seconds — your cluster stays available. You never need to think about control plane capacity.

🔐
IAM Integration — No Separate Auth

EKS natively integrates with IAM for cluster authentication. The aws-auth ConfigMap maps IAM users/roles to K8s RBAC groups. Use aws eks update-kubeconfig to generate a kubeconfig that authenticates via IAM — no separate certificates or tokens to manage.

🌐 DEEP DIVE: VPC CNI — Why Pods Get Real VPC IPs

The VPC CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin is what makes EKS networking unique. Unlike most K8s clusters that use an overlay network (e.g., Flannel, Calico), the VPC CNI assigns each Pod a real, routable VPC IP address from your subnet's CIDR range:

1
ENI Attachment

Each EC2 worker node has one or more Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) attached. Each ENI can hold multiple IP addresses — the number depends on the instance type (a t3.medium supports 3 ENIs × 6 IPs = 18 Pods).

2
Secondary IP Assignment

When a Pod is scheduled, the VPC CNI allocates a secondary private IP address from an ENI and assigns it to the Pod. This IP comes directly from your VPC subnet — no NAT, no overlay, no encapsulation.

3
Direct VPC Routing

Because Pods have real VPC IPs, they're directly routable within the VPC. The ALB can send traffic straight to a Pod's IP. Security Groups apply to Pods via Security Groups per Pod feature. AWS services see the Pod's actual IP in logs and flow logs.

📈
Prefix Delegation Mode

Default: each Pod consumes 1 secondary IP. Prefix delegation: assigns a /28 prefix (16 IPs) per ENI slot instead of 1 IP. A t3.medium goes from 18 Pods → ~50+ Pods. Critical for high-density workloads. Enable via ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION: "true" in the VPC CNI config.

🔒
Security Groups per Pod

Normally, all Pods on a node share the node's security groups. With Security Groups per Pod (enabled via VPC CNI add-on), each Pod can have its OWN security group — Pod A (anihpj) allows port 8000, Pod B (Redis) allows port 6379. Network-level Pod isolation without Network Policies.

20.3 Creating an EKS Cluster — Multiple Approaches

There are three paths to an EKS cluster, each suited to different stages of your journey. eksctl for speed, IaC for production, and the Console for exploration:

⚡ eksctl — One Command, Full Cluster (Dev/Prototyping)
eksctl — Single Command Cluster Creation
eksctl create cluster \
  --name anihpj-cluster \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --nodegroup-name workers \
  --node-type t3.medium \
  --nodes 3 \
  --nodes-min 2 \
  --nodes-max 6
✅
What It Creates

Control plane + managed node group + VPC (6 subnets across 3 AZs) + security groups + IAM roles + all mandatory add-ons. ~15 minutes from command to running cluster.

🎯
Best For

Getting started, development environments, learning, one-off experiments. Not for production — use IaC for repeatability and audit trail.

🏗️ IaC — CloudFormation / CDK / Terraform (Production)
CloudFormation — EKS Cluster Resource
Resources:
  EKSCluster:
    Type: AWS::EKS::Cluster
    Properties:
      Name: anihpj-cluster
      Version: "1.29"
      ResourcesVpcConfig:
        SubnetIds: !Ref PrivateSubnets
        EndpointPrivateAccess: true
        EndpointPublicAccess: false
📜
What It Gives You

Version-controlled infrastructure. Git commit = cluster state. Rollback = git revert. Audit trail of every change. Multi-environment: dev/staging/prod from same template with different parameters.

🎯
Best For

Production, team collaboration, compliance (SOC2, HIPAA), multi-account. CDK and Terraform approaches covered in Part 5 — same principles, different syntax.

🖥️ AWS Console — GUI Wizard (Exploration)

The EKS console provides a step-by-step wizard. Choose cluster name, K8s version, networking (VPC, subnets, endpoint access), logging (API, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler), and add-ons (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI). Best for: visually exploring options before writing IaC, one-off experiments where you don't need reproducibility. Not recommended for production — manual steps can't be versioned or reviewed.

eksctl Cluster Config — Production-Ready YAML
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig

metadata:
  name: anihpj-cluster
  region: us-east-1
  version: "1.29"

vpc:
  cidr: "10.0.0.0/16"
  subnets:
    private:
      us-east-1a: { cidr: "10.0.0.0/19" }
      us-east-1b: { cidr: "10.0.32.0/19" }
      us-east-1c: { cidr: "10.0.64.0/19" }
    public:
      us-east-1a: { cidr: "10.0.96.0/22" }
      us-east-1b: { cidr: "10.0.100.0/22" }
      us-east-1c: { cidr: "10.0.104.0/22" }

managedNodeGroups:
  - name: anihpj-workers
    instanceTypes: ["t3.medium", "t3a.medium"]
    desiredCapacity: 3
    minSize: 2
    maxSize: 10
    volumeSize: 50
    ssh:
      allow: false  # Use SSM Session Manager instead
    iam:
      withAddonPolicies:
        cloudWatch: true
        ebs: true
        efs: true

cloudWatch:
  clusterLogging:
    enableTypes: ["api", "audit", "authenticator", "controllerManager", "scheduler"]
🎯 Production EKS Checklist

1. Use private API endpoint (no public access). 2. Enable all control plane log types to CloudWatch. 3. Use Managed Node Groups for auto-patching. 4. Deploy across 3 AZs for HA. 5. Enable encryption with KMS for secrets. 6. Deploy Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter. 7. Set up IRSA for Pod-level IAM (not node-level). 8. Deploy AWS Load Balancer Controller for ingress.

🔄 DEEP DIVE: Managed Node Group Lifecycle — How Updates Actually Work

When you update a Managed Node Group (new AMI, new instance type, new K8s version), AWS orchestrates a rolling replacement that respects Pod availability:

1
New Launch Template Version Created

AWS creates a new Launch Template version with the updated configuration (new AMI ID, new user data). The old version remains for rollback. You never touch the Launch Template directly — EKS manages it.

2
Surge Node Launched

EKS launches a NEW EC2 instance with the updated configuration. This is called a surge node. The ASG temporarily exceeds maxSize by 1 to accommodate it. The new node runs the updated kubelet, container runtime, and AMI.

3
Old Node Cordoned & Drained

EKS cordons the OLDEST node (prevents new Pods), then drains it (evicts Pods gracefully). Pods reschedule on the new surge node and existing healthy nodes. PDBs are respected — if eviction would violate minAvailable, the drain waits or fails.

4
Old Node Terminated

Once all Pods are safely moved, the old EC2 instance is terminated. The ASG returns to desiredSize. EKS repeats steps 2-4 for each node in the group. The entire process runs serially — one node at a time — ensuring zero-downtime.

⚠️ Critical: MaxUnavailable Controls Speed vs Safety

Setting maxUnavailable: 2 allows EKS to update 2 nodes simultaneously — faster but riskier. Setting it to 1 (default) processes one node at a time — slower but safest. For production: keep maxUnavailable low and let the update run overnight during low-traffic hours. Always test in staging first.

🔌 EKS Add-ons — The Essential Components

EKS add-ons are pre-packaged software components managed through the EKS API. They extend the cluster with essential functionality:

Add-onTypeWhat It DoesWithout It...
VPC CNI🔴 MandatoryAssigns VPC IPs to Pods. Enables direct VPC routing, SG per Pod.Pods can't get IPs — cluster unusable
CoreDNS🔴 MandatoryInternal DNS: Pods resolve Service names to ClusterIPs.Service discovery broken — Pods can't find each other by name
kube-proxy🔴 MandatoryMaintains iptables/IPVS rules for Service → Pod traffic routing.Services don't work — no Pod-to-Service routing
AWS LB Controller🟡 RecommendedCreates ALB/NLB from Ingress/Service resources automatically.Must manually create load balancers — no K8s-native ingress
EBS CSI Driver🟡 RecommendedPersistent volumes backed by EBS (block storage).No persistent storage — Pods are stateless only
EFS CSI Driver🟢 OptionalShared file storage across multiple Pods/AZs (ReadWriteMany).No shared filesystem between Pods
CloudWatch Agent🟢 OptionalSends container logs and metrics to CloudWatch (Container Insights).Limited visibility — must use kubectl logs or third-party tools

20.4 EKS vs ECS vs Self-Managed K8s — Decision Guide

The AWS compute landscape offers three primary ways to run containers. Choosing the right one depends on your team's skills, scale, and requirements:

DimensionEKS (Managed K8s)ECS (AWS-Native)Self-Managed K8s on EC2
Control PlaneAWS managed, $0.10/hrFully managed, FREEYou manage, you pay for EC2
K8s EcosystemFull — Helm, Istio, ArgoCD, CRDsNone — AWS-onlyFull — identical to EKS
Learning CurveHigh (K8s knowledge required)Medium (ECS concepts)Very High (K8s + infra)
Multi-CloudPortable (K8s is K8s)AWS-onlyPortable, but you manage infra
Best ForMicroservices, platform teams, K8s shopsSimpler container workloads, AWS-native teamsSpecific hardware, custom networking, learning
anihpj Fit✅ Best: Django + Celery + Redis on K8s✅ Good: Simpler, but less flexible❌ Overkill for our use case
🧠 DEEP DIVE: EKS vs ECS — The Real Trade-off
☸️ Choose EKS When...
  • Your team already knows Kubernetes
  • You need Helm charts, CRDs, service mesh (Istio), GitOps (ArgoCD)
  • You want multi-cloud portability (EKS → AKS → GKE → on-prem)
  • You have multiple services that need K8s-native orchestration
  • You want the richest ecosystem of open-source tooling
🐳 Choose ECS When...
  • You want AWS-native simplicity — no K8s concepts to learn
  • You don't need Helm, Istio, or CRDs
  • Deepest integration with other AWS services
  • You want to run containers without managing any control plane
  • You're all-in on AWS and don't need multi-cloud portability
🚀 DEEP DIVE: EKS Fargate — Serverless Pods, No Nodes to Manage

EKS Fargate runs Pods directly on AWS Fargate — no EC2 worker nodes to provision, patch, or scale. Each Pod gets its own isolated micro-VM (Firecracker) with dedicated resources:

⚡
Zero Node Management

No ASG, no AMI patching, no node scaling decisions. You define a Fargate Profile that says "Pods in namespace X with label Y run on Fargate." AWS handles everything below the Pod level — the ultimate serverless K8s experience.

🔒
Pod-Level Isolation

Each Fargate Pod runs in its own dedicated micro-VM. No shared kernel between Pods — if one Pod is compromised, there's no neighbor to attack. This is stronger isolation than traditional containers sharing a kernel. Required for highly regulated workloads.

💡
When to Use Fargate

Great for: bursty workloads, dev/staging environments, batch jobs, isolated tenants. Not great for: DaemonSets (not supported), privileged containers, GPU workloads, workloads needing hostPath volumes. Fargate Pods also have vCPU/RAM limits (up to 16 vCPU / 120 GB).

Fargate Profile — Run anihpj Dev on Serverless
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
fargateProfiles:
- name: anihpj-dev
  selectors:
  - namespace: anihpj-dev
    labels:
      env: dev
# Pods in anihpj-dev with env=dev automatically run on Fargate
# No node group needed for dev workloads — pay per Pod per second

📝 Chapter 20 — Amazon EKS (10 Questions)

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q1

What components of Kubernetes does AWS manage in EKS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

AWS manages the control plane: API server, etcd (encrypted, auto-backup, 3-AZ HA), scheduler, and controller manager. You manage the data plane: worker nodes (EC2/Fargate), kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime, and CNI. The control plane runs in an AWS-managed VPC; you never SSH into it.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

How much does EKS cost for the control plane?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

$0.10 per hour per cluster (~$73/month). This flat fee covers: HA control plane across 3 AZs, managed etcd with automated backups, IAM integration, automatic K8s upgrades, and 24/7 support. Worker node costs (EC2 or Fargate) are additional and separate.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q3

What is the difference between Managed and Self-Managed Node Groups?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Managed Node Groups: AWS handles node provisioning, lifecycle (draining, termination, replacement), auto-scaling, and AMI updates. Self-Managed Node Groups: you create an ASG, choose the AMI, write the bootstrap script, and manage scaling/updates yourself. Managed = less ops; Self-managed = more control (custom AMIs, GPU instances, spot fleets).

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q4

What is eksctl and when should you use it?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

eksctl is the official EKS CLI tool. One command creates: control plane, node groups, VPC, subnets, security groups, IAM roles. Use it for: learning, development, one-off clusters, and prototyping. For production, use IaC (CloudFormation/CDK/Terraform) for repeatability and GitOps.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q5

How does EKS handle authentication differently from a self-managed K8s cluster?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

EKS integrates with AWS IAM for cluster authentication. Instead of client certificates or bearer tokens, you use aws eks update-kubeconfig which generates a kubeconfig that authenticates via aws-iam-authenticator (or the aws CLI). The aws-auth ConfigMap maps IAM users/roles to K8s RBAC groups. No separate certificate authority to manage.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q6

What are the three EKS API endpoint access modes?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

1. Public: accessible from the internet. 2. Public + Private: accessible from both the internet and within VPC. 3. Private only: accessible only from within your VPC (requires VPN/Direct Connect for remote access). Production best practice: Private only.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q7

How does the VPC CNI plugin work in EKS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The VPC CNI plugin assigns each Pod a real VPC IP address (from the ENI's secondary IP pool) rather than an overlay network IP. This means: Pods are directly routable within the VPC, security groups apply to Pods, and AWS services see the Pod's actual VPC IP. The trade-off: limited Pods per node (based on ENI secondary IP count). Use prefix delegation mode to increase Pod density.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q8

When would you choose EKS over ECS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Choose EKS when: (1) your team already knows K8s, (2) you need Helm charts, CRDs, service mesh (Istio), or GitOps (ArgoCD), (3) you want multi-cloud portability, (4) you need the full K8s open-source ecosystem. Choose ECS when you want simpler, AWS-native container orchestration without learning Kubernetes.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q9

What is the aws-auth ConfigMap and why is it critical?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The aws-auth ConfigMap in the kube-system namespace maps IAM users and roles to K8s RBAC groups. Without it, no IAM principal can access the cluster (except the cluster creator). If you delete or corrupt this ConfigMap, you lose all access to the cluster — only the AWS account root user can recover it.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q10

How do you update the Kubernetes version on an EKS cluster?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

EKS supports in-place version upgrades: (1) Update the control plane via AWS Console/CLI/IaC — takes ~10-15 minutes, no downtime. (2) Update each node group to the new AMI version — can be done with rolling updates. Rules: you can only upgrade one minor version at a time (1.28 → 1.29, not 1.28 → 1.30 directly). Always upgrade the control plane first, then node groups.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Networking. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Chapter 21: Deploying anihpj to EKS — Complete Walkthrough

This chapter takes you from a working EKS cluster to a fully deployed anihpj application. You'll push images to ECR, configure secrets with AWS Secrets Manager, deploy the full Kubernetes stack, and expose it via ALB Ingress — every step with production best practices.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~4 hours 🎯 Domain 1: SDLC 22% 📝 10 Questions

21.1 Preparation — Before You Deploy

Before deploying anihpj to EKS, ensure these prerequisites are in place. Each item is a gate — if any is missing, the deployment will fail:

1 ECR Repository Created
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name anihpj --region us-east-1

The ECR repository stores your Docker images. EKS pulls from here when creating Pods. Enable image scanning and immutable tags for security.

2 Docker Image Built & Pushed
docker build -t anihpj:v1.0 .
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker tag anihpj:v1.0 ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
docker push ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0

Tag with semantic version (v1.0), not latest. The image must be in ECR before the Pod spec references it.

3 EKS Cluster Running & kubectl Configured
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name anihpj-cluster --region us-east-1
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes  # Should show 3+ nodes in Ready state

Verify the cluster is accessible and nodes are Ready. If kubectl get nodes shows no resources, your kubeconfig isn't pointing to the right cluster.

4 AWS Load Balancer Controller Installed
helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \
  -n kube-system --set clusterName=anihpj-cluster

This controller watches for Ingress resources and automatically provisions ALBs/NLBs. Without it, Ingress resources stay in pending state forever.

21.2 Push Image to ECR — The Complete Flow

ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is your private Docker registry on AWS. Every EKS Pod pulls its image from ECR — here's the full push flow with security best practices:

Complete ECR Push Workflow
# 1. Authenticate Docker to ECR
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin \
  ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

# 2. Build multi-stage Docker image (from s3-5)
docker build -t anihpj:v1.0 -t anihpj:latest .

# 3. Tag for ECR
docker tag anihpj:v1.0 ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
docker tag anihpj:latest ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:latest

# 4. Push both tags
docker push ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
docker push ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:latest

# 5. Verify image exists
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name anihpj --region us-east-1
🔍
Image Scanning

ECR scans images for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). Enable on push: imageScanOnPush: true. Review findings in ECR console or via aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings.

🏷️
Immutable Tags

Enable imageTagMutability: IMMUTABLE to prevent overwriting tags. This ensures v1.0 always points to the exact same image — critical for deterministic rollbacks.

📜
Lifecycle Policies

Auto-clean old images to save costs. Example: keep last 10 images, expire untagged images after 7 days. Set via ECR lifecycle policy rules.

21.3 Create Namespace, ConfigMap & Secrets

Organize anihpj resources into their own namespace with resource quotas, and configure application settings via ConfigMap and Secrets:

Namespace + Resource Quota + ConfigMap
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod

---
# Resource Quota — prevent runaway resource usage
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: anihpj-quota
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
    pods: "20"

---
# ConfigMap — non-sensitive configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-config
  namespace: anihpj-prod
data:
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "anihpj.settings"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "anihpj.example.com,anihpj-prod.ALB_ID.elb.amazonaws.com"
  DEBUG: "False"
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"

---
# Secret — sensitive data (use AWS Secrets Manager + External Secrets for production!)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-secret
  namespace: anihpj-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  SECRET_KEY: "django-insecure-CHANGE-ME-in-production-use-secrets-manager"
  DB_PASSWORD: "anihpj-db-password"
  DB_HOST: "anihpj-rds.CLUSTER_ID.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com"
🔐 Production Secret Management

For production, never store secrets directly in K8s Secret YAML. Use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager: create an ExternalSecret CRD that maps Secrets Manager entries to K8s Secrets. The operator auto-refreshes secrets and rotates them according to Secrets Manager's rotation schedule. IRSA is required so the operator can access Secrets Manager.

🔐 DEEP DIVE: External Secrets Operator — Complete Setup

The External Secrets Operator (ESO) is the production-standard way to get AWS Secrets Manager secrets into Kubernetes. Here's the full setup:

1 Install ESO via Helm
helm repo add external-secrets https://charts.external-secrets.io
helm install external-secrets external-secrets/external-secrets \
  -n external-secrets --create-namespace

Creates the ESO controller, CRDs (SecretStore, ExternalSecret), and RBAC. The controller watches for ExternalSecret resources and syncs them.

2 Create SecretStore (AWS Provider)
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secretsmanager
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: eso-sa  # IRSA-enabled SA

The SecretStore defines HOW to authenticate to AWS. Here we use IRSA via a ServiceAccount. The eso-sa SA must be annotated with an IAM role that has secretsmanager:GetSecretValue.

3 Create ExternalSecret (Map AWS → K8s)
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-secrets
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secretsmanager
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: anihpj-secret  # K8s Secret to create/update
  data:
  - secretKey: SECRET_KEY
    remoteRef:
      key: anihpj/django
      property: secret_key
  - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD
    remoteRef:
      key: anihpj/db
      property: password

ESO now continuously syncs: every hour (refreshInterval: 1h) it fetches the latest values from Secrets Manager and updates the K8s Secret anihpj-secret. The Deployment references this Secret — no code changes needed. If a secret rotates in Secrets Manager, ESO updates the K8s Secret within 1 hour (configurable).

🗄️ RDS PostgreSQL Setup for anihpj

anihpj needs a production database. RDS PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ) is the managed choice — AWS handles backups, patching, and failover:

1 Provision RDS — Private, Encrypted, Multi-AZ
CloudFormation — RDS for anihpj
Resources:
  AnihpjDB:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.medium
      Engine: postgres
      EngineVersion: "16.3"
      MultiAZ: true
      StorageEncrypted: true
      StorageType: gp3
      AllocatedStorage: "50"
      BackupRetentionPeriod: 35
      DeletionProtection: true
      VPCSecurityGroups:
        - !Ref EKSNodeSG
      DBSubnetGroupName: !Ref PrivateSubnetGroup
🔒
Network Isolation

SG allows PostgreSQL (5432) only from EKS node SG. No public IP. Deployed in private subnets — reachable only from within the VPC.

🔄
Multi-AZ Failover

Synchronous standby in different AZ. Primary fails → DNS flips (60-120s). No data loss. Django reconnects via connection pool automatically.

📅
Automated Backups

Daily snapshots + continuous transaction logs. Point-in-time recovery to any second within 35 days. Snapshots in S3 (11 nines durability).

2 Store Credentials in Secrets Manager
AWS Secrets Manager — anihpj/db Secret
{
  "host": "anihpj.CLUSTER.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com",
  "port": 5432,
  "dbname": "anihpj",
  "username": "anihpj_admin",
  "password": "CHANGE-ME-auto-generated"
}

Never hardcode credentials. Secrets Manager: auto-rotation (Lambda, every 30 days), CloudTrail audit, KMS encryption at rest. External Secrets Operator syncs to K8s Secret — credentials never touch YAML files.

3 Connect Django to RDS — TLS & Connection Pooling
settings.py — Production Database Config
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'NAME': os.environ.get('DB_NAME', 'anihpj'),
        'USER': os.environ.get('DB_USER', 'anihpj_admin'),
        'PASSWORD': os.environ.get('DB_PASSWORD'),
        'HOST': os.environ.get('DB_HOST'),
        'PORT': os.environ.get('DB_PORT', '5432'),
        'CONN_MAX_AGE': 300,  # Persistent connections (5 min)
        'OPTIONS': {'sslmode': 'require'},  # Enforce TLS
    }
}
🔗
Connection Pooling

CONN_MAX_AGE: 300 keeps DB connections open 5 min. Without it, Django opens a new connection per request — crushing RDS. High traffic: add PgBouncer sidecar.

🔐
TLS Enforcement

sslmode: require encrypts all Django→RDS traffic. RDS natively supports TLS 1.2/1.3. Defense in depth: encrypt even within private networks.

21.4 Deploy anihpj with kubectl — Full Stack

Here's the complete Kubernetes Deployment for anihpj, with all production best practices: health checks, resource limits, security context, and rolling update strategy:

anihpj Deployment — Production-Ready
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    tier: backend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa  # IRSA
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: anihpj-config
        - secretRef:
            name: anihpj-secret
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5

---
# ClusterIP Service — internal access only
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-svc
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
  type: ClusterIP
💓
Health Checks

Liveness probe: restarts the container if it becomes unhealthy (crash loop). Readiness probe: removes Pod from Service endpoints if not ready (don't send traffic to unready Pods). Both are essential for zero-downtime deployments.

📊
Resource Requests & Limits

Requests: minimum guaranteed resources (scheduler uses this to place Pods). Limits: hard cap — Pod gets throttled or OOM-killed if exceeded. Setting both prevents noisy-neighbor problems.

🔒
Security Context

runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser: 1000 ensure the container never runs as root. If an attacker compromises the container, they can't escape to the host. Enforced cluster-wide via Pod Security Standards.

21.5 Expose with ALB Ingress

The AWS Load Balancer Controller automatically provisions an Application Load Balancer when you create an Ingress resource. Here's how to expose anihpj via HTTPS with automatic TLS termination:

ALB Ingress for anihpj
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:ACCOUNT:certificate/CERT-ID
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /health/
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: anihpj-alb
spec:
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-svc
            port:
              number: 8000
User Request Flow

https://anihpj.example.com/ → Route 53 → ALB (TLS termination, ACM cert) → Target Group (IP mode) → anihpj Pod (10.0.x.x:8000). End-to-end encrypted: HTTPS user→ALB, HTTP ALB→Pod (within VPC, considered trusted).

Path-Based Routing

Add multiple path rules: / → anihpj Django app, /static/ → S3 + CloudFront (for serving static files), /api/ → separate API service. One ALB can route to multiple backend services based on URL path.

21.6 Verify Everything — Testing Your Deployment

After deploying, verify that every component works correctly. Here's the complete verification checklist:

1 Check Pods are Running & Healthy
Pod Health Verification
kubectl get all -n anihpj-prod
kubectl describe pod -n anihpj-prod -l app=anihpj
kubectl logs -f deployment/anihpj -n anihpj-prod
✅
Healthy: Running

All 3 Pods show READY 1/1, STATUS Running, RESTARTS 0. Gunicorn logs show "Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8000".

🔄
CrashLoopBackOff

Pod crashes in a loop. Run kubectl logs POD --previous for crash reason. Common: missing ConfigMap/Secret keys, DB unreachable, wrong image.

⏳
Pending

Pod can't schedule. Run kubectl describe pod → Events. Common: insufficient CPU/memory, PVC unbound, affinity rules can't be satisfied.

2 Verify Ingress & ALB Provisioning
Ingress Status & ALB Check
kubectl get ingress -n anihpj-prod --watch
# ADDRESS column → ALB DNS (takes 2-3 min on first creation)
kubectl describe ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj-prod
curl -k https://ALB-DNS-NAME/jobs/
502
502 Bad Gateway

ALB can't reach Pods. Check: health check path (/health/), target group healthy targets, Pod readiness probe passing. ALB only routes to healthy targets.

404
404 Not Found

ALB works but routing wrong. Check: Ingress path rules, Django URL patterns. Use kubectl port-forward to test Pod directly without ALB.

3 Run Django Migrations (Kubernetes Job)
Migration Job — Run BEFORE Deployment Update
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: anihpj-migrate
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  backoffLimit: 3
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 300
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef: {name: anihpj-config}
        - secretRef: {name: anihpj-secret}

Applies schema changes once, then exits. backoffLimit: 3 retries on DB connection failures. Verify: kubectl logs job/anihpj-migrate -n anihpj-prod — should show "Applying migrations... OK".

4 Static Files — Init Container + S3/CloudFront
Init Container — collectstatic Before Main App
initContainers:
- name: collectstatic
  image: ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
  command: ["python", "manage.py", "collectstatic", "--noinput"]
  envFrom:
  - configMapRef: {name: anihpj-config}
  volumeMounts:
  - name: static-files
    mountPath: /app/staticfiles
# django-storages → S3 → CloudFront for global edge caching

Init Containers run before the main app, in sequence, must succeed. If collectstatic fails, main container never starts — no stale files served. Production: django-storages uploads to S3, CloudFront caches at 600+ edge locations.

5 End-to-End Smoke Test — Full Stack
Full-Stack API Validation
# GET — verify read path
curl -s https://anihpj.example.com/jobs/ | jq .
# Expected: []

# POST — verify write path (ALB→Ingress→Svc→Pod→Django→RDS)
curl -s -X POST https://anihpj.example.com/jobs/ \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"DevOps Engineer","company":"AWS","location":"Remote"}' | jq .
# Expected: 201 Created

# GET again — verify persistence
curl -s https://anihpj.example.com/jobs/ | jq .
# Expected: [{"id":1,"title":"DevOps Engineer",...}]
✅
All Systems Go

GET 200 + POST 201 + GET again confirms: ALB → Ingress Controller → Service → Pod → Django ORM → RDS → and back. All 7 layers verified end-to-end.

🔍
Debug: Port Forward Bypass

If ALB fails but Pods are Running: kubectl port-forward -n anihpj-prod deploy/anihpj 8000:8000 then curl localhost:8000/jobs/. If this works, the issue is in Ingress/ALB config, not the app.

Q1

What must be done before a Pod can pull an image from ECR?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The Pod's node (or the Pod itself via IRSA) must have IAM permissions to call ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchGetImage, and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer. With IRSA, the Pod's Service Account is annotated with an IAM role that has these permissions. Without IRSA, the node's instance profile needs them.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

What's the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Liveness probe: "Is the container alive?" If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. Use for detecting deadlocks or crashes. Readiness probe: "Is the container ready to serve traffic?" If it fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from Service endpoints. Use for warm-up periods or when a dependency (like DB) is temporarily unavailable.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q3

How does the AWS Load Balancer Controller provision an ALB?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The controller watches for Kubernetes Ingress resources with kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb. It creates an AWS ALB, Target Group, and Listener Rules based on the Ingress annotations and spec. Target type ip means Pod IPs are registered directly (VPC CNI makes this possible). The controller also manages the lifecycle: deleting the Ingress deletes the ALB.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q4

Why use a ResourceQuota in the anihpj namespace?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

ResourceQuota prevents a single application from consuming all cluster resources. Without it, a bug (memory leak) or misconfigured HPA could starve other applications. Quotas set hard limits on CPU, memory, and Pod count per namespace — protecting cluster-wide stability and enforcing multi-tenancy.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q5

What happens if you set replicas: 3 and one node fails?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Kubernetes detects the node is NotReady (via kubelet heartbeat). After a timeout (~5 minutes), it marks the Pods on that node for deletion and the Deployment controller creates replacement Pods on healthy nodes. With anti-affinity rules, Pods are spread across AZs — a single AZ failure means only 1 Pod (of 3) is affected.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q6

How do you handle Django database migrations during deployment?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Run migrations as a Kubernetes Job before the Deployment update: create a Job that runs python manage.py migrate --noinput with backoffLimit: 3 and ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 300. The Job runs once, applies schema changes, and exits. Only after the Job succeeds should you proceed with the Deployment rollout. Use Helm hooks or ArgoCD sync waves to orchestrate this order.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q7

What is the advantage of ALB Ingress over a NodePort Service?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

ALB Ingress: layer 7 routing (path-based, host-based), TLS termination at the ALB, WAF integration, built-in health checks, automatic DNS via Route 53 alias. NodePort: layer 4 only, exposes a port on every node (30000-32767), no TLS termination, no path-based routing. ALB Ingress is the production standard for HTTP/HTTPS workloads on EKS.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q8

Why use External Secrets Operator instead of storing secrets directly in K8s?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

K8s Secrets are only base64-encoded (not encrypted at rest by default). External Secrets Operator syncs from AWS Secrets Manager, which provides: automatic secret rotation via Lambda, audit trail via CloudTrail, fine-grained IAM access control, and cross-account sharing. If a secret rotates in Secrets Manager, the operator auto-updates the K8s Secret — no Pod restart needed if the app reads from the filesystem.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q9

What does maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0 mean in a RollingUpdate?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

maxSurge: 1: during the rollout, Kubernetes can create 1 extra Pod above the desired replica count. With 3 replicas, you'll temporarily have 4 Pods (3 old + 1 new). maxUnavailable: 0: no existing Pods can be taken down until new Pods are Ready. Combined: zero-downtime rollout — capacity is never below the desired count.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Storage. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q10

How do you troubleshoot a Pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

1. kubectl logs POD_NAME -n anihpj-prod --previous — checks the crashed container's logs. 2. kubectl describe pod POD_NAME — look at Events section for OOMKilled, ImagePullBackOff, or FailedMount. 3. Check if ConfigMap/Secret references exist and have correct keys. 4. Verify the image exists in ECR and the node has pull permissions. 5. Try kubectl run --rm -it debug --image=busybox -- sh to debug network/DNS issues from within the cluster.

Chapter 22: EKS Scaling & Availability

Scaling on EKS happens at two levels: Pods scale horizontally via HPA, and nodes scale via Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter. Together they ensure your application always has the right capacity — no more, no less — automatically.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 Domain 3: Resiliency 15% 📝 10 Questions

22.1 Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) automatically scales the number of Pod replicas based on observed CPU, memory, or custom metrics. It's the first line of defense against traffic spikes:

📈 HPA — Metrics → Decision → Scale

The HPA continuously watches your Pods and makes scaling decisions based on actual usage. Here's the complete pipeline from metric to new Pod:

1 Metrics Collection — The Input
Install Metrics Server on EKS
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
kubectl top pods -n anihpj-prod  # Verify: shows CPU/Memory per Pod

The Metrics Server is NOT installed by default on EKS — you must deploy it manually. It scrapes CPU and memory usage from each Pod via the kubelet's summary API every 15 seconds. For custom metrics (request rate, queue depth, SQS messages), connect HPA to CloudWatch, Prometheus, or any external metrics adapter.

📊
Resource Metrics

CPU + Memory per Pod. Requires Metrics Server. Built-in, simplest to use. averageUtilization: 60 means scale when average Pod CPU hits 60% of request.

📈
Custom Metrics

Any metric from your apps: HTTP requests/sec, active WebSocket connections, queue depth. Requires Prometheus Adapter or CloudWatch adapter. More relevant than CPU for many workloads.

🌐
External Metrics

Metrics from AWS services: SQS queue depth, ALB request count, DynamoDB consumed capacity. Requires CloudWatch metrics adapter. Perfect for event-driven scaling.

2 HPA Calculation — The Decision

Every 15 seconds, the HPA controller evaluates the formula:

🧮 The HPA Formula

desiredReplicas = ⌈ currentReplicas × (currentMetricValue ÷ targetMetricValue) ⌉

📈
Example: Scale Up

3 Pods running at 85% CPU, HPA target = 50%
ceil(3 × 85/50) = ceil(5.1) = 6 Pods
HPA increases replicas from 3 → 6. Traffic spike handled.

📉
Example: Scale Down

6 Pods running at 10% CPU, HPA target = 50%
ceil(6 × 10/50) = ceil(1.2) = 2 Pods
But minReplicas: 3 prevents going below 3 — HPA respects your minimum.

🧠 Multiple Metrics: HPA Picks the HIGHEST

If you define both CPU (target 60%) and memory (target 75%) metrics, HPA calculates desired replicas for EACH and picks the highest number. CPU says 6 Pods, memory says 4 Pods → HPA scales to 6. This ensures you never violate ANY metric threshold — the most constrained metric wins.

3 Scale Action — The Execution

HPA updates the Deployment's spec.replicas field. The Deployment controller creates or terminates Pods to match. HPA enforces cooldown windows to prevent flapping:

⬆️
Scale-Up Cooldown

Default: 3 minutes between scale-up events. If a traffic spike lasts 10 seconds, HPA won't overreact. The stabilizationWindowSeconds (default 60s for scale-up) looks at the highest recommendation in the window — preventing thrashing.

⬇️
Scale-Down Cooldown

Default: 5 minutes between scale-down events. A brief dip in traffic won't immediately kill Pods. The stabilization window (default 300s) uses the highest recommendation, so HPA waits for sustained low usage before scaling down.

HPA for anihpj — CPU + Memory Based
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hpa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 75
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300  # Wait 5 min before scaling down
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60   # React quickly to spikes
📐 DEEP DIVE: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) — Right-Size Your Pods

While HPA scales the NUMBER of Pods (horizontal), VPA adjusts the SIZE of existing Pods — changing CPU and memory requests/limits based on actual usage. Used together, HPA handles traffic spikes and VPA prevents over-provisioning:

📊
Recommender

Watches Pod resource usage over time and calculates optimal CPU/memory requests. If a Pod's container requests 500m CPU but only uses 50m, VPA recommends lowering to 100m — saving cluster capacity for other workloads.

🔄
Updater

Evicts Pods that need resizing so they restart with new resource settings. Respects PDBs — won't evict if it would violate minAvailable. Works with RollingUpdate: evicts one Pod at a time, waits for it to be Ready, then evicts the next.

🚫
Admission Controller

Intercepts new Pod creation and adjusts their resource requests to VPA's recommendation. This catches Pods created by Deployments, Jobs, and StatefulSets before they're scheduled with wrong values.

⚠️ VPA + HPA: Use Together, But Carefully

VPA and HPA can conflict if both scale based on CPU. Best practice: VPA scales based on memory (which HPA doesn't handle well), and HPA scales based on CPU or custom metrics. Never use VPA with CPU target if HPA also uses CPU — they'll fight each other. For production: enable VPA in "Recommend only" mode first, review its suggestions, then enable auto-update.

22.2 Cluster Autoscaler (CA) — Node-Level Scaling

HPA scales Pods, but what if there's no node with enough capacity? The Cluster Autoscaler watches for pending Pods and adds nodes to accommodate them:

⚠️ Without Cluster Autoscaler
  • HPA creates 2 new Pods → Pods stuck in Pending state
  • kubectl describe pod shows: "0/3 nodes are available: insufficient cpu"
  • Application is under-provisioned during traffic spike
  • Manual intervention required: resize node group, wait, then Pods schedule
✅ With Cluster Autoscaler
  • CA detects Pending Pods → calculates that adding one t3.medium node will satisfy them
  • CA calls AWS ASG API: increase DesiredCapacity by 1
  • New EC2 instance launches (~2 min), joins cluster, Pods schedule
  • Fully automatic: no human intervention, no alert fatigue
Cluster Autoscaler Deployment on EKS
helm repo add autoscaler https://kubernetes.github.io/autoscaler
helm install cluster-autoscaler autoscaler/cluster-autoscaler \
  --set autoDiscovery.clusterName=anihpj-cluster \
  --set awsRegion=us-east-1 \
  --set rbac.serviceAccount.create=true

22.3 Karpenter — Just-in-Time Nodes

Karpenter is the next-generation node autoscaler for EKS, built by AWS. Unlike Cluster Autoscaler (which works at the ASG level), Karpenter provisions individual EC2 instances directly — faster, more flexible, and cost-optimized:

DimensionCluster AutoscalerKarpenter
Provisioning SpeedMinutes (ASG scale-out)Seconds (direct EC2 launch)
Instance SelectionFixed instance type in ASGIntelligent: picks best instance from 500+ types
Spot OptimizationMixed instances policyNative spot-first with fallback to on-demand
ConsolidationNoYes — replaces underutilized nodes with fewer/smaller ones
Node TerminationASG scale-in (random instance)Targeted: removes least-utilized nodes first
Best ForSimplicity, existing ASG setupsCost optimization, high-scale, dynamic workloads
🚀 Karpenter for anihpj

Karpenter would automatically: choose t3a.medium (cheaper AMD equivalent) over t3.medium, use spot instances for dev/staging with on-demand fallback, consolidate 3 underutilized t3.medium nodes into 2 t3.small nodes after a traffic dip, and add GPU instances (g4dn) only if a resume-parsing batch job requests GPUs — then terminate them immediately after. This is the future of EKS scaling.

22.4 Multi-AZ High Availability

For production, anihpj must survive the loss of an entire Availability Zone. Here's the HA architecture:

💰 DEEP DIVE: Spot Instances for EKS — 60-90% Cost Savings

Spot Instances let you bid on unused EC2 capacity at massive discounts. For fault-tolerant workloads (dev/staging, batch processing, stateless web Pods), they're a game-changer for cost optimization:

1
Spot Interruption Notice (2-Minute Warning)

AWS sends a 2-minute interruption notice via EC2 metadata and EventBridge when it needs the capacity back. The AWS Node Termination Handler (DaemonSet on each node) detects this notice and immediately cordons the node (no new Pods scheduled).

2
Graceful Pod Drain

The Termination Handler drains all Pods: sends SIGTERM, waits for terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s), then force-kills. Pods on OTHER nodes are already handling traffic. If using Karpenter, a replacement node (possibly on-demand) is provisioned simultaneously.

3
Mixed Instance Policies

Configure your ASG/Karpenter with multiple instance types and purchase options: 60% spot + 40% on-demand. If spot capacity is reclaimed, on-demand instances absorb the load. Karpenter can intelligently diversify across instance types and AZs to minimize interruption risk.

✅ Good for Spot
  • Stateless web Pods (anihpj with 3+ replicas across AZs)
  • CI/CD build jobs (CodeBuild runners)
  • Dev/staging environments (can tolerate interruptions)
  • Batch processing (resumable)
❌ NOT for Spot
  • Stateful workloads (databases) without replication
  • Single-replica critical services
  • Real-time processing with strict latency SLAs
  • Production primary workloads without on-demand fallback
📐
Pod Anti-Affinity
affinity:
  podAntiAffinity:
    requiredDuringScheduling:
    - labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone

Forces Pods to be scheduled in DIFFERENT AZs. With 3 replicas across 3 AZs: lose one AZ, you lose 1 Pod, 2 remain serving traffic.

🗄️
RDS Multi-AZ

RDS Multi-AZ deployment maintains a synchronous standby in a different AZ. If the primary fails, RDS auto-failovers (1-2 min). anihpj Django reconnects automatically. No data loss — synchronous replication.

⚖️
ALB Cross-Zone LB

ALB distributes traffic across all AZs equally. If one AZ has no healthy targets (Pod crashed), ALB stops routing to it. Combine with health checks: ALB detects unhealthy Pods in seconds.

🛡️ DEEP DIVE: Pod Disruption Budgets — Protecting Pods During Voluntary Disruptions

A Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) limits how many Pods can be simultaneously unavailable during voluntary disruptions — node drains, rolling updates, cluster autoscaler scale-in. PDBs do NOT protect against involuntary disruptions (node crash, AZ failure).

📏
PDB: minAvailable
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pdb
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj

"At least 2 Pods must always be running." With 3 replicas, only 1 can be disrupted at a time. If a node drain would drop below 2, the drain command blocks until another Pod is Ready elsewhere.

📊
PDB: maxUnavailable
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pdb
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj

"At most 1 Pod can be unavailable at any time." Useful when you don't know the exact replica count (HPA varies it). The PDB adapts: with 10 Pods, 1 unavailable = 90% available. With 3 Pods, 1 unavailable = 67% available.

⚠️ PDB Gotchas

1. A PDB with minAvailable: 3 and only 3 replicas makes node drains impossible — the eviction API blocks forever because it can never satisfy the budget. 2. PDBs don't apply to involuntary disruptions — if a node crashes, Pods are gone regardless of PDB. 3. Cluster Autoscaler respects PDBs — it won't scale-in a node if Pod eviction would violate the budget. Karpenter has similar logic.

Q1

What metrics can HPA use to scale Pods?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

HPA supports resource metrics (CPU, memory — requires Metrics Server), custom metrics (any metric from CloudWatch, Prometheus, Datadog), and external metrics (SQS queue depth, number of connected users). You can define multiple metrics — HPA scales to the highest calculated replica count.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

What happens if HPA creates more Pods but nodes are full?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

New Pods remain in Pending state with the reason "insufficient cpu/memory." This triggers the Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter), which provisions a new node. Once the node joins the cluster, the scheduler assigns the pending Pods to it. Without CA/Karpenter, Pods stay Pending indefinitely — the HPA can't fix node-level capacity.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q3

Karpenter vs Cluster Autoscaler — which provisions faster?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Karpenter is significantly faster: it launches EC2 instances directly (seconds) rather than going through ASG scale-out (minutes). Karpenter also selects the optimal instance type from 500+ options based on Pod requirements, while CA is locked to whatever instance types the ASG defines.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q4

How does podAntiAffinity help with high availability?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Pod anti-affinity with topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone ensures that no two Pods with the same labels are scheduled in the same AZ. If one AZ fails, only the Pod(s) in that AZ are affected — Pods in other AZs continue serving. This is the K8s-native way to achieve AZ-level fault tolerance.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q5

What is the stabilization window in HPA behavior?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The stabilization window prevents HPA from "flapping" (rapidly scaling up and down). scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 means HPA looks at the last 5 minutes of metrics and uses the HIGHEST recommendation — it won't scale down during a brief traffic dip. For scale-up, a shorter window (60s) ensures HPA reacts quickly to real spikes.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q6

How does Karpenter handle spot instance interruptions?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Karpenter watches for the spot interruption notice (2 minutes before termination). It immediately cordons the affected node, drains Pods gracefully, and provisions a replacement node — potentially on-demand if no spot capacity is available. Pods are rescheduled on the new node before the spot instance is terminated.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q7

What is the difference between HPA and VPA?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

HPA: scales the NUMBER of Pods (horizontal scaling). Adds more replicas when traffic increases. VPA: adjusts the SIZE of existing Pods (vertical scaling) — changes CPU/memory requests and limits. VPA requires Pod restart. Use both: VPA right-sizes resource requests, HPA handles traffic fluctuations. They complement each other.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q8

How do you ensure zero-downtime during node termination?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

1. Node is cordoned (no new Pods schedule on it). 2. Pods are drained gracefully: SIGTERM sent, Pod has terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s) to finish requests and shut down. 3. Pod is removed from Service endpoints (readiness probe fails or Pod terminates). 4. New Pods on other nodes are already running and handling traffic. 5. Node is terminated. Managed Node Groups + Karpenter automate all of this.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q9

What happens when RDS Multi-AZ fails over?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

The RDS DNS endpoint stays the same — it now points to the standby instance (promoted to primary). Failover takes 60-120 seconds. During this window: Django returns database connection errors. After failover: Django reconnects automatically (connection pool detects broken connections). No data loss — synchronous replication ensures the standby is up-to-date.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q10

What is the recommended PodDisruptionBudget for anihpj with 3 replicas?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

A PDB with minAvailable: 2 ensures at least 2 Pods are always running, even during voluntary disruptions (node drains, rolling updates). This means: Kubernetes can only evict 1 Pod at a time. With anti-affinity across AZs and 2/3 Pods always available, you survive both voluntary disruptions AND single-AZ failures.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — EKS Scaling. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Chapter 23: EKS Security — Defense in Depth

Security on EKS follows a layered approach: IAM (who can access the cluster), RBAC (what they can do inside), Network Policies (Pod-to-Pod communication), Pod Security (what Pods are allowed to do), and Encryption (protecting data at rest). Each layer is an independent security control.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 Domain 5: Security & Compliance 17% 📝 10 Questions

23.1 IRSA — Pod-Level IAM (Revisited)

IRSA was covered in depth in Chapter 10.4. On EKS, IRSA is THE way to grant AWS permissions to Pods. Quick recap with an EKS-specific deployment example:

IRSA for anihpj — S3 + DynamoDB Access
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/anihpj-app-role
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa  # Pods get IAM role credentials

23.2 RBAC for EKS — Role-Based Access Control

Kubernetes RBAC controls what users and ServiceAccounts can do INSIDE the cluster. Combined with IAM (which controls who can authenticate), RBAC defines the authorization layer:

RBAC — Developer Role for anihpj Namespace
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  name: anihpj-developer
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log", "services", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update", "patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  name: anihpj-developer-binding
subjects:
- kind: Group
  name: anihpj-developers  # Mapped from IAM via aws-auth ConfigMap
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: anihpj-developer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

23.3 Network Policies — Pod-to-Pod Firewall

By default, all Pods in a Kubernetes cluster can communicate with each other. Network Policies restrict this — defining exactly which Pods can talk to which:

Network Policy — anihpj Isolation
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-netpol
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: ingress-nginx
    ports:
    - port: 8000
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: redis
    ports:
    - port: 6379
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - port: 5432

This policy says: anihpj Pods can ONLY receive traffic from the ingress controller on port 8000, and can ONLY send traffic to Redis (port 6379) and PostgreSQL (port 5432). Everything else is denied — defense in depth at the network layer.

🗺️ DEEP DIVE: The aws-auth ConfigMap — IAM to K8s RBAC Bridge

The aws-auth ConfigMap in kube-system is the critical piece that connects AWS IAM identities to Kubernetes RBAC. Without it, only the cluster creator can access the cluster:

aws-auth ConfigMap — Complete Example
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: aws-auth
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  mapRoles: |
    # Map IAM Role → K8s RBAC Group
    - rolearn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/eks-admin-role
      username: admin
      groups:
        - system:masters       # Full cluster admin
    - rolearn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/anihpj-developer-role
      username: developer
      groups:
        - anihpj-developers   # Maps to K8s RoleBinding
    - rolearn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/eks-readonly-role
      username: readonly
      groups:
        - view-only           # Built-in K8s view ClusterRole
  mapUsers: |
    # Map IAM User → K8s RBAC Group (use roles, not users!)
    - userarn: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:user/breakglass
      username: breakglass
      groups:
        - system:masters
🎭
mapRoles (Preferred)

Maps IAM Roles to K8s groups. Always use roles over users — roles have temporary credentials, no access keys to leak. The cluster creator's role is permanently stored in the cluster's identity — it survives aws-auth deletion.

👤
mapUsers (Avoid)

Maps IAM Users with long-lived access keys. Avoid for production — use SSO/IAM Identity Center with Roles instead. Only exception: emergency break-glass user for disaster recovery.

⚠️
Recovery if Deleted

If aws-auth is deleted or corrupted: 1. Only the cluster creator can still access (their identity is baked into the cluster). 2. The creator edits aws-auth via kubectl edit -n kube-system configmap/aws-auth. 3. If the creator also loses access: only AWS Support can recover the cluster.

23.4 Pod Security Standards (PSS)

Pod Security Standards replace the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy. They define three profiles — Privileged, Baseline, Restricted — that control what Pods can do at the security level:

🔓
Privileged

Unrestricted. Allows: hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged containers, hostPath volumes. Use for: system components (kube-proxy, CNI plugins). Never for application Pods.

🔒
Baseline

Prevents known privilege escalations. Blocks: hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged containers, hostPath. Use for: most application workloads. This is the minimum acceptable standard.

🔐
Restricted

Hardened. Requires: non-root user, read-only root filesystem, seccomp profile, drop ALL capabilities. Use for: highly sensitive workloads. Recommended for production.

23.5 Secrets Encryption — KMS Envelope Encryption

Kubernetes Secrets are stored in etcd as base64-encoded strings — NOT encrypted by default. EKS supports envelope encryption using AWS KMS:

1 Enable Encryption on Cluster Creation

Create a KMS key, then enable envelope encryption on the EKS cluster. All new Secrets written to etcd are encrypted with the KMS key. Existing Secrets are NOT retroactively encrypted — you must recreate them.

2 Encryption Flow

1. K8s generates a data encryption key (DEK) for each Secret. 2. DEK encrypts the Secret data. 3. DEK is encrypted with the KMS key (envelope). 4. Both encrypted DEK + encrypted data are stored in etcd. Without the KMS key, the Secret is unrecoverable.

3 IAM Control

Even if someone gains access to etcd (which AWS manages), they can't decrypt Secrets without kms:Decrypt permission on the KMS key. CloudTrail logs every encrypt/decrypt operation — you have an audit trail of Secret access.

Q1

What's the difference between IAM and RBAC in EKS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

IAM: authentication — "Who are you?" Controls who can call the EKS API. RBAC: authorization — "What can you do?" Controls what operations you can perform inside the cluster. IAM maps to K8s RBAC groups via the aws-auth ConfigMap. You need both: IAM to get in, RBAC to do anything once inside.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

What happens if you delete the aws-auth ConfigMap?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

All IAM users lose access to the cluster — no one can authenticate via kubectl. Only the original cluster creator (whose IAM identity is permanently stored) retains access. Recovery: the cluster creator can recreate the aws-auth ConfigMap. This is why you should never modify aws-auth without a backup.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q3

Can Pod A talk to Pod B by default?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Yes. Kubernetes has a flat network model — all Pods can communicate with all other Pods across all namespaces by default. Network Policies are required to restrict this. Without Network Policies, a compromised logging sidecar in namespace "monitoring" can connect to anihpj's database Pod in namespace "anihpj-prod."

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q4

Which Pod Security Standard should you use for anihpj?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Baseline at minimum. This prevents: hostPath volumes (can't mount host filesystem), privileged containers (can't run as root on the host), and hostNetwork (can't sniff host traffic). Restricted is better for production: adds non-root user requirement, read-only root filesystem, and drops all Linux capabilities.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q5

Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default in EKS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

No. Secrets are stored as base64-encoded strings in etcd. Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption — anyone with etcd access can decode them. You must explicitly enable envelope encryption with KMS on the EKS cluster. This is a critical production security control.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q6

How does a Network Policy enforce egress rules?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Egress rules define which Pods/IPs/ports a Pod can SEND traffic to. In the anihpj policy: anihpj Pods can only egress to Redis (port 6379) and PostgreSQL (port 5432). If an attacker compromises anihpj and tries to call out to a command-and-control server, the CNI plugin blocks the egress — the outbound connection is dropped before it leaves the Pod.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q7

What is the principle of least privilege applied to K8s RBAC?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Create a separate Role for each team/application with only the verbs and resources they need. The developer role above allows get/list/watch on Pods and Services, but NOT delete. If a developer's credentials are compromised, the attacker can only view resources — they can't delete Deployments or access Secrets. Scope to specific namespaces and resource names whenever possible.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q8

When would you use IRSA vs node-level IAM roles?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Always use IRSA for application Pods. IRSA gives each Pod (via its ServiceAccount) its own IAM role — least privilege per Pod. Node-level IAM roles are shared by ALL Pods on that node — if one Pod needs S3, all Pods get S3. Node-level roles are only appropriate for daemonset/system components (CNI plugin, CSI driver) that need AWS API access.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q9

What does runAsNonRoot: true actually enforce?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

It prevents the container from starting if the image's USER is root (UID 0) or if no USER is specified (defaults to root). If the container tries to run as root, kubelet refuses to start it with an error. This blocks container escape exploits that rely on root privileges. Combine with runAsUser: 1000 for explicit non-root UID.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q10

How does KMS envelope encryption protect Secrets if etcd is compromised?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Each Secret is encrypted with a unique data encryption key (DEK). The DEK itself is encrypted with the KMS CMK and stored alongside the encrypted data. Even if an attacker dumps all of etcd, they see only encrypted blobs. Without kms:Decrypt permission on the KMS key, the DEK cannot be decrypted, and without the DEK, the Secret data cannot be decrypted. CloudTrail logs all KMS key usage — you'll have an audit record of any decryption attempts.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security) — EKS Security. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.
