24.1 GitOps with ArgoCD on EKS

ArgoCD implements GitOps — your Git repository is the single source of truth for your cluster state. ArgoCD continuously reconciles the cluster to match the Git repo:

❌ Push-Based CI/CD (Traditional)
  • CI pipeline runs kubectl apply
  • CI needs cluster credentials
  • What's deployed ≠ what's in Git (drift)
  • "It worked in CI, why is production broken?"
✅ GitOps with ArgoCD (Pull-Based)
  • ArgoCD pulls from Git every 3 minutes
  • Only ArgoCD has cluster write access
  • Cluster = Git. Always. No drift possible.
  • Rollback = git revert + ArgoCD sync
ArgoCD Application for anihpj
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihs-canvas/anihpj-gitops
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true      # Delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true   # Revert manual changes
🔄 DEEP DIVE: ArgoCD Sync Waves & Hooks — Ordered Deployments

By default, ArgoCD syncs all resources simultaneously. For anihpj, you need ordering: ConfigMap → Secret → PVC → Deployment → HPA → Ingress. Sync waves and hooks give you precise control:

🪝 PreSync Hook: Django Migrations
Migration Job — runs BEFORE any resource sync
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: anihpj-secret

PreSync hooks run BEFORE any Sync-wave resources. This Job applies schema changes before the new Deployment rolls out — the new code never meets an old database schema. If migration fails, ArgoCD marks the sync as failed and nothing gets deployed.

0 Wave 0: ConfigMap & Secret (First)
annotations on ConfigMap & Secret
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"

Configuration and secrets must exist before anything that references them. ArgoCD deploys all wave-0 resources first, waits for every one to be Healthy, then proceeds to wave 1.

1 Wave 1: PVC & Service

Persistent Volume Claims and Services are infrastructure — ready before Pods mount volumes or receive traffic. The Service ClusterIP is assigned here and remains stable. Annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1".

2 Wave 2: Deployment

The main anihpj Deployment rolls out with RollingUpdate. ArgoCD waits for all Pods to be Ready (readiness probe passing) before considering this wave complete. Annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "2".

3 Wave 3: HPA

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler targets the now-running Deployment. If HPA were created before the Deployment, it would reference a non-existent target and error. Annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "3".

4 Wave 4: Ingress (Last)

The ALB Ingress is created last — only after the Service and Pods are healthy. This prevents the ALB from ever routing traffic to non-existent backends, avoiding 502 errors during deployment. Annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "4".

✅ PostSync Hook: Smoke Test (Optional)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PostSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: smoke-test
        image: curlimages/curl
        command: ["curl", "-f", "https://anihpj.example.com/health/"]

PostSync runs AFTER all waves complete successfully. A smoke test validates the full stack end-to-end. If curl returns non-200, the sync is marked failed — but resources remain deployed (unlike PreSync failure which blocks everything).

🌊
Waves: Sequential Resource Ordering
  • 0 ConfigMap → Secret
  • 1 PVC → Service
  • 2 Deployment
  • 3 HPA
  • 4 Ingress

Integers from negative to positive. Each wave waits for all its resources to be Healthy before the next. Use negative waves for cleanup-before-create patterns.

🪝
Hooks: Phase-Specific One-Time Actions
  • PreSync — Before any wave. Migrations, cert generation. Failure blocks sync.
  • Sync — During sync, alongside resources. DB seeding.
  • PostSync — After all waves. Smoke tests, cache warm, notifications. Failure marks sync failed, doesn't roll back.
  • SyncFail — On failure. Cleanup, alerting, rollback trigger.

Hook resources are one-shot — not part of desired state. hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation (replaces old), HookSucceeded, HookFailed.

24.2 Helm Charts for anihpj

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A Helm chart packages all the YAML for anihpj (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, HPA) into a single, versioned, templated package:

Helm Install anihpj
helm repo add anihpj https://charts.anihpj.dev
helm install anihpj-prod anihpj/anihpj \
  --namespace anihpj-prod \
  --set image.tag=v1.2.3 \
  --set replicaCount=3 \
  --set ingress.host=anihpj.example.com \
  --set resources.requests.cpu=250m
📦
Chart Structure

Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (default config), templates/ (K8s YAML with Go templates), charts/ (sub-charts for Redis, PostgreSQL). One helm install deploys everything.

🔄
Helm + ArgoCD

ArgoCD can deploy Helm charts directly from Git. Point the Application at a chart directory, and ArgoCD runs helm template then applies the rendered YAML. Best of both worlds: Helm's templating + ArgoCD's GitOps reconciliation.

24.3 Service Mesh — Istio on EKS

A service mesh injects an Envoy proxy sidecar into every Pod, handling all network traffic transparently. Your application code doesn't change — the sidecar intercepts every request and applies TLS, routing, retries, and telemetry automatically:

🔒 DEEP DIVE: mTLS — How Istio Encrypts Pod-to-Pod Traffic

In a standard K8s cluster, Pod-to-Pod traffic is unencrypted. Anyone who compromises the network can see database queries, API calls, secrets in transit. Istio's mTLS fixes this transparently:

1
Sidecar Injection (Automatic)

Label the namespace istio-injection: enabled. Istio's mutating webhook injects an Envoy sidecar into every new Pod. The sidecar runs alongside your app container, sharing the same network namespace — it intercepts ALL inbound and outbound traffic via iptables rules without the app knowing.

2
Certificate Provisioning

Istio's control plane (istiod) acts as a Certificate Authority. It provisions an X.509 certificate + private key to each Envoy sidecar. Certificates are short-lived (24 hours) and auto-rotated. The app never touches certificates — Envoy handles the TLS handshake entirely.

3
Mutual TLS Handshake

When Pod A calls Pod B: Envoy A intercepts the HTTP request → initiates TLS handshake with Envoy B → both present certificates signed by the SAME Istio CA → mutual trust established → traffic encrypted with ephemeral session keys. The applications think they're talking plain HTTP. Envoy transparently upgrades to mTLS.

Enable mTLS — PeerAuthentication Policy
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT  # Every Pod-to-Pod call MUST use mTLS
🐤 DEEP DIVE: Istio Canary — Traffic Splitting at the Mesh Level

Unlike ALB canary (which works at the edge — internet → ALB), Istio canaries work inside the cluster — any service can canary any other service:

VirtualService — Canary Traffic Splitting for anihpj
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-canary
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  hosts:
  - anihpj-svc
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-canary:
          exact: "true"     # Internal test traffic → v2
    route:
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-svc
        subset: v2
        port: {number: 8000}
      weight: 100
  - route:                   # All other traffic
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-svc
        subset: v1           # 90% → stable v1
        port: {number: 8000}
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: anihpj-svc
        subset: v2           # 10% → canary v2
        port: {number: 8000}
      weight: 10
🎯
Header-Based Routing

Send x-canary: true header → routed to v2. Internal test traffic validates the new version while real users stay on v1. Unlike ALB canary (IP-based splitting), Istio routes based on ANY request attribute: headers, cookies, path, method.

📈
Progressive Rollout

Start at 5% → monitor latency/errors → 25% → 50% → 100%. Istio + Flagger auto-detects regression: if error rate spikes on v2, Flagger auto-reverts to v1. No human intervention needed.

📊 DEEP DIVE: Observability — Every Call, Measured

Envoy sidecars emit telemetry for every single Pod-to-Pod call — no code instrumentation needed. This gives you a real-time map of your entire application:

📈
Golden Signals (RED)

Rate (requests/sec), Errors (5xx rate), Duration (p50/p95/p99 latency). Envoy emits these for every service call. Prometheus scrapes Envoy metrics every 15s. Grafana dashboards visualize them — no application code changes.

🗺️
Service Dependency Graph

Kiali (Istio's UI) auto-generates a real-time topology map: anihpj → Redis (cache) → PostgreSQL (database). Green lines = healthy, red = errors. Click any edge to see request rate, latency, and error % between those two services.

🔍
Distributed Tracing

Envoy propagates trace headers (Zipkin/Jaeger format) across service calls. A single user request to /jobs/ generates a trace spanning: Ingress → anihpj → Redis → PostgreSQL. Pinpoint exactly where latency happens.

Istio Install on EKS — Minimal Production Profile
istioctl install --set profile=default -y
kubectl label namespace anihpj-prod istio-injection=enabled
# All new Pods in anihpj-prod now get Envoy sidecars automatically

24.4 EKS Anywhere & Hybrid Deployments

EKS Anywhere lets you run EKS on your own infrastructure — on-premises data centers, edge locations, or even other clouds. Same EKS API, same tooling, anywhere:

FeatureEKS (AWS-Managed)EKS Anywhere
Control PlaneAWS managed ($0.10/hr)You manage (on your hardware)
InfrastructureAWS EC2 or FargatevSphere or bare metal
K8s VersionAWS maintainsYou maintain (EKS Distro)
Best ForCloud-native workloadsData residency, latency-sensitive, edge, hybrid
Managementeksctl, AWS Console, IaCeksctl anywhere CLI

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q1

What is GitOps and how does ArgoCD implement it?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

GitOps means Git is the single source of truth for cluster state. ArgoCD watches a Git repo and continuously reconciles the cluster to match. If someone manually changes a Deployment (kubectl edit), ArgoCD reverts it within 3 minutes (selfHeal). All changes go through Git → PR review → merge → ArgoCD sync. This gives you audit trail, rollback, and drift detection for free.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

What is the difference between Helm and Kustomize?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Helm: templating engine — uses Go templates with {{ .Values.replicaCount }} placeholders. Values defined in values.yaml. Good for: distributing apps (Helm Hub), complex conditional logic. Kustomize: overlay engine — patches base YAML without templates. Good for: environment-specific overlays (base → dev/staging/prod overrides), simpler mental model. Both work with ArgoCD.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q3

How does mTLS work in Istio?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Istio injects an Envoy sidecar proxy into every Pod. When Pod A calls Pod B: (1) Envoy A intercepts the request, (2) Envoy A and Envoy B perform mutual TLS handshake (both present certificates signed by Istio CA), (3) traffic is encrypted between them. Neither application knows about TLS — it's transparent. Certificate rotation happens automatically every 24 hours.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q4

What does selfHeal: true do in ArgoCD?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

When enabled, ArgoCD continuously monitors the cluster and reverts any manual changes that deviate from the Git state. If someone runs kubectl scale deployment anihpj --replicas=10 but Git says replicas=3, ArgoCD resets it to 3 within 3 minutes. This enforces the GitOps principle: the only way to change production is through Git.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q5

When would you use EKS Anywhere instead of EKS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Use EKS Anywhere when: (1) data residency laws require on-premises processing, (2) you need ultra-low latency (edge manufacturing, 5G), (3) you have existing data center investments, (4) you need a consistent K8s experience across cloud and on-prem. EKS Anywhere gives you the same EKS API and tooling on your own hardware.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q6

What is the advantage of Helm chart dependencies?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Helm charts can declare dependencies on other charts (Redis, PostgreSQL, Prometheus). One helm install anihpj can automatically deploy Redis and PostgreSQL as dependencies. Version locking ensures compatibility: anihpj v1.2 requires Redis v7.x. This eliminates "works on my machine" issues — the entire stack is versioned as one unit.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q7

How does Istio canary differ from ALB canary?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

ALB canary: works at the edge (internet → ALB). Can split traffic between two target groups. Good for external traffic. Istio canary: works Pod-to-Pod INSIDE the mesh. Canary ANY service call, not just ingress. More granular: send 10% of /api/checkout to v2, but 100% of /api/search to v1. Istio uses request headers (user-id, device-type) for routing decisions.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q8

What does prune: true do in ArgoCD sync policy?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

When enabled, ArgoCD deletes resources from the cluster that are removed from Git. If you delete anihpj-service.yaml from the repo, ArgoCD deletes the corresponding Service from the cluster. Without prune, removing a file from Git leaves the resource running in the cluster (orphaned). Prune ensures Git is the EXACT representation of cluster state.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q9

How do you rollback a Helm release?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

helm rollback anihpj-prod 1 — rolls back to revision 1. Helm stores release history (default 10 revisions). helm history anihpj-prod shows all revisions with timestamps. Rollback creates a new revision — you can roll forward again. With ArgoCD, rollback is even simpler: git revert the commit and ArgoCD syncs the previous state.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 4 (Monitoring, 15%) — CloudWatch. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q10

What is the EKS Distro and how does it relate to EKS Anywhere?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

EKS Distro (EKS-D) is the open-source Kubernetes distribution that powers EKS. It's the same binaries, same patches, same versions that AWS uses for EKS. EKS Anywhere packages EKS-D with tooling to run it on-premises. The relationship: EKS → uses EKS-D internally; EKS Anywhere → packages EKS-D for your data center. Both provide the same K8s experience.

📖 EXPLANATION

Chapter 25: CloudWatch — Metrics, Logs & Alarms

CloudWatch is the central nervous system of AWS observability. It collects metrics from every AWS service, aggregates logs from your applications, triggers alarms when things go wrong, and gives you dashboards to visualize it all. Mastering CloudWatch is essential for the DOP-C02 exam.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 Domain 4: Monitoring 15% 📝 10 Questions

25.1 CloudWatch Metrics — The What & When

Metrics are time-series data points about your AWS resources. Every AWS service sends metrics to CloudWatch automatically. You can also publish your own custom metrics:

📊 DEEP DIVE: CloudWatch Metrics Pipeline
1
Namespace

A container for metrics. AWS services use namespaces like AWS/EC2, AWS/EKS, AWS/RDS. Custom metrics use your own namespace: anihpj/production. Namespaces isolate metrics from different applications.

2
Dimensions

Name/value pairs that identify a metric uniquely. Example: CPUUtilization metric with dimensions {InstanceId: i-abc123}. A single metric can have up to 30 dimensions — the combination defines a unique time series.

3
Statistics & Period

CloudWatch aggregates raw data points into statistics: Average, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, SampleCount, Percentile (p95, p99). The period is the aggregation window: 1 minute (detailed) or 5 minutes (standard). Shorter period = more granular but costs more.

📏
Standard Monitoring

Free, 5-minute granularity. AWS sends metrics every 5 minutes by default. Enough for trend analysis and basic dashboards. Not granular enough for rapid auto-scaling or real-time alerting.

⚡
Detailed Monitoring

Paid, 1-minute granularity. Enable per-instance for EC2. Costs ~$2.10/instance/month. Required for fast auto-scaling reactions and sub-minute alarm evaluation.

🔧
Custom Metrics

Publish your own via PutMetricData API. Example: anihpj/orders-per-minute. $0.30 per metric per month. High-resolution (sub-minute) available. Use CloudWatch Agent or AWS SDK.

🧮 Metric Math — Derived Metrics Without Storing Them

Metric Math lets you create expressions that combine multiple metrics in real-time. No need to store the derived result — it's computed on the fly:

Metric Math Examples
# Error Rate = (5xx Errors / Total Requests) × 100
m1 = SUM(METRICS("AWS/ALB", "HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count"))
m2 = SUM(METRICS("AWS/ALB", "RequestCount"))
ERROR_RATE = (m1 / m2) * 100

# Headroom = Available Memory in GB
MEMORY_HEADROOM = (AVG(METRICS("mem_used_percent")) / 100) * AVG(METRICS("mem_total"))

25.2 CloudWatch Logs — The Why & Where

CloudWatch Logs collects, stores, and lets you query application and system logs. Every EKS Pod, Lambda function, and EC2 instance can send logs here:

📁
Log Groups

Containers for log streams. Typically one per application or service: /aws/eks/anihpj-cluster/cluster. Set retention: 1 day to never expire. Default: never expire (costs build up — always set retention!).

📄
Log Streams

Individual sequences of log events. EKS creates one stream per Pod per container. Stream names follow the pattern: kube-system/aws-node-abc123. Each stream is an ordered sequence.

🔍
Logs Insights

SQL-like query engine for logs. Search across multiple log groups, filter with patterns, aggregate with stats. 15-minute queries are free. Queries scan GB-scanned — optimize your time ranges.

CloudWatch Logs Insights — Debug anihpj Issues
-- Find ERROR logs in the last hour
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 50

-- Count errors by Pod (top contributors)
fields @logStream
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count() as error_count by @logStream
| sort error_count desc
| limit 10

-- Find slow requests (Django logs with duration > 1000ms)
fields @timestamp, @message
| parse @message "duration:*ms" as duration
| filter duration > 1000
| sort duration desc
💡 Metric Filters — Turn Logs into Metrics

Create a metric filter that counts occurrences of "ERROR" in your logs. This becomes a CloudWatch metric you can alarm on: "If ERROR count > 10 in 5 minutes → trigger alarm." This closes the loop: logs → metrics → alarms → actions.

📡 DEEP DIVE: Subscription Filters & Live Tail — Real-Time Log Streaming
📤
Subscription Filters

Stream logs in near real-time to: Kinesis Data Streams (real-time processing with Lambda consumers), Kinesis Firehose (deliver to S3, OpenSearch, Redshift), or Lambda (custom processing — parse, transform, alert). Create a filter pattern to only stream matching logs (e.g., only ERROR-level). Multiple subscriptions per log group — send to analytics AND archive simultaneously.

🔴
CloudWatch Live Tail

Stream logs to your terminal in real-time — like tail -f for CloudWatch. Select a log group, apply filters, and watch events appear as they happen. Perfect for: live debugging a deployment, watching for errors during a canary rollout, verifying that a fix stopped the error flood. Three session types: focused (one log group), aggregated (multiple), filter (with pattern matching).

25.3 CloudWatch Alarms — Automated Response

Alarms watch a metric over time and trigger actions when thresholds are breached. They're the bridge between observation and action:

CloudWatch Alarm — anihpj High CPU → Auto-Scale
HighCPUAlarm:
  Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
  Properties:
    AlarmName: anihpj-high-cpu
    MetricName: CPUUtilization
    Namespace: AWS/ECS
    Dimensions:
      - Name: ServiceName
        Value: anihpj-svc
    Statistic: Average
    Period: 60
    EvaluationPeriods: 3
    Threshold: 80
    ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
    AlarmActions:
      - !Ref AlertTopic  # SNS → PagerDuty/Slack
    OKActions:
      - !Ref AlertTopic  # Notify when recovered
🔴
Alarm States

OK: metric within threshold. ALARM: threshold breached. INSUFFICIENT_DATA: not enough data to evaluate. Always decide what to do for each state.

🔗
Composite Alarms

Combine multiple alarms with AND/OR logic. "Alert only if CPU > 80% AND memory > 90%" — reduces false positives. Up to 100 alarms per composite.

🤖
Anomaly Detection

ML-powered: CloudWatch learns the metric's normal pattern and alarms on deviations. No static thresholds needed.

🌐 DEEP DIVE: CloudWatch Synthetics — Canaries That Test Your App 24/7

CloudWatch Synthetics runs scripted browser checks (called canaries) against your endpoints on a schedule. Unlike metric alarms that only detect symptoms, canaries test the actual user experience:

🐤
API Canary
// Node.js canary — checks anihpj API every 5 minutes
const synthetics = require('Synthetics');
const apiCanary = async function () {
    const response = await synthetics.executeHttpStep(
        'GET', 'https://anihpj.example.com/jobs/');
    if (response.statusCode !== 200) {
        throw new Error('API not healthy: ' + response.statusCode);
    }
};
exports.handler = async () => { return apiCanary(); };

Runs every 5 min from multiple AWS regions. Publishes success/failure + duration as CloudWatch metrics. Alarm on failure rate or latency. Catches "the site looks up but API returns 500" — invisible to infrastructure metrics.

🖥️
Visual Monitoring Canary

Records a browser session (Headless Chromium): navigate to anihpj, click "Search Jobs," verify results appear, take screenshots. Detects frontend JavaScript errors, broken CSS, missing elements. Duration + success metrics go to CloudWatch. Har file for debugging failures.

25.4 CloudWatch Dashboards — See Everything at Once

Dashboards are customizable views that aggregate metrics, alarms, and logs widgets into a single pane of glass:

📊
Widget Types

Line/Stacked Area: time-series. Number: latest value. Gauge: value within a range. Text: markdown. Logs table: Insights results. Alarm status: red/green indicators.

🌐
Cross-Account / Cross-Region

One dashboard can pull metrics from multiple accounts and regions. Centralize dev, staging, and production monitoring on one screen. Requires cross-account IAM roles.

🌐 DEEP DIVE: CloudWatch Cross-Account Observability

In a multi-account setup (dev, staging, prod in separate accounts), you don't want to log into each account to check dashboards. CloudWatch cross-account lets you centralize monitoring:

👁️
Cross-Account Dashboards

Create a dashboard in a central monitoring account that pulls metrics from ALL other accounts. Each widget specifies the source account ID. Requires: IAM role in source accounts with cloudwatch:GetMetricData trusted by the monitoring account. One URL to see dev, staging, and production health side-by-side.

📊
Cross-Account Cross-Region

One dashboard can aggregate: anihpj-prod (us-east-1), anihpj-dr (us-west-2), anihpj-eu (eu-west-1). Set region per widget. Combine with cross-account for a truly global view: "Show me the 99th percentile latency for anihpj across all accounts and all regions."

25.5 Container Insights for EKS

Container Insights provides pre-built dashboards and metrics for EKS clusters. It shows cluster, node, Pod, and container-level metrics out of the box:

1 Deploy CloudWatch Agent on EKS
Install CloudWatch Agent + Fluent Bit
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws-samples/amazon-cloudwatch-container-insights/latest/k8s-deployment-manifest-templates/deployment-mode/daemonset/container-insights-monitoring/quickstart/cwagent-fluent-bit-quickstart.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

The CloudWatch Agent (DaemonSet) runs on every node collecting infrastructure metrics. Fluent Bit (DaemonSet) collects application logs from Pods and forwards them to CloudWatch Logs.

2 Pre-Built Dashboards

Once deployed, Container Insights auto-creates dashboards: Cluster performance, Node performance, Pod performance, Service performance — all without writing a single dashboard widget.

3 Control Plane Logging

Enable EKS control plane logs: API server, audit, authenticator, controller manager, scheduler. These flow to CloudWatch Logs under /aws/eks/anihpj-cluster/cluster. Critical for security auditing.

Chapter 26: CloudTrail & AWS Config — Audit & Compliance

CloudTrail records who did what in your AWS account. AWS Config records what your resources looked like at any point in time. Together they form the audit backbone required for SOC2, HIPAA, and PCI compliance.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 4: Monitoring 15% & Domain 6: Security 17% 📝 10 Questions

26.1 CloudTrail — API Activity Audit

CloudTrail records every AWS API call as an event: who called it, when, from which IP, what parameters, and the response. It's the definitive source for security forensics and compliance auditing:

📋
Management Events

Control plane operations: creating/deleting resources, modifying security groups, IAM changes. Always enabled, always free. Example: RunInstances, CreateBucket, AttachRolePolicy.

📊
Data Events

Data plane operations: S3 object-level API calls (GetObject, PutObject), Lambda invocations, DynamoDB operations. Paid, must be explicitly enabled.

🏢
Organization Trail

One trail at the organization level — automatically applies to ALL accounts. Centralized S3 bucket. Member accounts can't disable or modify it.

✅ CloudTrail Best Practices
  • Enable across ALL regions
  • Enable log file validation (detects tampering)
  • Encrypt with KMS CMK
  • Send to dedicated log archive account
  • Set retention via S3 lifecycle policies
❌ Common CloudTrail Mistakes
  • Only enabling in one region
  • Not enabling data events
  • Storing in the same account as workloads
  • Never reviewing trails (collecting but not analyzing)

26.2 CloudTrail vs CloudWatch — What Tells You What

DimensionCloudTrailCloudWatch LogsCloudWatch Metrics
What it recordsAWS API calls (who did what)Application logs (Pod stdout)Numeric data over time
FormatJSON eventsUnstructured textTime-series data points
Use caseSecurity forensics, complianceDebugging, Logs InsightsAlarms, dashboards, auto-scaling
RetentionS3 (set lifecycle)CloudWatch Logs (set per group)15 months (auto-retained)
🔍 DEEP DIVE: CloudTrail Lake — SQL Analytics on API History

CloudTrail Lake runs SQL queries against your CloudTrail events without setting up Athena:

-- Who deleted resources in the last 7 days?
SELECT userIdentity.arn, eventName, eventTime
FROM CLOUD_TRAIL_EVENT
WHERE eventName LIKE '%Delete%'
  AND eventTime > now() - interval '7' day

-- Top 10 most active IAM users
SELECT userIdentity.arn, count(*) as api_calls
FROM CLOUD_TRAIL_EVENT
GROUP BY userIdentity.arn
ORDER BY api_calls DESC LIMIT 10
🔍 DEEP DIVE: CloudTrail Insights — ML-Powered Anomaly Detection on API Activity

CloudTrail Insights automatically analyzes your management events and detects unusual API activity — spikes in write operations, calls from new IPs, or changes to sensitive resources outside normal patterns:

📈
What It Detects

API call spikes: "Normally 5 TerminateInstances per day, today: 150." New geolocation: "First API call from China in 2 years." Unusual resource changes: "IAM policy modified 30 times in 1 hour (normal: 2/day)." CloudTrail learns your baseline over 7 days and flags deviations as Insight events.

⚡
Investigation Workflow

1. CloudTrail generates an Insight event → 2. Event appears in CloudTrail console → 3. Click to see ALL API calls during the anomalous period → 4. Identify the specific user/role and affected resources → 5. Take action: revoke credentials, rotate keys, investigate breach. Insights bridge the gap between "we collect logs" and "we detect threats from logs."

26.3 AWS Config Rules — Continuous Compliance

AWS Config continuously evaluates your resources against rules. Unlike CloudTrail (which records what happened), Config proactively checks if your resources ARE compliant right now:

📏
Managed Rules

400+ pre-built rules from AWS. Examples: s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, encrypted-volumes, rds-instance-public-access-check. Deploy in minutes.

🔧
Custom Rules

Write Lambda functions that evaluate resources against your own logic. "All anihpj S3 buckets must have tag DataClassification set." Lambda evaluates and reports COMPLIANT/NON_COMPLIANT.

🔄 Auto-Remediation — Config + SSM Automation
1
Config Detects Non-Compliance

Config rule evaluation finds a public S3 bucket → NON_COMPLIANT.

2
EventBridge Triggers Remediation

Config sends non-compliance event to EventBridge → triggers SSM Automation runbook.

3
SSM Automation Fixes It

Runbook blocks public access, verifies the fix, reports success. Config re-evaluates — COMPLIANT.

🌐 DEEP DIVE: Config Aggregator — Single View Across All Accounts & Regions

When you have 20 accounts × 5 regions = 100 scopes, checking compliance individually is impossible. Config Aggregator pulls all compliance data into one central dashboard:

🏢
How It Works

Designate one account as the aggregator. Authorize source accounts to send their Config data. The aggregator collects: resource configurations, compliance status, and configuration timelines from ALL accounts and regions. One dashboard to rule them all — every resource, every account, every region.

🔍
Advanced Query

SQL-based query across ALL aggregated data: "Show me all S3 buckets across ALL accounts that are NOT encrypted" or "List all security groups with port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 in any account." Results link directly to the non-compliant resource for remediation. No more account-by-account hunting.

26.4 Compliance Dashboard & Conformance Packs

AWS Config aggregates compliance across all accounts and regions into a single dashboard. Conformance Packs deploy collections of rules as code:

Conformance Pack — anihpj Security Baseline
Resources:
  S3PublicAccessCheck:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:
      ConfigRuleName: s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited
      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: S3_BUCKET_PUBLIC_READ_PROHIBITED
  EncryptedVolumesCheck:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:
      ConfigRuleName: encrypted-volumes
      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: ENCRYPTED_VOLUMES
  RdsEncryptionCheck:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:
      ConfigRuleName: rds-storage-encrypted
      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: RDS_STORAGE_ENCRYPTED
🔐 DEEP DIVE: CloudTrail Log Integrity — Prove Logs Weren't Tampered

For compliance (SOC2, HIPAA, PCI), you must prove audit logs haven't been modified. CloudTrail provides cryptographic validation:

1
CloudTrail Creates Digest Files

Every hour, CloudTrail creates a digest file containing SHA-256 hashes of every log file delivered in that hour. Each digest is RSA-signed and references the previous digest — creating an immutable hash chain.

2
Validate Integrity

Run aws cloudtrail validate-logs — checks: each log file's hash matches the digest, each digest signature is valid, the chain is unbroken. If any file was modified → validation fails. This is admissible evidence for legal/compliance.

3
Multi-Layer Protection

Combine: log file validation (detect tampering) + KMS encryption (prevent reading) + S3 Object Lock (prevent deletion) + separate audit account (prevent access). Defense in depth for your audit trail — logs are tamper-evident, encrypted, immutable, and isolated.

Q1

What's the difference between CloudTrail Management and Data events?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Management events: control plane (create/delete/modify resources). Free, always on. Data events: data plane (S3 GetObject, Lambda Invoke). Must be explicitly enabled, paid.

📖 EXPLANATION

Chapter 27: AWS X-Ray — Distributed Tracing

X-Ray traces requests as they flow through your distributed application — from the user's browser through API Gateway, Lambda, EKS Pods, RDS, and back. It shows you exactly where latency happens and which service caused an error.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 4: Monitoring 15% 📝 10 Questions

27.1 What is Distributed Tracing?

A single user request to anihpj might touch: ALB → Django Pod → Redis (cache) → PostgreSQL (database) → S3. Without tracing, when that request is slow, you don't know which service is the bottleneck:

🔗
Trace

The complete journey of a single request across ALL services. A trace is composed of multiple segments. A GET /jobs/ request generates a trace spanning ALB, anihpj Pod, Redis, and PostgreSQL.

📐
Segment

A single service's work within a trace. The Django Pod's segment includes subsegments for Redis and PostgreSQL — showing exactly how much time was spent in each dependency.

🔍
Subsegment

Fine-grained timing within a segment: Redis GET (2ms), PostgreSQL SELECT (45ms), template rendering (10ms). Pinpoints exactly where the bottleneck is.

27.2 X-Ray Architecture

The X-Ray daemon runs as a DaemonSet on EKS. Your application sends trace data to the daemon via UDP, and the daemon batches and forwards to the X-Ray service:

X-Ray Daemon DaemonSet on EKS
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: xray-daemon
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: xray-daemon
        image: amazon/aws-xray-daemon:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 2000
          protocol: UDP
        env:
        - name: AWS_REGION
          value: us-east-1

27.3 Instrumenting anihpj with X-Ray

Django Middleware — X-Ray Instrumentation
# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS += ['aws_xray_sdk.ext.django']
MIDDLEWARE = ['aws_xray_sdk.ext.django.middleware.XRayMiddleware'] + MIDDLEWARE

XRAY_RECORDER = {
    'AUTO_INSTRUMENT': True,
    'SAMPLING_RULES': {
        'version': 2,
        'rules': [{
            'fixed_target': 10,
            'rate': 0.05  # 5% + 10/sec
        }]
    }
}

The SDK auto-instruments: incoming HTTP requests, outgoing HTTP calls, SQL queries (as subsegments), and AWS SDK calls. Set sampling appropriately:

🎯 DEEP DIVE: X-Ray Sampling Strategy — Balance Cost vs Coverage
🧮 The Reservoir Formula

Total Traces = fixed_target + rate × (RPS − fixed_target)

At 1000 req/sec, fixed_target: 10, rate: 0.05:

10 + 0.05 × (1000 − 10) = 10 + 49.5 ≈ 60 traces/sec

~6% effective sampling rate — covers low-traffic AND high-traffic periods

📏 Rule Evaluation Order
1
/checkout — 100%

Revenue-critical. Every transaction traced.

2
/search — 10%

Important path. Sample for latency trends.

3
/health — 1%

Noisy but uninteresting. Minimal sampling.

*
Catch-All — 5% + 10/sec

Default reservoir + rate for all other paths.

ⓘ Rules evaluated top-to-bottom. First match wins — put high-priority paths first, catch-all last.

🪣
Reservoir (Fixed Target)

Guaranteed N traces per second before sampling kicks in. fixed_target: 10 — always trace at least 10 req/sec. Ensures data even at 3 AM when traffic is low. Reservoir fills first, then rate applies to remainder.

✅ Best for: ensuring baseline coverage at all traffic levels

📊
Rate (Percentage)

Sample X% of remaining requests after reservoir. rate: 0.05 → 5% beyond reservoir. Controls cost at scale — at 10K req/sec, 5% rate still gives 500 traces/sec for analysis.

⚡ Best for: controlling cost while maintaining statistical significance

📏
Rule-Based Priority

Different rates per endpoint. 100% on /checkout (revenue), 10% on /search, 1% on /health. Put high-value paths first — first match wins.

⚠️ Pitfall: catch-all too high → cost explosion at scale

27.4 X-Ray Service Map — Visualize Your Architecture

🗺️
Service Map

Nodes = services, edges = calls colored by health (green = ok, yellow = errors, red = faults). Circle size = request volume — spot bottlenecks instantly. Click any edge → p50/p95/p99 latency + error count. Auto-updates in real-time.

🖥️→🗄️→🐳 anihpj-frontend → anihpj-api → PostgreSQL
🔍
Trace View

Full waterfall timeline: every segment and subsegment with duration bars. Hover any bar → exact latency. Pinpoint that the 200ms delay is in PostgreSQL:SELECT, not your code. Share trace URLs with your team for collaborative debugging.

🔵 anihpj-api245ms
├─ 🟢 Redis:GET2ms
└─ 🔴 PostgreSQL:SELECT198ms
🔗 DEEP DIVE: X-Ray ServiceLens — Unified Observability

ServiceLens integrates X-Ray traces with CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms into a single view — connecting all three pillars of observability:

🔗
Traces
X-Ray
↔
📊
Metrics
CloudWatch
↔
📋
Logs
CloudWatch
↔
⚠️
Alarms
CloudWatch
🔗
Traces → Metrics

Click a node in Service Map → see correlated CloudWatch metrics (CPU, memory, errors) at the same timestamp. Correlate "latency spike at 2:15 PM" with "CPU hit 95% at 2:15 PM" — instant root cause.

🎯 Pattern: trace shows WHAT slowed down → metrics show WHY

📋
Traces → Logs

Click a trace segment → CloudWatch Logs from that exact Pod at that exact time. No guessing which log stream — ServiceLens links trace ID to log entries automatically via correlation.

🎯 Pattern: trace pinpoints the timestamp → logs show the error message

⚠️
Traces → Alarms

Service Map shows alarm status on each node. If anihpj node is red, click to see which CloudWatch Alarm fired → drill into the trace. Closed-loop: alarm fires → trace identifies the bottleneck → fix it.

🎯 Pattern: alarm alerts you → ServiceLens tells you exactly where to look

What is a trace in X-Ray?

Chapter 28: OpenSearch & Centralized Logging

When you have hundreds of Pods across multiple clusters, kubectl logs doesn't scale. OpenSearch provides a centralized, searchable, and visualizable log platform — managed Elasticsearch by AWS. Combined with Fluent Bit on EKS, you get a production-grade logging pipeline.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 4: Monitoring 15% 📝 10 Questions

28.1 OpenSearch Service — Managed Search & Analytics

🔍
Full-Text Search

Search across ALL Pod logs: "ERROR AND (database OR connection) NOT healthcheck". Results in milliseconds, even across terabytes of logs.

📊
Dashboards

OpenSearch Dashboards (Kibana fork): error rate over time, top errors by Pod, latency histograms. Pre-built EKS observability dashboards.

⚠️
Alerting

Define monitors that run queries on a schedule. "ERROR count spikes" → alert to Slack/PagerDuty/SNS. Built-in, no CloudWatch intermediary needed.

28.2 Log Centralization Patterns

PatternFlowBest For
Fluent Bit → OpenSearchDaemonSet collects Pod stdout → OpenSearch directlySimple setups, one cluster
Fluent Bit → Kinesis Firehose → OpenSearchFirehose buffers, transforms, retries deliveryProduction: resilient to OS downtime
Fluent Bit → CloudWatch → Subscription → OpenSearchCloudWatch as intermediate durable storeDual storage: retention + analytics

28.3 Fluent Bit on EKS — Log Collection Pipeline

Fluent Bit Config — EKS to OpenSearch
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: fluent-bit-config
  namespace: logging
data:
  fluent-bit.conf: |
    [SERVICE]
        Flush         5
    [INPUT]
        Name          tail
        Path          /var/log/containers/*.log
        Parser        docker
        Tag           kube.*
    [FILTER]
        Name          kubernetes
        Match         kube.*
        Merge_Log     On
    [OUTPUT]
        Name          es
        Match         *
        Host          search-anihpj-logs.us-east-1.es.amazonaws.com
        Port          443
        Index         anihpj-logs
        AWS_Auth      On
        AWS_Region    us-east-1
📥
INPUT: Tail

Reads container log files from /var/log/containers/. Handles log rotation gracefully.

🔧
FILTER: Kubernetes

Enriches logs with K8s metadata: Pod name, namespace, labels, container name. Makes logs searchable by Pod/namespace.

📤
OUTPUT: OpenSearch

Sends enriched logs with IAM authentication. Indexed by date for efficient querying.

🗄️ DEEP DIVE: OpenSearch Index State Management — Tiered Storage & Lifecycle

Logs grow fast and old logs are queried less. OpenSearch ISM (Index State Management) automatically moves data through storage tiers to optimize cost:

1
Hot Phase (SSD — gp3) — Days 0-7

New logs are actively written and frequently queried. Fastest storage, highest cost. Use for: today's logs, active debugging, real-time dashboards. Index is open for both reads and writes.

2
Warm Phase (SSD — gp2) — Days 8-30

Logs are read-only, queried occasionally for recent investigations. Move index to warm nodes after 7 days. Still on SSD but less expensive configuration. Index transitions to read-only.

3
Cold Phase (HDD) — Days 31-90

Logs are rarely queried — only for compliance checks or post-mortems. Move to cold storage (UltraWarm nodes). Much cheaper than hot/warm. Queries are slower but still possible. Index is closed, data stored on S3-backed storage.

4
Delete Phase — Day 90+

Logs past retention are deleted to control costs. Set based on compliance requirements (SOC2: 1 year, HIPAA: 6 years). ISM policy auto-deletes indices. Always set a retention policy — never store logs indefinitely in OpenSearch.

🔐 DEEP DIVE: OpenSearch Security — Fine-Grained Access Control

OpenSearch supports multiple security layers to control who can see what:

🔑
IAM Master User

One IAM user/role designated as the master. Used for initial configuration only. After setup, create fine-grained roles and remove direct IAM access for day-to-day operations. The master is the break-glass account.

👥
Internal User Database

Create users directly in OpenSearch with username/password. Assign them to roles: anihpj-readonly (can search logs, can't modify), anihpj-admin (full access). Good for small teams. Simpler than integrating with external identity providers.

🔗
SAML / Cognito Federation

Integrate with your corporate SSO (Okta, Azure AD) via SAML or Amazon Cognito. Users log in with their corporate credentials. Map SAML groups to OpenSearch roles: devops-team → anihpj-admin, developers → anihpj-readonly. Enterprise-grade, no separate credentials.

Chapter 29: AWS Security Services Deep Dive

AWS provides a suite of security services that work together: GuardDuty detects threats, Inspector finds vulnerabilities, Security Hub centralizes findings, WAF blocks attacks at the edge, and KMS encrypts everything. Security is 17% of the DOP-C02 exam — mastery here is non-negotiable.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~4 hours 🎯 Domain 6: Security 17% 📝 10 Questions

29.1 GuardDuty — ML-Powered Threat Detection

GuardDuty continuously analyzes AWS CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and EKS audit logs using machine learning. It detects threats without you writing a single rule:

🔍
Threat Categories

Reconnaissance: port scanning, failed login patterns. Instance compromise: crypto mining, malware C2 communication. Data exfiltration: unusual S3 data transfers, suspicious IAM behavior. EKS Protection: privileged container launched, anonymous API access.

☸️
EKS Protection

GuardDuty monitors K8s audit logs for: pod launched with sensitive hostPath, cluster admin role binding created, anonymous user granted access, secrets accessed from unusual source IP. Findings appear in GuardDuty console with K8s-specific context (Pod name, namespace, action).

⚡
Auto-Remediation

GuardDuty → EventBridge → Lambda: "CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B detected" → Lambda isolates the EC2 instance (removes from ASG, tags as quarantined, sends Slack alert). Response time: seconds from detection to containment.

🛡️ DEEP DIVE: GuardDuty EKS Protection — What It Actually Monitors

GuardDuty EKS Protection analyzes Kubernetes audit logs from your EKS clusters. It doesn't need a DaemonSet, sidecar, or agent — it reads the audit log stream directly from the EKS control plane. It watches for patterns that indicate compromise:

🔓 Privilege Escalation 📌 Persistence 🚪 Defense Evasion 📤 Data Exfiltration 👤 Anonymous Access
🔴 Finding 1: PrivilegedContainer
HIGH PrivilegeEscalation:Kubernetes/PrivilegedContainer
Clusteranihpj-cluster
Namespacedefault
Podunknown-pod
Containersuspicious-container

💀 Impact: Container has root access to the node kernel. Escape to host is trivial.

🟡 Finding 2: ContainerWithSensitiveMount
MEDIUM Persistence:Kubernetes/ContainerWithSensitiveMount
Namespaceanihpj-prod
Podcompromised-pod
Mount/var/run/docker.sock

💀 Impact: Docker socket mounted → attacker can launch privileged containers, escape to host, or hijack other containers.

⚡
Auto-Remediation Path: GuardDuty Finding → EventBridge Rule → Lambda (isolate-compromised-pod) → delete Pod + annotate namespace as quarantined → SNS notification to #anihpj-security. Response time: <30 seconds.

29.2 Amazon Inspector — Vulnerability Management

Inspector continuously scans your workloads for software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and network exposure. Unlike GuardDuty (behavioral threats), Inspector finds misconfigurations and unpatched CVEs:

🛡️ GuardDuty

"Who is attacking me?"

ML-powered behavioral threat detection. Analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, CloudTrail, and Kubernetes audit logs to find: reconnaissance, C2 communication, data exfiltration, cryptomining.

🔍 Inspector

"What's vulnerable?"

Continuous vulnerability scanning across EC2, ECR, and Lambda. Finds CVEs (OS + language packages), open network ports, CIS benchmark violations — before attackers do.

🐳

🛡️ DEEP DIVE: Shield Advanced — DDoS Response Team (DRT) Workflow

Shield Advanced ($3,000/month) gives you access to AWS's DDoS Response Team — security engineers who actively help during attacks:

1
Attack Detected

Shield detects a DDoS attack against your protected resource (ALB, CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator). Auto-mitigation kicks in immediately — Shield's inline mitigations absorb the attack without your involvement. Metrics flow to CloudWatch.

2
DRT Engaged (if needed)

If the attack exceeds auto-mitigation capacity or targets application layer (L7), you can escalate to the DRT. Prerequisite: pre-authorize the DRT via IAM role (AWSShieldDRTAccessPolicy). DRT can create WAF rules, modify Route 53, and engage AWS edge network — all with your pre-approval.

3
Post-Attack: Cost Protection

Shield Advanced includes cost protection: if your protected resources scale up due to a DDoS attack (CloudFront data transfer, ALB LCU consumption), AWS credits the scaling costs back. No surprise bills from attack-induced scaling.

Chapter 30: Compliance-as-Code & Policy-as-Code

Compliance-as-Code means your compliance rules are version-controlled, testable, and automatically enforced — just like infrastructure. Policy-as-Code brings the same principle to Kubernetes: Gatekeeper and OPA enforce rules at admission time, preventing non-compliant resources from ever being created.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 6: Security 17% & Domain 2: Config Mgmt 17% 📝 10 Questions

30.1 AWS Config Managed Rules — Automated Compliance Checks

AWS Config rules are the backbone of compliance-as-code on AWS. 400+ managed rules check your resources continuously:

Config Managed Rules for anihpj
Resources:
  EksEndpointPublicAccessCheck:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:
      ConfigRuleName: eks-endpoint-public-access-check
      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: EKS_ENDPOINT_NO_PUBLIC_ACCESS
  EksSecretsEncryptedCheck:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:
      ConfigRuleName: eks-secrets-encrypted
      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: EKS_SECRETS_ENCRYPTED
  S3BucketPublicReadCheck:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:

      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: S3_BUCKET_PUBLIC_READ_PROHIBITED
🔗 DEEP DIVE: SCP Inheritance & Evaluation — How AWS Decides What's Allowed

When a principal makes an API call, AWS evaluates SCPs in a specific order. Understanding this chain is critical for the exam:

1
Root SCPs

SCPs attached to the organization root apply to ALL accounts. Attach your "deny leaving organization" and "require MFA" here — they cascade to every OU and account.

2
OU SCPs (Inherited Downward)

Each OU's SCPs apply to accounts in that OU AND all child OUs. A Dev OU SCP that denies expensive instance types applies to dev accounts but NOT to Prod OU. SCPs only restrict — child OUs can be MORE restrictive but never LESS.

3
Account SCPs

SCPs attached directly to the account. These are the final layer. Effective SCP = intersection of root SCPs ∩ OU SCPs ∩ account SCPs. If root allows s3:* but OU denies s3:DeleteBucket → effective = s3:* minus DeleteBucket.

4
Result: Effective Permissions

Effective permissions = (Root SCPs ∩ OU SCPs ∩ Account SCPs) ∩ IAM Policies. SCPs define the ceiling; IAM builds up to that ceiling. An explicit Deny in ANY layer (SCP or IAM) blocks the action. Deny always wins.

30.2 SCPs — Service Control Policies (Preventive Guardrails)

SCPs are JSON policies applied at the OU or account level that define the maximum available permissions. They prevent actions even if IAM allows them:

SCP — Deny Leaving Organization + Block Public S3
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLeavingOrg",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["organizations:LeaveOrganization"],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyPublicS3",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "s3:x-amz-acl": "private"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
🛡️ DEEP DIVE: CloudFormation Guard — Policy-as-Code Before Deployment

CloudFormation Guard (cfn-guard) validates CloudFormation templates against policy rules BEFORE they're deployed. It's like a linter for infrastructure — catches security violations at the template level:

Guard Rules — anihpj Security Policies
# Rule: EKS clusters must have private endpoints
rule ensure_eks_private_endpoint {
    when Resources.%Type == "AWS::EKS::Cluster" {
        Resources.Properties.ResourcesVpcConfig.EndpointPublicAccess == false
        << "EKS cluster must use private endpoint only" >>
    }
}

# Rule: S3 buckets must have encryption enabled
rule ensure_s3_encryption {
    when Resources.%Type == "AWS::S3::Bucket" {
        Resources.Properties.BucketEncryption exists
        << "S3 bucket must have encryption enabled" >>
    }
}

Run in CI/CD: cfn-guard validate -r anihpj-rules.guard template.yaml. If any rule FAILs → pipeline stops. Catches violations before they reach AWS. Companion tool cfn_nag scans for known insecure patterns (wildcard IAM, public S3, unencrypted resources).

☸️ DEEP DIVE: OPA/Gatekeeper — Kubernetes-Native Policy Enforcement

Gatekeeper is the Kubernetes admission controller that enforces OPA (Open Policy Agent) policies. It validates, mutates, or rejects resources BEFORE they're created in the cluster:

Gatekeeper Constraint — Require Resource Limits on anihpj
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredResources
metadata:
  name: anihpj-must-have-limits
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    namespaces: ["anihpj-prod", "anihpj-staging"]
  parameters:
    limits:
      - cpu
      - memory
    requests:
      - cpu
      - memory
# Result: Any Pod in anihpj namespaces WITHOUT cpu/memory limits & requests is REJECTED

Gatekeeper uses Constraint Templates (reusable policy logic written in Rego) and Constraints (specific instances with parameters). Audit mode: logs violations without blocking — test policies before enforcing. Dry-run: see what would be rejected before enabling enforcement.

30.3 AWS Audit Manager — Evidence Collection Automated

Audit Manager automates evidence collection for compliance audits. Instead of manually gathering screenshots and logs, it continuously collects evidence from your AWS environment:

📋
Pre-Built Frameworks

Frameworks for SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS, CIS, NIST, ISO 27001. Each framework maps controls to AWS data sources. Audit Manager automatically collects evidence: CloudTrail logs, Config snapshots, Security Hub findings, and user activity reports.

📁
Assessment Reports

Generate auditor-ready reports with: control description, evidence collected, compliance status (compliant/non-compliant), and remediation recommendations. Share with external auditors via read-only access — no need to export data.

🐍 DEEP DIVE: Custom Lambda Config Rule — anihpj Compliance Check

When 400+ managed rules aren't enough, write your own Lambda-based Config rule:

Custom Config Rule — Check anihpj Tags
import boto3

def evaluate_compliance(configuration_item):
    """Check if all anihpj resources have DataClassification tag."""
    resource_type = configuration_item['resourceType']
    tags = configuration_item.get('tags', {})
    
    if 'DataClassification' not in tags:
        return {
            'compliance_type': 'NON_COMPLIANT',
            'annotation': f'{resource_type} missing required tag: DataClassification'
        }
    
    valid_values = ['Public', 'Internal', 'Confidential', 'Restricted']
    if tags['DataClassification'] not in valid_values:
        return {
            'compliance_type': 'NON_COMPLIANT',
            'annotation': f'Invalid value: {tags["DataClassification"]}. Must be one of: {valid_values}'
        }
    
    return {'compliance_type': 'COMPLIANT'}

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    config = boto3.client('config')
    invoking_event = event['invokingEvent']
    result = evaluate_compliance(invoking_event['configurationItem'])
    config.put_evaluations(
        Evaluations=[{
            'ComplianceResourceType': invoking_event['configurationItem']['resourceType'],
            'ComplianceResourceId': invoking_event['configurationItem']['resourceId'],
            'ComplianceType': result['compliance_type'],
            'Annotation': result.get('annotation', ''),
            'OrderingTimestamp': invoking_event['notificationCreationTime']
        }],
        ResultToken=event['resultToken']
    )

30.4 Compliance for anihpj — Putting It All Together

1 Preventive Layer: SCPs

SCP at OU level: deny public S3, deny leaving organization, restrict regions. These are the "walls" — nothing gets past them, not even admin users.

2 Detective Layer: Config Rules

Config rules continuously evaluate: EKS endpoints private, secrets encrypted, S3 buckets private, RDS encrypted. Findings → Security Hub for centralized visibility.

3 Corrective Layer: Auto-Remediation

Config non-compliance → EventBridge → SSM Automation → auto-fix (block S3 public access). Escalation to humans only if auto-fix fails.

4 Evidence Layer: Audit Manager

Collects continuous evidence for SOC 2/HIPAA. Auditor-ready reports generated automatically. Proof of compliance without manual effort.

Q1

What's the difference between preventive and detective controls?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Preventive: stop bad things from happening (SCPs, IAM policies, WAF rules, encryption requirements). Detective: find bad things that happened (Config rules, GuardDuty, CloudTrail, Security Hub). Corrective: fix bad things automatically (auto-remediation, Lambda fixers). Best practice: layer all three.

How do SCPs differ from IAM policies?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

SCPs: applied at OU/account level, define MAXIMUM permissions for ALL principals in the account. Don't grant permissions — only remove them. IAM policies: attached to users/roles/groups, grant specific permissions. Effective permissions = SCP_Allows ∩ IAM_Allows. SCPs are the ceiling; IAM builds up to that ceiling.

Q6

What makes SCPs "preventive" rather than "detective"?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

SCPs block actions BEFORE they happen. When a user calls an API, AWS evaluates SCPs FIRST. If an SCP denies the action, the API call is rejected immediately — the resource is never modified. Detective controls (Config rules, CloudTrail) only notice AFTER something changed. SCPs are the stronger control.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — Compliance. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q7

Can SCPs grant permissions?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

No. SCPs can only restrict permissions. They define the boundary of what's possible. Even with an SCP that "allows" s3:*, the user still needs an IAM policy that allows s3:* — and then the effective permissions are the intersection. SCPs are a filter, not a grant.

📖 EXPLANATION

What is the Config rule evaluation trigger?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Two trigger types: Configuration changes (resource created/modified/deleted — near real-time evaluation) and Periodic (evaluated on schedule: 1h, 3h, 6h, 12h, 24h). Use change triggers for critical resources, periodic for infrequent changes or where immediate detection isn't critical.

Chapter 31: Secrets & Certificate Management

Secrets (database passwords, API keys) and certificates (TLS) are the keys to your kingdom. AWS provides Secrets Manager for automated rotation, Parameter Store for simple config, ACM for TLS certificates with auto-renewal, and KMS for encryption keys. Master these and you've secured the foundation.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 6: Security 17% 📝 10 Questions

31.1 AWS Secrets Manager — Automated Rotation

Secrets Manager stores and automatically rotates secrets. It natively integrates with RDS, DocumentDB, and Redshift for automatic credential rotation:

🔄
Auto-Rotation

RDS rotation: Secrets Manager calls a Lambda that creates a new database password, updates both the database AND the secret simultaneously. Old password still works during the transition. Staging labels: AWSPENDING (new), AWSCURRENT (active). Rotation complete in seconds.

🌐
Cross-Account Access

Share secrets across accounts via resource-based policies. Central security account stores all secrets; workload accounts read them via ESO. Audit: CloudTrail records every access. No copying secrets between accounts.

📅
Versioning

Every rotation creates a new version with a staging label. Roll back to previous version if rotation fails. Retention: keep N versions, auto-delete oldest. Audit trail: who rotated, when, which version.

31.2 SSM Parameter Store — Simple Configuration Storage

Parameter Store is the simpler, free alternative for configuration that doesn't need rotation:

FeatureSecrets ManagerParameter Store
Rotation✅ Automatic (Lambda-based)❌ Manual only
Cross-Account✅ Resource policy❌ Not natively supported
Cost$0.40/secret/month + APIStandard: FREE, Advanced: $0.05/param/month
Best ForDatabase passwords, API keys that rotateConfig values, feature flags, AMI IDs
Max Size64 KBStandard: 4 KB, Advanced: 8 KB

31.3 AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) — TLS Made Easy

ACM provisions, manages, and deploys public and private TLS certificates. It auto-renews certificates before they expire — no more 3 AM "cert expired" emergencies:

🔒
Public Certificates

Free TLS certificates for your domains. ACM validates ownership via DNS (CNAME record) or email. Auto-renewed 60 days before expiry. Deploy to: ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, Elastic Beanstalk. Certificates are regional (except CloudFront — us-east-1 only).

🏢
Private CA

Your own internal Certificate Authority. Issue certificates for internal domains (.internal, .corp), mTLS between services, IoT devices. Integrates with AWS App Mesh and EKS for service-to-service mTLS. Pay $400/month per CA (shared-mode available for cheaper dev use).

📧 DEEP DIVE: ACM Validation Methods — DNS vs Email

ACM must prove you own the domain before issuing a certificate. Two methods, one clear winner:

✅ DNS Validation — Set and Forget
Route 53 — One-Click CNAME Record
# ACM provides this CNAME record:
Name:  _abc123.anihpj.example.com.
Type:  CNAME
Value: _xyz789.acm-validations.aws.

# Add to Route 53 → ACM validates → cert issued in minutes
# 60 days before expiry: ACM checks CNAME → auto-renews
🔄
Auto-Renewal Works

CNAME record stays in Route 53 forever. ACM checks it exists → renewal succeeds. No human intervention. Ever.

⭐
Wildcard Support

*.anihpj.example.com covers ALL subdomains with ONE certificate. Email validation doesn't support wildcards.

❌ Email Validation — The Silent Killer

🔴 This method WILL cause a production outage:

  • ACM emails: admin@, postmaster@, webmaster@ + WHOIS contacts
  • Someone must click the approval link within 72 hours
  • At renewal: ACM sends the SAME emails again — if nobody clicks → cert silently expires
  • Your site goes down. At 3 AM. On a Saturday.

🎯 The Rule: Production = DNS validation, ALWAYS. Email only for one-off tests.

31.4 AWS KMS — Key Management Service

KMS creates and manages encryption keys. It's the foundation for encryption across ALL AWS services — S3, EBS, RDS, Secrets Manager, SQS, SNS, and more all use KMS under the hood:

🔑
AWS-Managed CMK
AWS Owned 3yr Rotation
CreatedAutomatically by AWS service
Nameaws/service-name
PolicyAWS controls — you can't edit
Best ForDefault encryption, no fine-grained control
🗝️
Customer-Managed CMK
YOU Own Yearly Rot. Cross-Acct
CreatedManually by YOU
PolicyFull control — IAM + Key Policy
AuditCloudTrail logs every use
Best ForCompliance, access control, audit
🌐
Multi-Region Key
Global Same Material
🗝️ Primary ↔ 🗝️ Replica
Encrypt in us-east-1, decrypt in eu-west-1 — same key. Replicas can be promoted to primary.
🔐 DEEP DIVE: KMS Envelope Encryption
1
Customer Master Key (CMK)

Stored in KMS — NEVER leaves AWS. Used only to encrypt/decrypt data keys (small operations). Customer-managed CMKs: YOU control the key policy (who can use it, who can administer it). AWS-managed CMKs: AWS controls the policy. Supports automatic yearly rotation.

2
Generate Data Key

Your application calls KMS: GenerateDataKey. KMS returns TWO copies: plaintext data key (use to encrypt YOUR data) and encrypted data key (store WITH your data). The data key does the actual heavy lifting — encrypting gigabytes of data.

3
Envelope: Store Both Together

Encrypted data + encrypted data key stored together (S3 object, EBS volume, RDS instance). To decrypt: send encrypted data key to KMS → KMS decrypts using CMK → use plaintext data key to decrypt data. CMK never leaves KMS. Only data keys travel.

🔐 DEEP DIVE: HashiCorp Vault vs AWS Secrets Manager — When to Use Which

Both manage secrets. The choice depends on your architecture and requirements:

☁️
AWS Secrets Manager

Best for: AWS-native workloads. Managed, no servers to run. Native RDS rotation. Cross-account via resource policies. $0.40/secret/month. Integrated with EKS via External Secrets Operator. Choose this unless you need multi-cloud or dynamic secrets.

🏗️
HashiCorp Vault

Best for: multi-cloud, dynamic secrets, advanced PKI. You run the servers (EC2 or EKS). Dynamic database credentials (auto-created, short-lived, auto-revoked). PKI engine (your own CA). Kubernetes auth method (Pod identity → Vault role). More powerful but more ops overhead. Vault Sidecar Injector for EKS.

Q1

How does Secrets Manager auto-rotation work for RDS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Lambda function: creates new password in RDS, updates secret with staging label AWSPENDING, updates RDS with new password, confirms connection works, promotes AWSPENDING to AWSCURRENT. Old password continues working during transition. Zero-downtime rotation.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — Secrets & Certs. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store — when to use which?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Secrets Manager: database passwords, API keys needing rotation, cross-account sharing. Paid but with auto-rotation. Parameter Store: config values, feature flags, AMI IDs, non-sensitive data. Free for standard params. Use Secrets Manager for anything that rotates or is shared across accounts.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — Secrets & Certs. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q3

How does ACM handle certificate renewal?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

ACM auto-renews certificates 60 days before expiry. No action needed — as long as the domain validation (DNS CNAME or email) is still valid. ACM provisions the new certificate and updates all associated resources (ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway) automatically. Imported certificates must be renewed manually.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — Secrets & Certs. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q4

What is envelope encryption in KMS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

CMK encrypts a data key (small). Data key encrypts actual data (large). Store encrypted data + encrypted data key together. CMK never leaves KMS — only data keys travel outside. Enables encrypting terabytes with a single CMK without hitting KMS API limits.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — Secrets & Certs. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q5

When would you use AWS Private CA?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Internal PKI for: mTLS between microservices (Istio/App Mesh), internal domains (.internal, .corp), IoT device certificates, code signing. $400/month per CA. Shared-mode for cheaper dev use. Integrates with ACM — issue private certs through the same API as public certs.

📖 EXPLANATION

Q6

What are KMS key policies vs IAM policies?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Key policy: resource-based policy on the KMS key itself. Required — without it, nobody can use the key. Defines key administrators and key users. IAM policy: identity-based policy on the user/role. Must also allow kms:Encrypt/Decrypt. BOTH key policy AND IAM policy must allow access — intersection of permissions.

Q7

Where can you deploy ACM certificates?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, Elastic Beanstalk, AppSync, Amplify, and Nitro Enclaves. NOT directly on EC2 (use ACM to get the cert, then export to EC2 via AWS Private CA). CloudFront requires certificates in us-east-1 region; all other services use the same region as the resource.

Q8

What are Secrets Manager staging labels?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

AWSCURRENT: the active version being served to clients. AWSPENDING: the new version being tested during rotation. AWSPREVIOUS: the previously current version (for rollback). Rotation works: create AWSPENDING → test → promote to AWSCURRENT → old becomes AWSPREVIOUS. Rollback: promote AWSPREVIOUS back to AWSCURRENT.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — Secrets & Certs. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q9

Does KMS support automatic key rotation?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Yes — for customer-managed CMKs with AWS-generated key material. Automatic rotation: yearly. KMS creates new backing key material but keeps the same key ID and ARN — transparent to applications. Manually rotate on-demand if needed. AWS-managed CMKs: rotated every 3 years automatically. Imported key material: never auto-rotated — you must import new material.

How do you share a secret across AWS accounts?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Attach a resource-based policy to the secret allowing the target account's principals. Target account uses ESO or SDK to read the secret. Both accounts need KMS access to the encryption key. CloudTrail records cross-account access. No copying secrets — single source of truth in the central account.

Chapter 32: Secure CI/CD — DevSecOps

DevSecOps shifts security left — instead of checking for vulnerabilities before release, you check at every commit. SAST scans source code, DAST tests running apps, SCA audits dependencies, and image scanning catches CVEs in containers. Security becomes part of the pipeline, not a gate at the end.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 6: Security 17% & Domain 1: SDLC 22% 📝 10 Questions

32.1 Shift Left Security — The DevSecOps Philosophy

"Shift left" means moving security testing earlier in the development lifecycle. The earlier you find a vulnerability, the cheaper it is to fix:

1
Developer's IDE

SAST plugins (SonarLint, Snyk, Checkmarx) scan code as you type. Secrets detection (git-secrets, truffleHog) catches credentials before commit. Pre-commit hooks block secrets from being committed.

2
Pull Request

Automated SAST scan on PR. Dependency check (SCA) for known CVEs. Infrastructure-as-Code scanning (cfn_nag, Checkov, tfsec). If any critical finding → PR blocked from merge. Review required from security team for sensitive changes.

3
CI/CD Pipeline

Build: image scanning on docker build. Test: DAST against staging. Deploy: admission control (Gatekeeper) validates K8s manifests. Post-deploy: penetration testing, compliance scanning.

32.2 SAST, DAST & SCA — The Security Testing Triad

TypeWhat It ScansWhenTools
SAST (Static)Source code — finds patterns like SQL injection, hardcoded secretsAt commit / PRSonarQube, Checkmarx, CodeGuru, Bandit (Python)
DAST (Dynamic)Running application — finds runtime vulnerabilitiesStaging / Pre-prodOWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, AWS Inspector
SCA (Composition)Dependencies — finds known CVEs in librariesAt buildSnyk, Dependabot, OWASP Dependency-Check

32.3 ECR Image Scanning — Container Security

ECR scans container images for OS and language package vulnerabilities on every push:

ECR Scanning Pipeline
# Enable scan on push
aws ecr put-image-scanning-configuration \
  --repository-name anihpj \
  --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true

# Push triggers automatic scan
docker push ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0

# Check scan results
aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings \
  --repository-name anihpj \
  --image-id imageTag=v1.0

# Common findings: CVE-2023-XXXX in libssl (HIGH), CVE in pip packages (MEDIUM)
# Pipeline gate: if CRITICAL findings → fail build → block deployment

32.4 Pipeline Security Best Practices

A secure pipeline protects every stage: source code integrity, build isolation, artifact trust, and deployment authorization. Here's the complete security flow from commit to cluster:

1 Source: Protect the Code
🔒
Branch Protection

Require PR reviews before merge. Block direct pushes to main. Require status checks to pass (tests, SAST, linting). Signed commits verify author identity. Protected branches prevent force-push overwrites.

🔍
Secret Detection

Pre-commit hooks scan for credentials patterns. If an AWS access key (AKIA...) is detected → commit is BLOCKED. Tools: git-secrets, truffleHog, detect-secrets. Catches secrets BEFORE they enter the repo — not after.

2 Build: Isolate & Scan
🔑
Secrets Injection
# buildspec.yml — NEVER put secrets here
env:
  secrets-manager:
    DB_PASSWORD: "anihpj/db:password"
    SECRET_KEY: "anihpj/django:secret_key"
  variables:
    ECR_REPO: "anihpj"  # Non-sensitive only

CodeBuild fetches secrets at build time from Secrets Manager. Secrets appear as masked **** in logs. IAM role must have secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on specific secrets only — never wildcard.

🔬
Multi-Layer Scanning

SAST: Bandit (Python), SonarQube. SCA: pip-audit, Snyk. Image: ECR scan-on-push (OS + package CVEs). IaC: cfn_nag, Checkov. Gate: CRITICAL finding → build FAILS → deployment BLOCKED. No exceptions without security team approval.

3 Artifact: Sign & Trust
Cosign — Sign Image After Build + Scan
# Generate key pair (once per pipeline)
cosign generate-key-pair

# Sign image ONLY after ALL scans pass
cosign sign --key cosign.key \
  ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0

# Verify signature before deployment (admission controller)
cosign verify --key cosign.pub \
  ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0
# Verification FAILS → Pod creation BLOCKED
✍️
Why Sign?

Proves the image came from YOUR pipeline — not an attacker who compromised ECR credentials. Signature is a separate OCI artifact stored alongside the image. Admission controller verifies signature before allowing Pod creation. Keyless signing (Sigstore/OIDC) eliminates key management.

📜
SLSA Provenance

Build provenance records: which commit, which build pipeline, which builder image, what inputs. SLSA Level 2+: hosted build service + signed provenance. SLSA Level 3: non-falsifiable attestations. Every production artifact is traceable back to its source.

4 Deploy: Least-Privilege Gates
📥
Source Role

codecommit:GitPull only. Cannot deploy, build, or read secrets.

🔨
Build Role

ecr:PutImage, specific secret reads. Cannot deploy to EKS.

🚀
Deploy Role

eks:DescribeCluster, codedeploy:CreateDeployment. Cannot read source or modify builds.

Each stage has its OWN IAM role. Compromise one stage → only that stage's permissions are exposed. Combined with SCPs at the account level, this is defense in depth for your delivery pipeline.

What does "shift left" mean in DevSecOps?

The earlier a vulnerability is found, the cheaper it is to fix. A vulnerability found in IDE costs minutes; found in production costs days and potentially data breaches.

Scans your dependencies (requirements.txt, package.json, pom.xml) for known CVEs. Example: Django 4.2.1 has CVE-2023-XXXX. SCA flags it and suggests upgrade to 4.2.3. Tools: Snyk, Dependabot, OWASP Dependency-Check. Run at every build — new CVEs are discovered daily.
