PART 9 Incident & Event Response

Chapter 33: Event-Driven Automation on AWS

Event-driven automation is the backbone of DevOps at scale. AWS provides four core services that turn "something happened" into "something responded automatically" — EventBridge routes events, SNS notifies people/systems, SQS decouples workloads, and Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows. Together, they eliminate manual toil and reduce MTTR from hours to seconds.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 Domain 5: Incident Mgmt 14% 📝 10 Questions

33.1 Amazon EventBridge — The Central Nervous System

EventBridge is AWS's serverless event bus — it ingests events from AWS services, your custom applications, and SaaS partners, then routes them to targets based on rules. Think of it as the central nervous system of your event-driven architecture:

📥 Event Sources
AWS Services Custom Apps Scheduled SaaS Partners

EC2 state changes, CodeDeploy status, RDS backup complete, custom "order placed" events, cron schedules, Datadog/PagerDuty/Auth0 events

🎯 Event Bus → Rules → Targets
EventBridge Rule — React to EC2 Termination
{
  "Source": ["aws.ec2"],
  "DetailType": ["EC2 Instance State-change Notification"],
  "Detail": { "state": ["terminated"] }
}
// Targets: Lambda → SNS → SQS → Step Functions → CloudWatch Logs
// ONE event can fan out to up to 5 targets per rule
🔀
Event Bus Types

Default Bus: AWS service events auto-published here (EC2, S3, CodeDeploy). Custom Bus: your application events (anihpj.order.placed). Partner Bus: SaaS provider events (Datadog, Auth0). Cross-account: send events to buses in other accounts via resource policy.

📐
Schema Registry

Auto-discovers event structure from your bus. Generates code bindings (Python/Java/TypeScript) so you know exactly what fields an event contains. No more guessing event.detail.someField — the schema tells you. Versioned schemas prevent breaking changes.

⏪
Event Replay

Replay past events for debugging or recovery. If a downstream Lambda was broken for 2 hours, replay those 2 hours of events to catch up. Archive events to S3 for long-term retention. Replay from archive: pick a time window → events are re-published to the bus.

💡 EVENTBRIDGE FOR anihpj — Real Automation Examples
📝
New Job Posted → Instant Search
anihpj app → Custom Bus → Rule: jobpost.created → Lambda: index→OpenSearch
⚠️
Spot Interruption → Graceful Node Drain
EC2 Spot Warning → Default Bus → Lambda: cordon+drain + SNS: notify ops
🚀
Deploy Failure → Slack Alert
CodeDeploy → Default Bus → SNS → #anihpj-deployments
🔀
Cross-Account Event Delivery
Acct A → Event Bus (B) → Acct B Targets

Resource policy on receiver bus allows PutEvents. No VPC peering. All accounts → Security account for centralized monitoring.

⏪
Archive & Replay — Event Sourcing
📦 Archive (S3) → ⏪ Replay → Bus

Store all events indefinitely. Replay any time window. Bug for 3 days → replay 3 days. KMS-encrypted archives.

🔄
Input Transformer — Reshape Events
Raw event → InputPath (extract) → InputTemplate (reshape) → Target

Reshape JSON without a Lambda. Extract fields with InputPath, build new payload with InputTemplate + static text. Zero Lambda cost, zero cold start.

🌐
API Destinations — Call External APIs
EventBridge → HTTPS (Slack/Datadog/GitHub)

Auth via Secrets Manager. Rate limiting built-in. No Lambda proxy. Deployment failure → direct Slack webhook.

33.2 SNS & SQS — Messaging That Scales

SNS (pub/sub push) and SQS (queue pull) form the messaging backbone. Together they enable the fanout pattern — one message distributed to multiple systems simultaneously:

📢
SNS — Push to Many

Publish once, deliver to ALL subscribers. Lambda, SQS, HTTP/S, Email, SMS, Mobile Push. Message filtering ensures each subscriber only gets relevant messages.

SNS Fanout — 1 Topic → Multiple SQS Queues
SNS Topic: anihpj-events
  ├── SQS Queue: order-processing (filter: type=order)
  ├── SQS Queue: notification-service (filter: type=notification)
  ├── SQS Queue: analytics-pipeline (filter: type=*)
  ├── Lambda: index-in-opensearch
  └── HTTP/S: Slack webhook

# Each team gets their OWN queue — decoupled processing
📬
SQS — Pull When Ready
Feature⚡ Standard📋 FIFO
ThroughputNearly unlimited300 msg/sec (batch), 3,000/sec (high throughput)
OrderingBest-effortStrictly preserved
DeduplicationOccasional duplicatesExactly-once (5-min window)
Use CaseDecoupling, bufferingFinancial transactions, order processing
📯
SNS FIFO Topics — Ordered + Deduplicated
✅ Exactly-Once 📋 Strict Order ⚡ 300/s
Group IDOrdering within one group (e.g., per userId)
Dedup IDPrevents duplicates within 5-min window
SubscribersSQS FIFO queues only — no mixing
🔄
SNS Retry & Durability — Never Lose a Message
Retry: 0s→ 1s→ 2s→ 4s→ 8s→ ... ×20
● SQS subscription never deleted — infinite retry
● Lambda/HTTP: 20 retries → DLQ captures failure
● Cross-region delivery: no VPC peering needed
☠️
Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)
📨 Source Queue → 🔄 3× retry → ☠️ DLQ
maxReceiveCount: 3 → after 3 failures → messages land in DLQ. Set CloudWatch Alarm on DLQ depth > 0 to auto-investigate.
⏱️
Visibility Timeout & Long Polling
👁️ Visibility

Message hidden for N sec. Not deleted → reappears (retry). Default: 30s. Max: 12h.

⏳ Long Polling

Wait up to 20s. 99% fewer empty responses. Always use in production.

📦
SQS Batch Processing — Efficiency at Scale
10 msg/call Lambda: 10K/batch 300s window
✅Partial failure: only failed messages retried, rest deleted
⚡FIFO throughput: 3,000 msg/sec. Standard: unlimited
🎯
Message Groups — FIFO Ordering at Scale
User A
msg₁ → msg₂ → msg₃
In Order
User B
msg₁ → msg₂ → msg₃
In Order

Both groups process in parallel — one group = one consumer at a time.

⏳
Delay Queues & Message Timers
⏳ Delay Queue0–900s, all messages invisible until delay elapses
⏱️ Message TimerPer-message override of queue-level delay

💡 anihpj: Send job approval msg now → invisible 24h → check if approved. No polling loop needed.

🔀
SNS Subscription Filter Policies
Filter: {"type": ["order"], "priority": ["high", "critical"]}
Only matching messages delivered → no wasted processing in consumer code.
🔗 SNS Filter Policy — Real anihpj Example
Subscription Filter Policy — Route by Event Type
{
  "order-processing-queue": {
    "FilterPolicy": {
      "event_type": ["job.created", "job.updated"],
      "priority": ["high", "critical"]
    }
  },
  "notification-queue": {
    "FilterPolicy": {
      "event_type": ["notification.email", "notification.slack"]
    }
  },
  "analytics-queue": {
    "FilterPolicy": {}  // Empty = receive ALL events
  }
}
// SNS publishes ONE message → each queue gets only what it needs

33.3 AWS Step Functions — Workflows as State Machines

Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows with built-in error handling, retries, and parallel execution. Instead of chaining Lambdas manually with fragile error logic, you define a state machine — and Step Functions handles the rest:

⚡ Standard Workflows

Duration: Up to 1 year. Pricing: per state transition ($0.025/1,000). Execution model: exactly-once, with execution history. Best for: long-running, auditable workflows — order processing, human approval steps, multi-day data pipelines.

✅ Guaranteed: if a step fails, Step Functions retries with exponential backoff. You define retry policy — no custom code needed.
🚀 Express Workflows

Duration: Up to 5 minutes. Pricing: per execution + duration ($1.00/million). Execution model: at-least-once (synchronous) or at-most-once (async). Best for: high-volume, short-duration — IoT ingestion, API orchestration, real-time event processing.

⚡ Speed: Express workflows execute ~10x faster than Standard. No execution history stored beyond CloudWatch Logs.
🔧 DEEP DIVE: Incident Response Workflow — Step Functions ASL

This state machine automates the entire incident response lifecycle — detect → isolate → notify → recover — without a human touching anything until the Slack notification fires:

Amazon States Language — Incident Response for anihpj
{
  "StartAt": "DetectAnomaly",
  "States": {
    "DetectAnomaly": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789:function:detect-anomaly",
      "Next": "IsolateResource"
    },
    "IsolateResource": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789:function:isolate-instance",
      "Retry": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "IntervalSeconds": 5, "MaxAttempts": 3, "BackoffRate": 2 }],
      "Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "Next": "NotifyFailure" }],
      "Next": "NotifySecurity"
    },
    "NotifySecurity": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:publish",
      "Parameters": { "TopicArn": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789:anihpj-security", "Message.$": "$" },
      "Next": "RecoverService"
    },
    "RecoverService": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789:function:recover-service",
      "End": true
    },
    "NotifyFailure": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:publish",
      "Parameters": { "TopicArn": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789:anihpj-oncall", "Message": "Auto-isolation FAILED — manual intervention required" },
      "End": true
    }
  }
}
Flow: 🔍 DetectAnomaly → 🔒 IsolateResource (retry×3) → 📢 NotifySecurity → 🔄 RecoverService
🔌
200+ Service Integrations

Call any AWS service directly from your state machine — no Lambda wrapper, no cold start, no custom code.

⚡ Request Response (Sync)
DynamoDB GetItem/PutItem • SQS SendMessage • ECS RunTask • Lambda Invoke • API Gateway
✅ Returns result immediately
⏳ Sync Run Job (Polling)
Athena StartQueryExecution • Glue StartJobRun • Batch SubmitJob • EMR AddJobFlowSteps
⏳ Polls until job completes. Configure HeartbeatSeconds + TimeoutSeconds
🔄
Parallel & Map States
Parallel: Run branches simultaneously — check 3 anomaly systems at once, aggregate results when all complete.
Map: Process each item in an array. 100 orders → 100 parallel executions. MaxConcurrency controls parallelism.
Map State — Process 100 Orders with Max 10 Concurrent
"ProcessOrders": {
  "Type": "Map",
  "ItemsPath": "$.orders",
  "MaxConcurrency": 10,
  "Iterator": {
    "StartAt": "ValidateOrder",
    "States": { "ValidateOrder": { "Type": "Task", ... } }
  }
}
⏸️
Human Approval Steps

Pause execution indefinitely and wait for a human to approve or reject — no timeout unless you set one.

Task Token → SNS → Email/Slack → Human Clicks → SendTaskSuccess(token)

⚡ HeartbeatSeconds: if no heartbeat received within the window, the task times out and routes to a Catch fallback state.

🔀 Choice States & Wait States — Conditional Logic + Timed Pauses
Choice State — Branch Without Lambda

A Choice state evaluates conditions and routes to different branches — no Lambda needed for branching logic. Rules: StringEquals, NumericGreaterThan, BooleanEquals, TimestampLessThan, and compound AND/OR/NOT. Example: if anomaly score > 0.8 → escalate to human; if 0.5-0.8 → auto-isolate; if <0.5 → log and continue. Default: a catch-all fallback when no rule matches — prevents stuck executions.

Wait State — Timed Pauses

Pause execution for a specified duration or until a timestamp. Seconds: "Seconds": 300 — wait 5 minutes before proceeding. Timestamp: "Timestamp": "2026-06-12T09:00:00Z" — wait until a specific UTC time. SecondsPath/TimestampPath: dynamically pick the value from input JSON. Use case: anihpj incident response — IsolateResource → Wait 60 seconds for drain → then RecoverService.

🔁 SQS Redrive Policy — Automated DLQ Recovery

The redrive policy lets you move messages FROM a DLQ back to the source queue for reprocessing — after you've fixed the bug that caused the failures:

1
Messages Fail → DLQ

After maxReceiveCount (e.g., 3) failed processing attempts, messages move to the DLQ. CloudWatch alarm fires on DLQ depth > 0.

2
Fix the Bug

Engineer investigates DLQ messages, identifies the root cause (e.g., malformed JSON, missing field), and deploys a fix to the consumer Lambda.

3
Redrive to Source Queue

Use the SQS console or CLI: aws sqs start-message-move-task — all DLQ messages are moved back to the source queue for reprocessing.

4
Messages Processed Correctly

The fixed Lambda processes messages successfully. DLQ empties. No data is lost — every message eventually gets processed.

33.4 Auto-Remediation Patterns — Self-Healing AWS

Auto-remediation is the holy grail of DevOps — the system detects a problem and fixes it before a human even notices. Here are the battle-tested patterns:

🔄
Pattern 1: Replace Unhealthy Resources
MTTR <2m$0
⚡ Trigger

CloudWatch Alarm: EC2 StatusCheckFailed or ELB UnhealthyHostCount

🎯 Action

ASG terminates unhealthy instance, launches replacement

☸️ EKS: Liveness probe fails → kubelet restarts. Readiness fails → Pod removed from Service.

🔐
Pattern 2: Security Auto-Block
MTTR <30s
⚡ Trigger

GuardDuty finding (CryptoCurrency:EC2) or WAF rate-limit breach

🎯 Action

EventBridge → Lambda → NACL DENY rule or WAF IP block

🐳 anihpj: GuardDuty → EventBridge → Lambda isolate instance + Slack alert.

📜
Pattern 3: Certificate Auto-Renewal
Silent
⚡ Trigger

ACM cert approaching expiry (60 days before)

🎯 Action

ACM checks CNAME → re-issues → deploys to ALB/CloudFront. Zero touch.

⚠️ DNS validation ONLY. Email-validated certs require manual click at renewal.

📈
Pattern 4: Auto-Scale Based on Load
Proactive
⚡ Trigger

CPUUtilization > 70% for 5 min, or custom SQS queue depth metric

🎯 Action

ASG scaling policy adds instances, KEDA/HPA scales EKS Pods

🐳 anihpj: SQS depth > 100 → HPA: jobpost-worker 2 → 8 replicas. Queue empties → scale back to 2.

⚡ Auto-Remediation Decision Flow — Choose the Right Pattern
1
Is the failure self-healing by AWS?

ASG health checks, K8s probes, ACM renewal → AWS handles it. No custom code needed.

2
Can EventBridge + Lambda handle it?

Security finding, spot interruption, deployment failure → EventBridge rule → Lambda. Write once, run forever.

3
Is it a multi-step workflow?

Incident response, disaster recovery failover → Step Functions state machine. Orchestrate 10+ steps with retries and error handling.

4
Does it need human judgment?

Any step requiring approval → SNS notification → human clicks approve via Slack/Jira → Step Functions resumes. Semi-automated with human in the loop.

Q1

What is the difference between EventBridge and SNS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

EventBridge: Event bus with rule-based routing — pattern matching on event content. Supports schema registry, event replay, cross-account buses. Used for event-driven architectures. SNS: Pub/sub messaging with topic-based routing — push to all subscribers. Simpler, but no content-based filtering (except subscription filter policies). Fanout: SNS → multiple SQS queues.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

When would you use SQS FIFO over Standard?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

When message order matters (financial transactions, order processing) and duplicates would cause problems (exactly-once processing needed). FIFO guarantees first-in-first-out and deduplication within 5 minutes. Tradeoff: 300 msg/sec (batch) vs nearly unlimited for Standard.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q3

What is a Dead Letter Queue and why use it?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

A DLQ captures messages that fail processing after a configured number of attempts (maxReceiveCount). Without a DLQ, poison-pill messages are retried indefinitely, blocking the queue. With DLQ: after N failures → move to DLQ → main queue continues processing. Set CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth > 0 to investigate failures.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q4

Standard vs Express Step Functions — when to use each?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Standard: Long-running (up to 1 year), exactly-once execution, full execution history, per-state pricing. Use for: order processing, human approval workflows, data pipelines. Express: Short (≤5 min), high-volume (100K+/sec), at-least-once or at-most-once, per-execution pricing. Use for: IoT ingestion, API orchestration, real-time event processing.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q5

How does the SNS fanout pattern work?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

One SNS topic → multiple SQS queues (one per team/service). Each team processes messages at their own pace. If one consumer fails, others are unaffected. SNS pushes the same message to all subscribed queues. Message filtering: each queue only receives messages matching its filter policy (e.g., type=order). Decoupled, resilient, scalable.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q6

What are EventBridge event buses and when do you need custom ones?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Default bus: AWS service events auto-published here (free). Custom bus: your application events — needed when you want to publish custom events that AWS doesn't generate. Partner bus: SaaS provider events. Custom buses give you: schema registry, event replay, cross-account sharing, and isolation from AWS events. anihpj would use a custom bus for jobpost.created, order.placed, etc.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q7

How does Step Functions handle errors and retries?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Built-in ASL constructs: Retry: exponential backoff with configurable interval, max attempts, and backoff rate. Catch: route specific errors to fallback states. Timeout: if a task exceeds its time limit, route to fallback. Example: Retry 3× with 5s/10s/20s intervals → catch all errors → notify on-call. No custom retry logic needed in Lambda code.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q8

What is SQS long polling and why use it?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Instead of returning immediately with empty response (short polling), SQS waits up to 20 seconds for a message to arrive. Reduces empty responses by ~99%, lowers CPU usage on consumers, and reduces costs (fewer API calls). Enabled by default on new queues via ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds. Always use long polling in production.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q9

How would you automate Spot Instance interruption handling for anihpj EKS?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

1. EventBridge rule captures EC2 Spot Instance Interruption Warning. 2. Rule triggers Lambda that: (a) uses kubectl cordon to mark the node as unschedulable, (b) uses kubectl drain to evict Pods gracefully, (c) publishes SNS notification to #anihpj-ops. 3. AWS Node Termination Handler (open-source) does this automatically — deploy as DaemonSet on spot node groups.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 6 (Security, 12%) — IAM Advanced. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q10

How do you set up EventBridge cross-account event delivery?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

1. In the RECEIVER account: add resource policy on the event bus allowing PutEvents from the SENDER account. 2. In the SENDER account: create a rule targeting the RECEIVER account's event bus ARN. 3. Events flow: Sender account → EventBridge → Receiver account event bus → Receiver account targets. Used for centralized security monitoring (all accounts → security account).

Chapter 34: Incident Response & Disaster Recovery

When things go wrong — and they will — your ability to detect, respond, and recover determines whether it's a 5-minute blip or a 5-hour outage. This chapter covers the full spectrum: from automated incident response runbooks to multi-region disaster recovery architectures for the anihpj EKS platform.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 Domain 5: Incident Mgmt 14% & Domain 3: Resiliency 15% 📝 10 Questions

34.1 RTO, RPO & DR Strategies — How Fast Must You Recover?

Two numbers define your disaster recovery requirements. Everything else — architecture, cost, tooling — flows from them:

⏱️ RTO — Recovery Time Objective

RTO

"How long can we be DOWN?"

Measured from the moment of disaster to the moment service is restored. RTO = 5 min means you need near-instant failover (Multi-Site Active/Active). RTO = 4 hours means Backup & Restore may suffice.

📊 RPO — Recovery Point Objective

RPO

"How much data can we LOSE?"

Measured in time — the maximum acceptable data loss window. RPO = 0 means synchronous replication (no data lost). RPO = 1 hour means hourly backups are acceptable.

� The Incident Response Lifecycle — NIST-Based 5-Phase Model

Before you design DR strategies, you need a response process. This is the industry-standard lifecycle every DevOps engineer must know — from the moment an alarm fires to the post-mortem review:

1
Detection

CloudWatch Alarm fires (or user reports issue). On-call engineer acknowledges via PagerDuty. Goal: confirm the incident is real, not a false alarm. Time target: <5 minutes. Tools: CloudWatch Alarms, X-Ray Service Map, GuardDuty findings.

2
Analysis

Determine scope and impact. Is it a single Pod or the entire region? Check X-Ray Service Map, CloudWatch metrics, recent deployments (CloudTrail). Goal: identify WHAT is broken and HOW bad it is. Time target: <15 minutes. Communicate: update status page, Slack #incident channel.

3
Containment

Stop the bleeding. Rollback the bad deployment. Isolate the compromised instance. Block the malicious IP. Goal: prevent the incident from getting WORSE, even if the root cause isn't yet known. Example: if anihpj /jobs/ is returning 500s → roll back to last known good deployment.

4
Eradication

Remove the root cause. Apply the missing database index. Fix the misconfigured security group. Patch the vulnerable library. Goal: permanently eliminate the cause so it can't recur. Difference from containment: containment stops damage NOW; eradication fixes the root cause.

5
Recovery

Restore full service. Verify all systems healthy. Monitor for 30+ minutes to confirm stability. Goal: return to normal operations with confidence. Post-recovery: schedule blameless post-mortem within 24-48 hours. Update runbooks based on lessons learned.

�🛡️
🛡️ DR STRATEGY SPECTRUM — Cost vs RTO/RPO Tradeoff
📞
Escalation Policies & On-Call

Primary on-call: First responder, acknowledged within 5 minutes. Secondary: Escalated if primary doesn't acknowledge within 15 minutes. Manager: Escalated after 30 minutes of no response. Tools: PagerDuty, Opsgenie, AWS Incident Manager. Best practice: Never alert a single person — always have a backup. Rotate weekly, not daily (context switching kills response quality).

🚨
Severity Levels — Standard Classification

SEV1 (Critical): Complete service outage, revenue impact. War room immediately. SEV2 (Major): Major feature broken, no workaround. Page on-call. SEV3 (Minor): Partial degradation, workaround exists. Create ticket, SLA: 4 hours. SEV4 (Low): Cosmetic issue, no user impact. Backlog. Rule: if you're not sure, escalate UP. It's always better to de-escalate later than to under-react.

StrategyCostRTORPOHow It WorksBest For
Backup & Restore$HoursHoursRegular backups to S3 cross-region. On disaster: restore EBS snapshots, RDS snapshots, Velero EKS restore.Dev/Staging, non-critical workloads
Pilot Light$$10-30 minMinutesMinimal core services running in DR region. Data replicated (RDS cross-region read replica, S3 CRR). On disaster: provision full environment from CloudFormation/Terraform.Production with moderate RTO
Warm Standby$$$5-15 minSecondsScaled-down copy running in DR region. ASG min=1. RDS read replica promoted to primary. On disaster: scale UP → switch Route 53 DNS.Production with aggressive RTO

34.2 Backup & Restore on AWS — The Foundation

Every DR strategy starts with backups. AWS provides managed backup services that automate scheduling, retention, and cross-region replication:

💾
AWS Backup — Centralized Command

Policy-driven backup for 15+ AWS services from a single console.

📅 Schedule
Daily + Weekly + Monthly
💿 Retention
7d + 4w + 12m
🌍 Cross-Region
Auto-copy to DR
🔒 Vault Lock
WORM — undeletable
CLI: Create Backup Plan for anihpj RDS
aws backup create-backup-plan \
  --backup-plan '{
    "BackupPlanName": "anihpj-daily-plan",
    "Rules": [{
      "RuleName": "DailyBackup",
      "ScheduleExpression": "cron(0 3 * * ? *)",
      "StartWindowMinutes": 60,
      "CompletionWindowMinutes": 120,
      "Lifecycle": { "DeleteAfterDays": 30 },
      "CopyActions": [{
        "DestinationBackupVaultArn": "arn:aws:backup:eu-west-1:vault:anihpj-dr",
        "Lifecycle": { "DeleteAfterDays": 90 }
      }]
    }]
  }'
🗄️
RDS Automated Backups

Daily snapshots + continuous transaction logs. Point-in-time recovery to any second within the retention window.

⏱️ Granularity
PITR within 5 min
📆 Retention
1 to 35 days
🌍 Cross-Region
Snapshot copy to DR
⚠️ Caveat
NEW instance — DNS changes
CLI: Restore RDS to a Point in Time
# Restore to 2:31:59 PM — just before table drop
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier anihpj-prod \
  --target-db-instance-identifier anihpj-prod-restored \
  --restore-time "2026-06-11T14:31:59Z" \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.xlarge

# ⚠️ Result: NEW endpoint — update app config!
📦
S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR)

Objects automatically replicated to a bucket in another region. Async replication — typically within seconds to minutes. CRR: Cross-region for DR compliance and latency reduction. SRR: Same-region for log aggregation and compliance.

✅ Requirements

Versioning on BOTH buckets + IAM replication role with S3 read permissions on source + S3 write permissions on destination.

⚠️ Critical Caveat

Existing objects are NOT auto-replicated. Use S3 Batch Replication to backfill. Replication is async — seconds to minutes of lag. Deletes can be replicated (optional).

CLI: Enable S3 CRR on anihpj-assets Bucket
# 1. Enable versioning on both buckets (REQUIRED)
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket anihpj-assets \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket anihpj-assets-dr-eu-west-1 \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# 2. Create replication configuration (IAM role must exist)
aws s3api put-bucket-replication --bucket anihpj-assets \
  --replication-configuration '{
    "Role": "arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/s3-crr-role",
    "Rules": [{"Status":"Enabled","Priority":1,
      "Destination":{"Bucket":"arn:aws:s3:::anihpj-assets-dr-eu-west-1"}
    }]}'

# 3. Backfill existing objects (NOT auto-replicated!)
aws s3api create-batch-job --manifest file://existing-objects.csv

🔄 Backup Lifecycle — How anihpj Data Flows to Safety

Your backup strategy needs to cover three layers: database state, file storage, and Kubernetes configuration. Here's how each service protects anihpj:

🗄️ Layer 1: Database (RDS Aurora PostgreSQL)
●Daily automated snapshots → S3
●5-min PITR via transaction logs
●Aurora Global DB → eu-west-1 (near-real-time)
●Manual snapshot before each migration
RPO:<1 second (Global DB), 5 min (PITR fallback)
📦 Layer 2: Object Storage (S3 anihpj-assets)
●S3 CRR → eu-west-1 (async, seconds)
●Versioning enabled — deleted objects recoverable
●Object Lock: resumes immutable for 7 years (compliance)
RPO:Seconds (CRR lag), minutes (version restore)
☸️ Layer 3: Kubernetes State (Velero → S3)
●Velero daily schedule → S3 (DR region)
●All K8s objects + EBS PV snapshots
●EKS managed etcd: AWS responsibility
RPO:24 hours (daily backup window)
🎯 anihpj Recovery Blueprint: Database → Aurora Global DB (RPO <1s). Files → S3 CRR (RPO seconds). Kubernetes → Velero (RPO 24h). DNS → Route 53 failover (RTO <2min).

Velero backs up your ENTIRE Kubernetes cluster — all resources (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps) AND persistent volumes — to an S3 bucket. On disaster, restore the cluster to any region:

Velero Backup Schedule for anihpj Cluster
apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-daily-backup
  namespace: velero
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"           # Every day at 2 AM
  template:
    includedNamespaces:
      - anihpj-prod
      - anihpj-staging
    excludedResources:
      - events.events.k8s.io
    storageLocation: aws-s3-dr    # S3 bucket in DR region
    snapshotVolumes: true          # Back up EBS PVs too
    ttl: 720h0m0s                  # Retain for 30 days

# Restore to a new EKS cluster in any region:
# velero restore create --from-schedule anihpj-daily-backup
📋 SSM Automation Documents — Runbooks as Code

SSM Automation Documents turn manual runbooks into executable code. Instead of an engineer following a wiki page (and possibly missing a step at 3 AM), the automation document executes the procedure consistently every time:

SSM Automation — Isolate & Snapshot Compromised Instance
---
schemaVersion: '0.3'
description: 'Isolate compromised EC2 instance + take forensic snapshot'
parameters:
  InstanceId:
    type: String
    description: 'The instance to isolate'
mainSteps:
  - name: DetachFromASG
    action: aws:executeAwsApi
    inputs:
      Service: autoscaling
      Api: DetachInstances
      InstanceIds: ["{{ InstanceId }}"]
  - name: QuarantineSG
    action: aws:executeAwsApi
    inputs:
      Service: ec2
      Api: ModifyInstanceAttribute
      InstanceId: "{{ InstanceId }}"
      Groups: ["sg-quarantine"]
  - name: ForensicSnapshot
    action: aws:createImage
    inputs:
      InstanceId: "{{ InstanceId }}"
      NoReboot: true
  - name: NotifySecurity
    action: aws:publishSnsTopic
    inputs:
      TopicArn: "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789:anihpj-security"
      Message: "Instance {{ InstanceId }} isolated and snapshotted"

Triggered by: EventBridge rule matching GuardDuty finding → SSM Automation → quarantined + snapshotted + notified. Consistent every time.

34.3 Multi-Region DR Architecture — Building Resilient Systems

A multi-region architecture means your application survives an entire AWS region going down. Here's the anihpj production reference architecture:

🌍
Route 53 — DNS Failover

Latency-based routing sends users to nearest healthy region. Health checks monitor ALB endpoints in both regions every 30 seconds. If us-east-1 ALB goes unhealthy → Route 53 automatically redirects all traffic to eu-west-1. Failover time: ~60-120 seconds (DNS TTL dependent).

🗄️
Database — Aurora Global Database

One primary region (read/write) + up to 5 secondary regions (read-only). Replication lag: typically <1 second. On disaster: promote secondary to primary in <1 minute. RPO: <1 second (cross-region storage-based replication). For anihpj: PostgreSQL-compatible Aurora Global DB.

☸️
EKS — Two Clusters, One CI/CD

Separate EKS clusters in each region (not stretched — K8s doesn't do well across regions). Same container images in both ECRs (replicated). Same Helm charts. CI/CD deploys to BOTH clusters. Route 53 weighted routing: 80% us-east-1, 20% eu-west-1 (or 100/0 with failover).

📦
S3 & ECR — Cross-Region Replication

S3 CRR: all anihpj assets (resumes, company logos) auto-replicated. ECR cross-region replication: container images pushed to us-east-1 → auto-replicated to eu-west-1. DynamoDB Global Tables: job metadata replicated across regions with conflict resolution (last-write-wins).

34.4 DR for anihpj on EKS — Practical Implementation

Putting it all together for the anihpj job board platform. Here's the complete DR lifecycle — from normal operations through disaster to full recovery:

🟢 Normal Ops → 🔴 Disaster → 🟡 Recovery → 🟢 Normal Ops
📋 Pre-Disaster — Preparation Checklist
☑Velero scheduled backups (daily 2 AM → S3 DR region)
☑Aurora Global DB secondary in eu-west-1
☑ECR cross-region replication enabled
☑CloudFormation templates ready in DR region (Pilot Light)
☑Route 53 health checks on both ALBs
☑Documented DNS failover procedure

🧪 Test quarterly with GameDay exercises

🚨 During Disaster — Execution Runbook
1
Confirm Outage

Is us-east-1 really down? Check AWS Health Dashboard + CloudWatch cross-region metrics.

2
Promote Database

Aurora Global DB: promote eu-west-1 secondary → primary (~1 minute).

3
Provision Infrastructure

Run CloudFormation: deploy EKS cluster in eu-west-1 (Pilot Light → full).

4
Restore Kubernetes

velero restore create from latest S3 backup → all Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps + PVs.

5
Switch DNS

Route 53 failover → eu-west-1 ALB. Health checks already monitoring both endpoints.

6
Verify Recovery

Run smoke tests: curl anihpj.com/api/jobs/ → 200 OK. Monitor for 30+ min.

⏱️ Target RTO: <30 minutes
📊 Post-Disaster — Failback Procedure
1
Sync Data Back

Aurora Global DB replicates from eu-west-1 back to us-east-1. Wait for replication lag = 0.

2
Promote Primary

Promote us-east-1 back to primary. Keep eu-west-1 as secondary for next disaster.

3
Deploy to Primary

Deploy latest anihpj release to us-east-1 EKS cluster. Verify pods are healthy.

4
Switch DNS Back

Route 53 weighted routing: 100% → us-east-1. Monitor for 30+ minutes.

5
Post-Mortem

Schedule within 24-48 hours. Update runbook with lessons learned. Failback must be as practiced as failover.

🧪 Chaos Engineering — Validation Through Destruction

AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) validates your DR plan BEFORE a real disaster:

🔴Node Termination: Kill 50% of EKS worker nodes → verify HPA scales + Pods reschedule
🟡Network Throttle: 500ms latency + 30% packet loss → verify circuit breakers work
🔵CPU Exhaustion: 90% CPU on anihpj-api → verify CloudWatch Alarm + HPA

🎮 GameDays: Quarterly team exercises. "What surprised us?" → update runbooks.

🧪 DEEP DIVE: AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) — Chaos Engineering Done Right

FIS runs controlled experiments on your production (or staging) environment to verify your system handles failure gracefully. It's chaos engineering with guardrails — you define exactly what to break and what the safety limits are:

🔴
EC2 Termination

Experiment: Terminate 50% of EKS worker nodes in a node group.

ValidatesASG auto-replacement, Pod rescheduling, HPA scaling

🗄️ DEEP DIVE: etcd Backup — EKS Control Plane DR

Velero backs up your workloads (Pods, Deployments, PVs), but etcd stores the entire cluster state — all K8s objects, RBAC, and configuration. For self-managed clusters (Kops, Kubeadm), you must back up etcd separately. For EKS (managed control plane), AWS handles etcd — but if you run EKS Anywhere or self-managed nodes:

etcd Backup — Save Cluster State to S3
# 1. Snapshot etcd
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%Y%m%d).db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# 2. Upload to S3 (cross-region)
aws s3 cp /backup/etcd-20260611.db \
  s3://anihpj-etcd-backup-dr/etcd-20260611.db

# 3. Restore on new cluster
etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-20260611.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored

💡 EKS managed: AWS handles etcd — you don't access it. Use Velero for workload backup. Self-managed: etcd backup is YOUR responsibility. Without it, you lose ALL cluster configuration on disaster.

🌐 Route 53 Routing Policies — Choose the Right Failover Strategy
PolicyHow It WorksFailover TimeBest For
FailoverActive/Passive — primary endpoint, secondary on standby. Health check monitors primary. If unhealthy → DNS flips to secondary.60-120s (TTL)Simple DR, single-region apps
Latency-BasedRoute users to region with lowest latency. Multiple active endpoints. Health check filters out unhealthy regions.60-120s (TTL)Multi-region active-active, global user base
GeolocationRoute based on user's geographic location. Compliant with data sovereignty laws.60-120s (TTL)GDPR compliance, regional content
WeightedDistribute traffic by weight (80/20). Gradual failover — shift weight from unhealthy endpoint.Manual (weight change)Blue/green deployments, canary testing
Global AcceleratorNot DNS-based. Anycast IPs route to nearest AWS edge → optimal path to your ALB. Instant failover.<30 secondsLatency-sensitive apps, gaming, real-time

Q1

What's the difference between RTO and RPO?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

RTO (Recovery Time Objective): How long can you be DOWN? Time from disaster to service restoration. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): How much data can you LOSE? Maximum acceptable data age at recovery. RTO = 5 min, RPO = 0 sec → Multi-Site Active/Active. RTO = 4h, RPO = 1h → Backup & Restore.

📖 EXPLANATION

This concept is tested on Domain 3 (Resilient, 20%) — Disaster Recovery. Understanding this is essential for DOP-C02 scenario-based questions.

Q2

Compare the four DR strategies by cost and RTO/RPO.

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Backup & Restore ($): RTO=hours, RPO=hours. Pilot Light ($$): RTO=10-30min, RPO=minutes. Warm Standby ($$$): RTO=5-15min, RPO=seconds. Multi-Site Active/Active ($$$$): RTO=<1min, RPO=near-zero. Cost increases exponentially as RTO/RPO approach zero.

Included/excluded namespaces and resources. Restore: recreate all K8s objects + PVs from snapshots in any EKS cluster (any region).

Q5

What is Aurora Global Database and why use it for DR?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

One primary region (read/write) + up to 5 secondary regions (read-only). Storage-based replication with <1 second lag. On disaster: promote secondary to primary in <1 minute. RPO: <1 second. Much faster than cross-region read replicas (which use logical replication). For anihpj: PostgreSQL-compatible Aurora Global DB.

Q6

How does Route 53 handle multi-region failover?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Route 53 health checks monitor ALB endpoints every 30 seconds. Latency-based routing sends users to nearest healthy region. If primary region ALB fails health checks → Route 53 removes that record from DNS → all traffic routed to secondary region. Failover time: 60-120 seconds (depends on DNS TTL). For faster failover: use Global Accelerator.

Q10

Why shouldn't you stretch a single EKS cluster across regions?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ ANSWER

Kubernetes uses etcd for state — etcd requires low-latency consensus (Raft). Cross-region latency (50-150ms) breaks etcd. Instead: run SEPARATE EKS clusters in each region. Use external tooling (Velero, GitOps) to keep them synchronized. Route 53 handles traffic routing. Each cluster is independent — if one region fails, the other continues unaffected.

Chapter 35: Root Cause Analysis & Post-Mortems

Every incident is a learning opportunity. Root Cause Analysis (RCA) transforms "something broke" into "here's exactly why and how we prevent it forever." Post-mortems turn incidents into actionable improvements — not blame. This chapter covers the methodology, the AWS toolchain, and how to build a culture of continuous improvement.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 5: Incident Mgmt 14% 📝 10 Questions

35.1 The 5 Whys Method — Drilling to Root Cause

The 5 Whys is deceptively simple: ask "why?" five times until you move past symptoms to the systemic root cause. Here it is applied to a real anihpj outage scenario:

🔍 5 WHYS — anihpj /jobs/ Endpoint 500 Outage

Incident: The anihpj /jobs/ endpoint returned HTTP 500 errors for 45 minutes during peak traffic.

1
Why did /jobs/ return 500 errors?

→ Because the database query timed out after 30 seconds.

2
Why did the database query time out?

→ Because the jobpost table has 5 million rows and no index on the skills column used in the WHERE clause.

3
Why is there no index on the skills column?

→ Because the database migration to add the index was written but never applied in production.

4
Why wasn't the migration applied in production?

→ Because the CI/CD pipeline deploys code but database migrations are run manually by a DBA who was on vacation.

5
Why are migrations manual and not automated?

→ Because the team feared automated migrations would corrupt data. No tested rollback strategy existed.

🎯 ROOT CAUSE

Lack of an automated, tested database migration pipeline with rollback capability. The missing index was a symptom; the manual migration process was the disease.

🐟 Fishbone (Ishikawa) Diagram — Categorize Contributing Factors

The Fishbone diagram complements the 5 Whys by categorizing all contributing factors. Draw a horizontal arrow pointing to the problem, then branch off into categories. For the anihpj /jobs/ outage:

🎯 EFFECT: /jobs/ endpoint returning HTTP 500
👤 People

DBA on vacation. No backup person trained. Manual process bottleneck — single point of human failure.

⚙️ Process

DB migrations are manual. No CI/CD integration. No pre-deployment checklist. No rollback plan.

🛠️ Technology

Missing index on skills column. No query performance monitoring. No circuit breaker for slow queries.

📊 Measurement

No CloudWatch alarm on query duration. No SLO for API latency. Issue discovered by users, not monitoring.

🌍 Environment

5M rows in jobpost table — dataset grew 3x in 2 months. No capacity planning. No load testing before deploy.

💡 When to use Fishbone vs 5 Whys: 5 Whys goes DEEP on one causal chain. Fishbone goes WIDE — capturing ALL contributing factors across people, process, technology, measurement, and environment. Use BOTH for a complete RCA.

🌲 Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) — Top-Down Failure Decomposition

While 5 Whys goes linear and Fishbone goes wide, Fault Tree Analysis works top-down. Start with the TOP event (the outage), then ask "What could cause this?" repeatedly, using AND/OR gates between contributing failures:

🔴 TOP EVENT: /jobs/ returns HTTP 500
OR
DB Query Timeout
AND
Missing index (basic event) 5M rows (condition) No query timeout (basic event)
App Code Panic
Unhandled exception (basic event) No circuit breaker (basic event)
Connection Pool Exhausted
Pool size too small (basic event) Slow queries holding connections (condition)

💡 FTA is best for: complex systems where multiple independent failures must align to cause an outage. AND gate = ALL conditions must be true. OR gate = ANY condition triggers the event. Use FTA for: safety-critical systems, complex microservice dependencies, compliance audits.

35.2 Blameless Post-Mortems — Learning Without Fear

A blameless post-mortem focuses on what happened and how to prevent it — not who caused it. When engineers fear punishment, they hide incidents. When they trust the process, they surface problems early:

✅ Blameless Culture
  • "What contributed to this incident?" — NOT "Whose fault was it?"
  • Assume good intent — the engineer made the best decision with the information they had
  • Focus on system failures, not human errors
  • Celebrate finding and fixing — every incident makes the system stronger
  • Psychological safety → engineers proactively report near-misses
❌ Blame Culture
  • "Who pushed the bad code?" — witch hunt mentality
  • Engineers hide mistakes to avoid punishment
  • Same incidents repeat because root causes (process gaps) are never addressed
  • Fear of on-call → burnout → attrition
  • Post-mortems become "cover your ass" exercises
📋 Post-Mortem Template — Standardize Your Incident Review
📝
Section 1: What Happened?
📛 Title

e.g., "/jobs/ 500 errors — 45 min outage"

📅 Date/Time

Start + end (UTC). Duration.

📊 Impact

Users, revenue, SLAs breached.

🔔 Detection

Alarm? User report? On-call?

🔍
Section 2: Root Cause & Timeline
⏱️ Timeline

Minute-by-minute reconstruction in UTC. Include all key events.

❓ 5 Whys

Full analysis from symptom → systemic root cause.

➕ Contributing

Missing monitoring? Manual process? Insufficient testing?

✅ Went Well

Auto-remediation worked? Fast team response?

🎯
Section 3: Action Items
🛡️ Prevent

Automate the database migration pipeline — no more manual DBA steps

🔍 Detect

Add CloudWatch Alarm on query duration > 1 second

⚡ Mitigate

Add circuit breaker for DB timeouts — fail fast, don't cascade

🔴 Each item MUST have: Description + Owner + Due Date. No "eventually."

🔄
Section 4: Lessons Learned
😲 Surprised Us

What did we NOT expect? What assumption was wrong?

🍀 Got Lucky

What could have been MUCH worse? Where did we dodge a bullet?

🔄 Patterns

3rd DB outage this quarter? Is there a systemic issue?

📈 Change

Process, tooling, or architecture changes. Share org-wide.

35.3 Incident Timeline Reconstruction — AWS Toolchain for RCA

When an incident strikes, you need to reconstruct exactly what happened — and AWS provides the forensic toolchain:

📜
CloudTrail — "Who Did What?"

Records EVERY API call in your AWS account. RCA question: "Was a security group rule changed 5 minutes before the outage?" → Filter CloudTrail by time + resource. Key fields: eventTime, userIdentity, sourceIP, requestParameters. Integrates with EventBridge for real-time alerting on sensitive API calls.

📋
CloudWatch Logs Insights — "What Happened?"

Query logs across ALL your services with SQL-like syntax. RCA question: "What errors occurred in the 2 minutes before the crash?" → Query: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 100. Time-range picker: zoom to incident window. Save queries for runbooks.

🔗
X-Ray — "Which Service Failed?"

Traces show the full request path across microservices. RCA question: "Why is the API slow?" → Open Service Map → find slowest edge → click Trace View → see that PostgreSQL subsegment took 30 seconds. Pinpoint: the database, not the application code. Share trace URL in the incident channel.

🕵️ EXAMPLE: anihpj Outage — Step-by-Step RCA with AWS Tools
1
CloudWatch Alarm Fires

Alarm: "HTTP 500 error rate > 5% for 2 minutes on anihpj ALB." SNS → PagerDuty → on-call engineer paged at 2:15 PM.

2
X-Ray Service Map

Engineer opens ServiceLens → anihpj-api node is red. Click → traces show ALL requests failing at PostgreSQL with timeout after 30s.

3
CloudWatch Logs Insights

Query anihpj-api logs: filter @message like /Database.*timeout/ → 500+ timeouts in last 5 minutes. All queries are SELECT * FROM jobpost WHERE skills LIKE '%python%' — full table scan.

4
CloudTrail Investigation

Check who deployed last: LookupEvents for UpdateService on ECS/EKS → CI/CD pipeline deployed v2.4.1 at 2:00 PM. Deployed code included new search feature using unindexed skills column.

5
RCA Conclusion

Root cause: missing database index. Immediate fix: create index → query time drops from 30s to 12ms. Long-term: automate DB migrations in CI/CD. Add CloudWatch alarm on query duration > 1s.

35.4 Action Items & Runbooks — From Incident to Improvement

The true value of RCA is the action items that prevent recurrence. Every incident should produce concrete, trackable improvements:

🎯
SMART Action Items
Specific"Add index on jobpost.skills" — not "fix database"
Measurable"Query time reduced to <50ms"
AssignableOne owner — @anihpj-dba
RealisticCan be done in 1 sprint
Time-boundDue by next Friday
📊
Track Completion
✅Create GitHub issues / Jira tickets for each item
📋Track in the post-mortem document
🔄Review at weekly ops meetings
🔴Rule:No incident is "closed" until ALL items are DONE
📖 Runbook Development — From Tribal Knowledge to Executable Code

Runbooks transform tribal knowledge ("ask Bob, he fixed this last time") into executable procedures. For every alert your system generates, there should be a runbook:

Runbook: Database Performance Degradation
Alert: RDS CPUUtilization > 80% for 5 minutes OR QueryDuration > 1s

Step 1: CHECK current connections
  aws rds describe-db-instances | grep DatabaseConnections

Step 2: IDENTIFY slow queries
  SELECT pid, now() - pg_stat_activity.query_start AS duration, query
  FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';

Step 3: KILL long-running queries if needed
  SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid);

Step 4: CHECK if recent deployment caused regression
  Review CloudTrail for UpdateService API calls

Step 5: SCALE UP if needed (temporary)
  aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-class db.r6g.2xlarge

Step 6: CREATE post-incident ticket → DBA team
  "Investigate + add missing indexes"
🔄 Continuous Improvement — The Feedback Loop
🚨 Incident → 📋 Post-Mortem → 🎯 Action Items → 🤖 Automation → 🛡️ Prevention

Each cycle: system becomes more resilient. Incidents that can't happen → never happen again.

📊 SLO, SLI, SLA — Measuring Reliability for Post-Mortems

Post-mortems are meaningless without measurement. SLOs define what "good enough" looks like, and every incident is measured against them:

📏
SLI — Service Level Indicator

The actual metric you measure. Examples: Request latency (p99 < 200ms), error rate (< 0.1%), availability (99.9% uptime), throughput (1000 req/sec). For anihpj: SLI = p95 latency of /jobs/ endpoint. If p95 > 200ms → SLI is violated. Measure SLI over a rolling window (28 days typical).

🎯
SLO — Service Level Objective

The target for your SLI. Example: "99.9% of requests complete in < 200ms over 28 days." This means you can have 0.1% of requests SLOWER than 200ms — that's your error budget. Error budget consumed: 0.1% of 1M requests = 1,000 slow requests allowed per month. When budget hits zero → freeze new features, focus on reliability.

📜
SLA — Service Level Agreement

The contract with your customers. Example: "99.5% uptime per month, or 10% credit." SLA is looser than SLO — you set SLO tighter to catch issues BEFORE they breach the SLA. Violation: refunds, credits, reputation damage. For anihpj: SLO = 99.9%, SLA = 99.5% — gives 0.4% buffer before penalties.

🔍 DEEP DIVE: CloudWatch Contributor Insights — Find the Needle

When an incident affects thousands of users, you need to know which users are impacted, not just that there's a problem. Contributor Insights analyzes CloudWatch Logs and identifies the top-N contributors to any pattern:

Contributor Insights Rule — Top Users Getting 500 Errors
{
  "Schema": { "Name": "anihpj-500-errors-by-user" },
  "LogGroupNames": ["/aws/eks/anihpj-cluster/containers"],
  "LogFormat": "JSON",
  "Fields": ["$.userId"],
  "Contribution": {
    "Keys": ["$.userId"],
    "Filters": [
      { "Match": "$.statusCode", "EqualTo": 500 }
    ]
  }
}
// Result: "User #4892: 1,247 errors, User #1201: 893 errors..."
// Now you know exactly who is affected — not just that errors exist.

💡 In a post-mortem: Contributor Insights tells you whether the incident affected ALL users (platform-wide outage) or specific cohorts (e.g., only users on mobile, only users in eu-west-1, only users with large datasets). This shapes your RCA direction.

Chapter 36: AWS Cost Management Fundamentals

Cost optimization isn't an afterthought — it's a continuous discipline. This chapter covers the four pillars of AWS cost management: understanding pricing models, visualizing spending with Cost Explorer, setting guardrails with Budgets, and driving accountability with cost allocation tags. Every dollar saved is a dollar that can fund more innovation.

36.1 AWS Pricing Models — Pay for What You Use (or Less)

AWS offers four pricing models, each trading flexibility for discount. The DevOps engineer's job is to match the right model to each workload:

⚡
On-Demand — Maximum Flexibility
No Commitment0% Discount

Pay per second (60s minimum). No upfront payment. Scale up or down instantly. Best for: unpredictable workloads, short-term projects, dev/test environments. Baseline price: this is what all discounts are calculated from.

📋
Reserved Instances — 1-3 Year Commitment
Up to 72% Off1-3yr Lock-in

Reserve specific instance type in a specific AZ. Payment: All Upfront (max discount), Partial, or No Upfront. Convertible RI: change instance family (54% discount). Standard RI: locked to family (72% discount). Scheduled RI: reserve for specific time windows (e.g., 9-5 weekdays — great for batch jobs). Marketplace: sell unused Standard RIs.

💎
Savings Plans — Flexible Commitment
Up to 72% OffFlexible

Commit to $/hour spend for 1-3 years. Compute SP: applies to EC2, Lambda, Fargate — any region, any family. EC2 Instance SP: locked to region + family (higher discount). Key advantage: automatically applies to any matching usage — no need to pre-select instances.

🎰
Spot Instances — Up to 90% Off
90% Off2-min Notice

Bid on spare EC2 capacity. AWS can reclaim with 2-minute warning. Best for: stateless workloads, batch jobs, CI/CD runners, fault-tolerant apps. Never use for: databases, stateful services. With EKS: mix Spot + On-Demand node groups for baseline + burst.

🔄
Reserved Instance Marketplace

Sell unused Standard RIs on the AWS marketplace. Buy short-term RIs from other sellers (discount varies). Seller: recoup costs from RIs you no longer need. Buyer: get RI pricing without 1-3 year commitment. Caveat: Convertible RIs cannot be sold on marketplace. Standard RIs only, US bank account required for sellers.

⚖️
Compute SP vs EC2 Instance SP

Compute SP: Applies to EC2 (any family/region), Lambda, Fargate. Up to 66% discount. Maximum flexibility — ideal for evolving architectures. EC2 Instance SP: Locked to instance family + region. Up to 72% discount. Higher savings but less flexible. Rule: Start with Compute SP for baseline, add EC2 Instance SP when confident about specific instance needs.

🧠 How Savings Plans Billing Actually Works
1️⃣
Commitment Applied Hourly

Your $1.00/hour SP commitment is applied against eligible usage every hour. If you only use $0.80 of compute that hour, the remaining $0.20 rolls forward within the same hour-family-region (EC2 Instance SP) or across all instance families (Compute SP).

Commit $1.00/hr → Used $0.80 → $0.20 rolls forward
2️⃣
Discount Application Order
1st
Reserved Instances
Most specific — AZ+instance → 2nd
Savings Plans
Covers what RIs don't → 3rd
On-Demand
Whatever remains
3️⃣
Example: anihpj Bill at 3 AM
5× t3.large running: 2×RI + 2×SP + 1×On-Demand

🎯 Optimal stack: RI (base) + SP (mid) + On-Demand (peak). Total discount: ~50% vs all On-Demand.

📊 Pricing Model Comparison — Choose the Right Mix
ModelDiscountCommitmentFlexibilityBest For anihpj
On-Demand0%NoneMaximumDev/staging, spikes
Savings PlansUp to 72%1-3 yearsHighProduction baseline
Reserved InstanceUp to 72%1-3 yearsLowRDS, ElastiCache
SpotUp to 90%NoneCan be reclaimedCI/CD, batch, burst

36.2 Cost Explorer & Budgets — See It, Control It

Cost Explorer visualizes your spending patterns. Budgets set guardrails. Together, they form the observe-and-control loop:

📊 Cost Explorer
📈Granularity: Hourly, daily, monthly. 12-month historical + 12-month forecast.
🔍Filters: Service, Region, Tag, Linked Account, Usage Type.
💡Recommendations: Rightsizing (underutilized EC2), Savings Plans suggestions.
📊Reports: Daily or monthly .csv to S3 for custom analysis.
💰 AWS Budgets
💸Cost Budget: Alert when spend exceeds $X/month. For anihpj: $500/mo dev, $2,000/mo prod.
📊Usage Budget: Alert when usage exceeds threshold (e.g., EC2 hours > 5,000).
📋RI/SP Budget: Alert when coverage drops below target (e.g., < 80% covered).
⚡Actions: Auto-apply IAM policy, SCP, or STOP EC2/RDS when budget exceeded.
🔔
Budget Alert Flow
Budget (e.g. $500/mo) → 85% threshold → SNS → Slack/Email

Set at 50%, 85%, and 100% thresholds. SNS → Lambda possible: auto-stop dev instances when 100% hit. Chatbot integration: alerts in Slack #anihpj-finops.

📋
Cost & Usage Report (CUR)

The most detailed billing data — published to S3 as .csv daily. Contains: resource-level pricing, tags, usage hours, amortized RI/SP costs. Use with: Athena (SQL queries on billing data), QuickSight (visual dashboards), third-party tools (CloudHealth). Frequency: daily update with 24-hour lag.

⚡ Budget Actions — Auto-Stop Resources When Budget Exceeded

Budget Actions go beyond alerts — they actively stop spending when budgets are breached. Three action types, from least to most powerful:

🔐
IAM Policy Action — Least Powerful, Most Targeted
📋 How It Works

Attaches an IAM policy denying specific API calls (e.g., Deny ec2:RunInstances) to users/roles in the account.

🎯 Best For

Dev accounts with spending caps. Blocks NEW resource creation but existing resources keep running.

Budget 100% → IAM Policy Attached → No new EC2/RDS
🏛️
SCP Action — Organization-Wide Enforcement
📋 How It Works

Applies Service Control Policy at the OU level. Overrides IAM — even if IAM allows ec2:*, the SCP can deny it.

🎯 Best For

Production guardrails, compliance. Prevents resource creation org-wide — no account can bypass.

Budget breach → SCP Applied to OU → Org-wide freeze
🛑
Target Resource Stop — Immediate Cost Halt
📋 How It Works

Stops specific EC2 or RDS instances you designate. Running resources are stopped — immediate cost halt. Can be restarted later.

🎯 Best For

Dev/staging instances that should not exceed daily budget. ⚠️ Stopped, not terminated — can be restarted.

Budget > daily limit → EC2/RDS STOPPED → Spending halts immediately

36.3 Trusted Advisor — Your Free AWS Consultant

Trusted Advisor scans your AWS account for 7 categories of optimization opportunities. Many checks are free — use them before spending a dime on optimization tools:

💰
Cost Optimization

Idle resources: unattached EBS volumes, idle RDS, underutilized EC2, idle load balancers, unassociated Elastic IPs. Savings: typically 10-20% of your bill. For anihpj: flagged 3 unattached EBS volumes ($18/mo savings).

⚡
Performance

High-utilization EC2, EBS throughput optimization, CloudFront header forwarding. Check: are any instances consistently > 90% CPU? Upgrade recommended. anihpj: t3.large at 92% CPU → upgrade to t3.xlarge.

🔒
Security

S3 bucket public access, IAM root MFA, security group unrestricted ports (0.0.0.0/0 for 22/3389), CloudTrail enabled, RDS public snapshots. All FREE. anihpj: found S3 bucket with public write access — CRITICAL fix.

CategoryFree (Basic)Paid (Business+)

PerformanceLimitedAll checks
SecurityAll checksAll checks
Fault ToleranceLimitedAll checks
Service LimitsLimitedAll checks

36.4 Compute Optimizer — Right-Sizing Recommendation Engine

Compute Optimizer uses ML to analyze your EC2, ASG, Lambda, and EBS configurations. It identifies over-provisioned (wasting money) and under-provisioned (risking performance) resources:

📉 Over-Provisioned → Downsize
🖥️EC2 instance at 15% avg CPU → downgrade from xlarge to large
⚡Lambda with 3GB memory, using only 512MB → reduce to 1GB
💾EBS gp2 at 200 IOPS using only 50 — switch to gp3

💡 Savings: 30-50% on affected resources

📈 Under-Provisioned → Upgrade
🖥️EC2 at 92% CPU + memory pressure → upgrade instance
⚡Lambda timing out at 3s → increase memory (= more CPU)
💾EBS volume burst credits exhausted → provisioned IOPS

⚡ Risk: degraded performance, timeouts, user-facing errors

📊 Cost Explorer Group By — Find Your Top Spenders

Cost Explorer's Group By dimension is the most powerful cost investigation tool:

🔍
5 Essential Dimensions to Group By
🖥️ Service

Which service costs most? EC2 is typically #1, then RDS, then data transfer.

🌍 Region

Is us-east-1 cheaper? Compare costs across regions to optimize placement.

👤 Account

Which linked account spends most? Shows per-team breakdown.

🏷️ Tag

Group by Environment=prod vs dev. Instantly see production vs non-prod spend.

📊 Usage Type

BoxUsage vs DataTransfer. Break down EC2 further — compute vs networking costs.

📈
Forecast Methodology — How It Predicts Your Bill
🧮 Linear Regression Model

Cost Explorer analyzes your last 30 days of actual spend and projects forward 12 months. More history = better accuracy. Seasonal patterns are detected automatically.

⚠️ Limitations

New services launched within 7 days are NOT captured. Sudden architectural changes (e.g., migrating to Graviton) won't reflect until 7+ days of data accumulate.

💡 Pro Tip

Compare "Actual vs Forecast" monthly. A deviation > 15% signals: unplanned spend, new services, or a forecast that needs recalibration.

Chapter 37: EKS Cost Optimization

EKS costs break down into compute (~70%), storage (~15%), networking (~10%), and control plane (~5%). Mastering EKS cost optimization means knowing exactly where each dollar goes and applying the right strategy for each layer. This chapter covers the practical techniques to cut your EKS bill by 40-60%.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Domain 3: Resiliency 15% 📝 10 Questions

37.1 EKS Pricing Breakdown — Where Your Money Goes

A typical production EKS cluster's cost structure for anihpj:

💰 TYPICAL EKS CLUSTER COST BREAKDOWN (anihpj Production)
☸️ Control Plane — 5% ($72/mo)
$0.10/hr flat rate per cluster. Managed by AWS — no cost tuning possible. Includes etcd, API server, scheduler.
💻 Compute — 70% ($220-$300/mo)
3× t3.large On-Demand ($182) + 2× Spot ($36). Biggest lever for savings. Apply Savings Plans + Spot mix.
💾 Storage — 15% ($22/mo)
EBS gp3 (50GB × 3 nodes: $12) + EFS (20GB: $6) + S3 ($4). Use gp3 over gp2 for 20% savings.
🌐 Networking — 10% ($58/mo)
NAT Gateway ($33) + ALB ($16) + Data Transfer ($9). Biggest trap: NAT GW costs are per-AZ. Use VPC Endpoints for S3.
🎯 Total Baseline: ~$370/mo | Optimized (Spot + SP): ~$220/mo | Savings: 40%

37.2 Spot Instances for EKS — 60-90% Savings on Compute

Spot instances are spare EC2 capacity sold at steep discounts. They're perfect for EKS stateless workloads — with proper handling of the 2-minute interruption warning:

✅ Spot Best Practices for EKS
✅Mix Spot + On-Demand node groups (70/30 split)
✅Use multiple instance types (t3 + t3a + m5) for availability
✅Deploy AWS Node Termination Handler as DaemonSet
✅Stateless Pods only — use PodDisruptionBudget for safety
⚡ Spot Interruption Handling
Spot gets 2-minute warning before termination. AWS Node Termination Handler (open-source) watches for the warning → cordons the node → drains Pods gracefully. EventBridge rule captures the warning → Lambda can also trigger automated failover. Critical: ensure PDBs are set so at least 1 Pod stays available during drain.
🦾
Graviton (ARM) Instances — 20% Cheaper + 20% Faster

AWS Graviton processors (ARM-based) offer 20% lower cost and 20% better performance vs comparable x86 instances. EKS support: Use t4g/m6g/c7g instance types. Requirement: multi-arch container images (docker buildx --platform linux/arm64,linux/amd64). Most interpreted languages (Python, Node.js, Go) work out of the box. For anihpj: Django app runs on ARM with zero code changes — just rebuild the image.

🚀
Karpenter — Intelligent Node Autoscaling

Karpenter is a next-gen K8s autoscaler that provisions the right instance type for each Pod — not just adds nodes to a fixed group. vs Cluster Autoscaler: Karpenter selects optimal instance type/size in real-time, handles Spot interruption gracefully, removes underutilized nodes faster. For anihpj: Karpenter provisions t3.large for API Pods, t3.medium for worker Pods — no wasted capacity.

37.3 Fargate vs EC2 Cost Analysis

Fargate charges per vCPU-hour + GB-hour for Pods — no node management. EC2 charges per instance-hour. The right choice depends on your workload pattern:

ScenarioFargateEC2Recommendation
Steady 24/7 workloadHigherLowerEC2 + Savings Plans
Bursty/spiky workloadLowerHigherFargate
Batch jobs (nightly)LowerLowerEC2 Spot (cheapest)
Variable microservicesDependsDependsRun Kubecost analysis
🧮 Fargate Pricing Calculation — Worked Example

Fargate charges per vCPU-second and GB-second that your Pod requests — NOT what it actually uses:

Pod: anihpj-worker | Requests: 1 vCPU, 2 GB memory | Runtime: 12 hours/day
vCPU cost: 1 × $0.04048/hr × 12h = $0.49/day
Memory cost: 2 × $0.004445/hr × 12h = $0.11/day
Total: $0.60/day × 30 days = $18/month per Pod
If Pod actually uses only 0.3 CPU → you still pay for the 1 CPU requested!

⚠️ Key insight: Fargate charges by REQUEST, not USAGE. This is why right-sizing is MORE critical on Fargate than EC2.

37.4 Right-Sizing Pods — Stop Over-Provisioning

The #1 EKS cost mistake: requesting far more CPU/memory than Pods actually use. Kubecost and Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) are your tools:

📊
Kubecost — Know Your Costs
📈Cost by Namespace • Deployment • Pod • Label
😴Idle costs: CPU/memory requested but UNUSED
📊Efficiency %: actual usage ÷ requested resources
🐳 anihpj: jobpost-worker requests 1 CPU, uses 0.3 CPU — 70% over-provisioned. Reduce to 0.5 CPU request → save 50% on compute.
⚡
VPA + HPA — The Right-Sizing Duo
📐 VPA (Vertical)

Recommends optimal CPU/memory per Pod. Off mode: recommendation only (safe for prod). Auto mode: updates Pods automatically (restarts required).

↔️ HPA (Horizontal)

Scales Pod count by CPU/memory/custom metrics. Works with VPA: VPA sets the right SIZE, HPA sets the right COUNT.

🌐 Network Cost Optimization — Cut Your Data Transfer Bill
🔌
VPC Endpoints — Keep Traffic in AWS
🚪 Gateway Endpoint

Free for S3 + DynamoDB. Traffic stays on AWS backbone. Zero NAT Gateway charges.

🔌 Interface Endpoint

$0.01/hr for all other services (ECR, SNS, SQS, etc.). Private IP in your VPC.

💡 Savings

EKS Pods pulling ECR images via NAT GW? Switch to Interface Endpoint → save $30-50/mo.

🌍
CloudFront Caching — Reduce Origin Traffic
User → CloudFront → ALB→EKS

Cache /jobs/ listing (TTL: 60s) + static assets (TTL: 1d). Result: 70% fewer origin requests.

📡
Inter-AZ Traffic — The Hidden Cost
⚠️ $0.01/GB Cross-AZ

Pods communicating across AZs generate data transfer charges. Adds up silently each month.

✅ Fix: Pod Anti-Affinity

podAntiAffinity: preferredDuringScheduling keeps related Pods in the same AZ. 10-15% savings.

🔗
PrivateLink — Cross-Account Without NAT
VPC A → PrivateLink → VPC B

No NAT GW, no IGW, no VPC peering. $0.01/hr + $0.01/GB. Everything on AWS backbone.

Chapter 38: FinOps — Financial Operations in the Cloud

FinOps brings finance, engineering, and business together to drive cloud cost accountability. It's not just about cutting costs — it's about understanding unit economics: what does each job posting, each API call, each user session actually cost? This chapter covers the FinOps framework, showback/chargeback models, and how to build a cost-conscious engineering culture.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 Cross-Domain: Cost Awareness 📝 10 Questions

38.1 FinOps Framework Overview — Inform → Optimize → Operate

The FinOps Foundation defines an iterative lifecycle. You don't "do FinOps once" — it's a continuous cycle:

📊 Inform → ⚡ Optimize → 🔄 Operate
📊
Inform — Visibility
🏷️ Define allocation tags for teams/services
📊 Build dashboards (Cost Explorer, Kubecost, QuickSight)
💰 Set budgets with alerts at multiple thresholds

🎯 Outcome: Every team knows their cloud spend. No more "the bill just arrived" surprises.

⚡
Optimize — Take Action
📐 Rightsizing: VPA recommendations, Compute Optimizer
📋 Commitments: Savings Plans + Reserved Instances
🗑️ Delete idle: unattached EBS, old snapshots, ECR images
🎰 Spot adoption: stateless workloads on Spot instances

🎯 Outcome: Reduce waste without impacting performance. Target: 30-40% savings in first cycle.

🔄
Operate — Sustain
📈 Continuous monitoring with anomaly detection
🛑 Budget automation: auto-stop dev instances
🏛️ Governance: SCPs + Config Rules for tag enforcement
🔄 Regular FinOps reviews: weekly ops sync

🎯 Outcome: Cost optimization becomes habit. FinOps embedded in engineering culture.

👥
The 4 FinOps Personas
👨‍💻
Engineering
Build efficient, tag resources, right-size Pods
💰
Finance
Set budgets, forecast, track commitments
📊
Business
Unit economics, feature investment decisions
🏢
Executive
Champion culture, approve commitments

🔴 Rule: FinOps fails if only finance cares — engineering MUST be invested.

📐
The 6 FinOps Principles
1. Teams collaborate across finance, engineering, and business
2. Decisions driven by business value of cloud
3. Everyone takes ownership of their cloud usage
4. FinOps data is accessible and timely
5. Centralized team drives FinOps across the org
6. Variable cloud model embraced — not treated like fixed data center cost

💡 Core idea: Cloud cost is a shared responsibility — not just "the finance team's problem."

💰 Understanding Cost Types — Amortized vs Unblended vs Blended

When looking at your AWS bill, which cost metric you use dramatically changes what you see:

📊
Unblended Costs

The raw amount you're charged for each resource at its actual rate. Example: 2× t3.large: one On-Demand ($0.0832/hr), one covered by SP ($0.058/hr). Unblended shows these at their actual different rates. Best for: day-to-day operations, seeing the real-time impact of optimization decisions.

📈
Amortized Costs

Upfront RI/SP payments spread evenly across the commitment period. Example: $1,200 All-Upfront RI for 1 year = $100/month amortized, even though you paid $1,200 in January. Best for: accurate monthly cost allocation, FinOps showback/chargeback, comparing total cost of ownership across architectures.

🔄
Blended Costs

Average of On-Demand and discounted rates across linked accounts (Consolidated Billing). Example: Account A uses On-Demand, Account B uses SP — blended rate averages both. Best for: high-level trending across organization. Caveat: masks individual account optimization opportunities.

💡 For anihpj: Use amortized costs for showback reports (fair allocation of RI/SP benefits). Use unblended for daily cost monitoring (catch anomalies fast).

38.2 Inform → Optimize → Operate — Applied to anihpj

Let's walk the FinOps lifecycle for the anihpj job board:

📊 Inform — What Does anihpj Cost?
Tags: Environment=prod, Team=backend, App=anihpj, CostCenter=engineering
Unit Cost: $0.03/job posting, $0.0005/API call, $0.12/user session
⚡ Optimize — Where Can We Save?
Spot: jobpost-worker on Spot (save 70%)
SP: Savings Plans for baseline ($0.058/hr)

🔄 Operate — Sustain the Gains

38.3 Chargeback & Showback Models

How do you make teams care about costs? You show them — or charge them:

📊 Showback — Visibility Only

Teams see their costs in dashboards but aren't billed. Psychology: "Our costs are visible, let's optimize." How: Kubecost per-namespace dashboards, Cost Explorer filtered by team tag. Best for: early FinOps adoption, building cost awareness without fear.

✅ Teams respond to visibility. No organizational friction. Start here.
💰 Chargeback — Teams Pay Their Bill

Each team's costs are deducted from their budget. Psychology: "This is MY money, I'll optimize aggressively." How: Cost Allocation Tags → CUR → calculate per-team spend → deduct from team budget. Best for: mature FinOps, large organizations with independent team budgets.

⚡ Powerful but needs organizational buy-in. Start with showback first.

38.4 Cost Allocation Tags — The Foundation of FinOps

Without tags, you know how much you spent — but not who spent it. Tags are the DNA of cloud cost accountability:

🏷️
Tag Strategy for anihpj
Environmentprod | staging | dev
Teambackend | frontend | data
Applicationanihpj | anihpj-worker
CostCenterengineering | marketing
🔐
Tag Enforcement
✅ SCP: deny resource creation without required tags
✅ AWS Config: required-tags managed rule
✅ IaC: Terraform/CloudFormation enforce tags in templates
⚠️ Activate tags in Billing Console (24-48h to appear in CUR)
🔍 Anomaly Detection & Third-Party FinOps Tools
📈 AWS Cost Anomaly Detection

AWS's built-in ML service monitors spending patterns and alerts on unusual spikes. How: Define monitors with cost impact threshold (e.g., alert on +$100/day deviation). Subscriptions: per-service (EC2 only) or account-wide. For anihpj: "Alert when daily EKS cost deviates > 20% from baseline" — catch runaway scaling or cryptomining early.

✅ Free service. Set up in Cost Management console. Integrates with SNS for Slack alerts.
🛠️ Third-Party FinOps Tools

CloudHealth (VMware): Multi-cloud cost management, rightsizing, governance. Enterprise-grade. CloudCheckr: Cost + security + compliance in one platform. Apptio Cloudability: Financial-grade cloud cost analytics. Open-source: Kubecost (K8s), OpenCost (CNCF sandbox). For anihpj: Kubecost for EKS visibility + AWS Budgets for guardrails. Add CloudHealth at enterprise scale.
